posts.title: Things I did right (and wrong) making this site in 2019
posts.excerpt: I made this Vue.js view of a headless WordPress backend in 2019. 6 years later, what would I do differently? ## What I did right First, let me say a few things that I am still happy with: 1. The minimalistic style still works. If my brand i
posts.content:
I made this Vue.js view of a headless WordPress backend in 2019. 6 years later, what would I do differently?

What I did right

First, let me say a few things that I am still happy with:

  1. The minimalistic style still works. If my brand is being a developer, I don't need flashy style. But I think the simplicity is clean and understated and does the content a favor. I stand behind it 6 years later, which in the world of design isn't half bad.
  2. The use of Vue as a PWA (progressive web app) on top of a WP backend still seems to me a solid choice. For a 1-person site, I don't need to waste time recreating the wheel. Vue is so light that this feels like a great use for it.
  3. The emphasis on content and the simple pages about who I am still serve the needs of the site well.
  4. The AWS deployment is right-sized for the site. It uses the services well without overkill, and has been faithfully chugging along with about a $6 a month expenditure for 6 years.
  5. The layout is appropriately responsive for multiple viewports and devices.

What I didn't do right

The PWA portion took up a lot of time. It was a fun experiment for me, but is definitely overkill for this site, except as a proof of ability. However, there's a few parts I didn't get right.

  1. The page numbering is 0-indexed, which isn't appropriate for user facing content. I'd never let that pass a merge request today and am surprised I didn't catch it in 2019.
    1. This is pretty easy to fix. It's just getting the code and offsets right. A key here was creating a getter in the store to isolate the logic for loading posts.
  2. The scroll position of posts does not reset when navigating through them. It's all the same page with different content, but that doesn't matter to the user. It should scroll up on a new article rendering.
    1. Super easy. A simple JS call to scroll to position 0 whenever the page content changes.
  3. The caching of the site content is overaggressive. If you load the list of posts, and a new one is added, you don't see it even after a hard refresh.
    1. I really thought this was the service worker configuration, since it is designed to serve content from a local cache. As it turns out, it was the actual browser cache. The WordPress API defaulted to a max-age of a day, so changing that to not allow caching fixed it right up!
  4. The header meta tags are not updating appropriately for each article. If you link directly to one, it should pull the title and description and image from that post in particular, not the site as a whole.
    1. This should be easier than it is. Because crawlers don't run (much) JavaScript, the meta has to be on the page when it's first loaded. An appropriate approach is server-side rendering, or pre-rendering. A simple workaround for a site from 2019 that I don't want to spend much time with is to add a few lines of PHP into the index file that directly queries the WordPress API for the title, description, and image of the slug in the URL.
  5. I wouldn't design the custom API endpoint the same way today. I created a summary endpoint that returned meta for all the posts, which I found helpful in designing the local storage of the service worker. It was a way around the limitation that the service worker is just caching all requests that it sees, so it will only cache specific queries. However, this isn't the most scalable solution and the real issue is that using an off-the-shelf service worker is just never going to do everything I'd want it to.

Service worker limitations

Let's break that last point down a bit. Here is a physical architecture diagram of viewing a page of results in the archive, as it exists today:

Each HTTP request is brokered through the service worker, which allows it to cache responses and, when necessary, serve the content locally. But it has no awareness of the shape of the data or how requests relate to each other. It's elegant in one sense and dumb in another.

This means that it will cache the response for posts?page=1 and posts?page=2 and posts?page=1&search=javascript separately. There's nothing wrong with this when caching for performance, but when caching for availability (i.e. offline access) it doesn't do much for the user.

If we really wanted to allow a good offline experience that included fetching results, I think we'd want to bring some of the searching logic down into the service worker (or application) layer.

Duplicated state

And while we have this nice architecture diagram, let me point out that there is a duplication of state. In fact, the state of posts exists in 3 places: in the WordPress backend, in the service worker cache, and in the Vuex state store (which uses rxjs). If we brought some of the data logic into the service worker, I'd also want to get rid of the Vue store. It'd be a simpler design with less potential for consistency issues and bugs in general.

Updated site

If you view the site now, you shouldn't actually see these issues. :)

posts.title: Modeling FlightGear: Predicting a Stalled Descent
posts.excerpt: As part of a my job interview last year with GTRI, I was required to create a tech talk presentation. I developed a short proof of concept project that combines flight simulation, data collection, and machine learning to predict a stalled d
posts.content:
As part of a my job interview last year with GTRI, I was required to create a tech talk presentation. I developed a short proof of concept project that combines flight simulation, data collection, and machine learning to predict a stalled descent using FlightGear. In this post, I’ll follow the basic layout of the presentation I gave that walks through the project, so...this may be a bit PowerPoint-y.

1. FlightGear Intro & Data Collection

FlightGear is a powerful open-source flight simulator built for a wide range of users””researchers, educators, engineers, hobbyists, and anyone interested in flight dynamics. What makes it particularly valuable for data-driven work is its flexibility and support for real-time telemetry logging.

For this project, I used:

  • FlightGear version 2020.3.19
  • Flight dynamics model: JSBSim
  • Aircraft: Beechcraft 1900D (a 19-passenger twin-engine turboprop)
  • Starting point: Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport (CVG)

FlightGear allows users to define a configuration XML file at launch to control what telemetry is collected, the logging frequency, and the output format. I configured the simulator to log key flight parameters””including latitude, longitude, altitude, roll, pitch, heading, and airspeed””at a 10ms interval.

These logs are part of FlightGear’s internal property tree and can be streamed to a CSV file. This data formed the basis for the analysis and modeling work that followed.

2. Visualizing the Flight Path

Once the data was collected, the next step was to load it into a Python environment for inspection and visualization. I used a Jupyter notebook (running locally or in Google Colab) and processed the telemetry using Pandas.

In the 3d plot below you are seeing the actual path of the plane in 3d real space. Note that the altitude - Z - is scaled differently from the X and Y. Planes fly relatively close to the earth. This is an embarrassingly awful flight that in no way correlates to a real one -- it was intentionally chaotic and designed to contain multiple stalls.

For visualizing flight paths and behavior over time, Plotly provided a convenient way to build interactive charts that made patterns””such as altitude changes and trajectory deviations””easy to interpret.

This initial visual inspection helped verify data quality, assess the completeness of each flight log, and establish a sense of how stall events appear in the raw data. It also provided early hints at irregularities in the logging interval, which became a key issue later.

3. Data Preprocessing

Although I specified a 10ms logging interval, the actual output was far from consistent. For example, in a test flight from CVG to Dayton (DAY), the latency varied significantly:

  • Minimum: 0.0s
  • Maximum: 0.81s
  • Mean: ~0.0099s
  • Standard deviation: ~0.0121s

This kind of irregularity matters because many machine learning models””including recurrent neural networks (RNNs)””assume uniform time steps. Irregular intervals can lead to misalignment in temporal sequences, reduce model performance, and introduce misleading correlations.

I used several strategies to mitigate this:

A. Improve Logging Interval

Reducing the logging interval helped the simulator to sample more consistently, but with the obvious tradeoff of less data resolution.

B. Reduce Resource Demand

Running the simulator at lower resolution (e.g., 800x600), disabling visual effects, and minimizing rendering quality helped improve performance and reduce variability in logging.

C. Preprocess Data

For the logged data, I ended up using techniques like forward-filling and interpolation to standardize time intervals. These helped smooth over irregularities and maintain the temporal integrity of the data. Preprocessing data is normal, but obviously less ideal as it can bias and subtly alter the data set.

In the long term, modifying FlightGear’s source code could provide more robust telemetry handling. I dove into the source code a bit and found both an easy fix (removing "catch up" entries) and a more important long term fix (using a multithreaded logging system that separates data collection from rendering and other simulator processes).

4. Training a Stall Predictor

The core goal of this project was to predict when a flight was entering a stalled descent. A stall occurs when the aircraft’s angle of attack exceeds a critical limit, causing a loss of lift. It’s not directly tied to speed””rather, it depends on the combination of speed and the angle required to maintain lift. As the aircraft slows down, it needs a higher angle of attack, and that’s when stalls can happen.

To build a predictor, I labeled sequences of data that showed clear signs of stall behavior. The plotly graphs made these rather obvious. I then trained a recurrent model (in TensorFlow) to detect these patterns over time.

At this point I have already standardized the data, which I've described above. I also adjusted the scale a bit.

Note here that the labeling had two parts: first, the actual stall events (red), and second the time leading up to a stall (yellow). To help automatically identify the stalling events I used the delta in vertical speed. Then I label the previous seconds as pre-stall.

def label_prestall_by_vertical_speed(df):
    df = df.copy()

    # Label 'stall' events
    df['altitude_rolling_avg'] = df['altitude'].rolling(window=10).mean()
    df['vertical_speed'] = df['altitude_rolling_avg'].diff() * 100 * 60  # Change per second
    df['vertical_speed'].fillna(0, inplace=True)
    df['stall'] = df['vertical_speed'] < -4000

    # Shift upwards 15 seconds for 'prestall'
    df['prestall'] = df['stall'].shift(-1500)
    df['prestall'].fillna(False, inplace=True)
    df['prestall'] = df['prestall'] & ~df['stall']

    return df

I also needed to break the flight up into sequences:

def build_sequences(df, label_col=None):
    num_sequences = len(df) - sequence_length
    num_features = len(feature_columns)

    # Preallocate memory (standard array appending is very slow here)
    features = np.zeros((num_sequences, sequence_length, num_features), dtype=np.float32)
    labels = np.zeros(num_sequences, dtype=np.float32) if label_col else None

    for i in range(num_sequences):
        features[i] = df[feature_columns].iloc[i:i + sequence_length].values

        if label_col:
            labels[i] = df[label_col].iloc[i + sequence_length]

    return (features, labels) if label_col else features

And of course I need to actually build the model. I used TensorFlow and based on some reading I did (listed at bottom) I used LSTM - long short term memory - layers.

def build_model(X_train):
    model = Sequential()
    model.add(LSTM(25, return_sequences=True, input_shape=(X_train.shape[1], X_train.shape[2])))
    model.add(LSTM(25, return_sequences=False))
    model.add(Dense(1, activation='sigmoid'))
    model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='binary_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])
    return model

The training set was small but sufficient to demonstrate proof-of-concept performance. There are some obvious limitations which I'll cover in a bit. But after training the model on the training set and applying it to the test set, we have results. Almost surely overfit to the data here, but that's going to be hard to avoid with a small sample set.

Model: "sequential"
_________________________________________________________________
 Layer (type)                Output Shape              Param #   
=================================================================
 lstm (LSTM)                 (None, 1000, 25)          3000      
                                                                 
 lstm_1 (LSTM)               (None, 25)                5100      
                                                                 
 dense (Dense)               (None, 1)                 26        
                                                                 
=================================================================
Total params: 8126 (31.74 KB)
Trainable params: 8126 (31.74 KB)
Non-trainable params: 0 (0.00 Byte)
_________________________________________________________________

2244/2244 [==============================] - 125s 54ms/step - loss: 0.0913 - accuracy: 0.9731 - val_loss: 0.0636 - val_accuracy: 0.9825
<keras.src.callbacks.History at 0x7cf7389954b0>

I also apply the trained model to a new flight to see how it does:

Not bad! Here the trained model correctly identifies 2 pre-stall events without any pre-labelling of any kind.

5. Real-Time Integration with FlightGear

Another goal might be to integrate the stall predictor back into the simulator to support real-time alerts during flight. FlightGear’s flexible architecture makes this plausible. I created a lightweight Python script that could monitor ongoing telemetry, run inference using the trained model, and issue a warning if a stall pattern is detected.

That said, there are a few technical challenges:

  • Latency and sync: Live integration would need tight timing coordination between the simulator and the inference system.
  • Telemetry frequency: Ensuring that live data is sampled consistently (same issue as before).
  • Model optimization: The model needs to be small and fast enough to run in real time without slowing down the simulation.

This type of integration could be useful not just for training pilots but also as part of prototyping smarter flight control systems or assistive safety tools.

Here is a video of this running on a live flight. There is an obvious induced stall that is correctly predicted around 3:15.

https://youtu.be/55Ve0gVw7uk

Looking Ahead

Here are a few areas I see as important next steps:

  • Telemetry consistency: Possibly by restructuring the logging system using a multithreaded approach.
  • Flight model realism: Using more sophisticated or validated aircraft models for better data.
  • Larger, more diverse datasets: Including different aircraft, weather conditions, and flight phases. This is almost surely the biggest flaw in this proof of concept.
  • Model improvements: Exploring more advanced RNN variants (like GRUs or LSTMs) and work with ML/AI specialists.
  • Stall source variety: Looking at different types of stall. One person I showed this PoC to remarked, "I don't know that you've created a stall predictor. I think you created an intentional-stall predictor.". That's a valid point.

References

  • Introduction ”“ FlightGear Flight Simulator. https://www.flightgear.org/about/
  • TensorFlow. Time series forecasting. https://www.tensorflow.org/tutorials/structured_data/time_series
  • Weerakody, P. B., Wong, K. W., Wang, G., & Ela, W. (2021). A review of irregular time series data handling with gated recurrent neural networks. Neurocomputing, 441, 161”“178.

posts.title: Fleet-Wide Asset Tracker Status with Google Map's Advanced Markers
posts.excerpt: Asset Tracking is a shining example of the power of IoT. We can see not only where our asset is, but also what’s happening to it ”” is it stuck in a distributor yard, sitting in a hot environment, or tipped on its side? We sometimes tal
posts.content:
Asset Tracking is a shining example of the power of IoT. We can see not only where our asset is, but also what’s happening to it ”” is it stuck in a distributor yard, sitting in a hot environment, or tipped on its side?

We sometimes talk as if there’s just one asset, but almost always we have many that we’re tracking. There are insights to be gained at the fleet level, too. Is there a bottleneck in the transit line, batteries consistently left to run down, or a certain receiving warehouse that handles our crates roughly?

We can make these insights visible at a glance by showing them directly on a map.

Jump over to the Losant blog for the rest of this tutorial!

posts.title: OpenAI and the future of programming
posts.excerpt: OpenAI's ChatGPT public access demo is remarkable. In some ways the Internet's collective experience harkens back to the first days of Siri, with people sharing the impressive responses and less-than-impressive gaffes of the virtual assista
posts.content:
OpenAI's ChatGPT public access demo is remarkable.

In some ways the Internet's collective experience harkens back to the first days of Siri, with people sharing the impressive responses and less-than-impressive gaffes of the virtual assistant.

In the past few days, I've had ChatGPT explain to me why the phase of the moon appears to not always point at the sun, give me encouragement for my morning exercises as Darth Vader ("feel the dark side flow through your arms"), and construct a circle story with me about a human programmer recruited by aliens to save the Earth.

The story we constructed could be its own blog post, not least for the highly suspicious lesson the AI tried to impose on the story's end:

The grateful humans hailed Sarah as a hero, and she returned to Earth as a changed person, with a newfound sense of purpose and a deep appreciation for the power of technology and the importance of trust.

This, after I had tried to turn Sarah into something of a murdering fugitive on the alien's home-world. Okay, chatbot, we humans will just always trust technology, then.

But as a software engineer, perhaps the most intriguing capabilities revolve around ChatGPT's ability to generate code snippets, which are after all text based.

Programming with ChatGPT

Here's an example:

"Write me a c function that takes a linked list as an argument, and returns a new linked list with n randomly chosen items from the list that have been put into a new linked list. The number of items should also come from an argument. The new linked list items should have their memory allocated correctly and not be pointing to the original list's items. "

And the result:

[code language="c"]#include #include // A linked list node typedef struct Node { int data; struct Node* next; } Node; // Returns a new linked list with n randomly chosen items from the // original list. The new linked list items will have their memory // allocated correctly and will not point to the original list's items. // // The original linked list is not modified. Node* random_sublist(Node* head, int n) { // Seed the random number generator srand(time(NULL)); // Initialize the new list Node* new_head = NULL; Node* new_tail = NULL; // Iterate through the original list Node* current = head; while (current != NULL) { // Generate a random number in the range [0, 1] double r = (double)rand() / RAND_MAX; // If the random number is less than the probability of selecting // this item, add it to the new list if (r < (double)n / current_position) { // Allocate memory for the new node Node* new_node = (Node*)malloc(sizeof(Node)); if (new_node == NULL) { // Handle allocation failure // ... } // Copy the data from the original node to the new node new_node->data = current->data; new_node->next = NULL; // Add the new node to the end of the new list if (new_head == NULL) { new_head = new_node; } else { new_tail->next = new_node; } new_tail = new_node; } // Move to the next node in the original list current = current->next; } return new_head; } [/code]

This is incredibly impressive. It's clear, well-commented, and mostly correct. There are some errors, including the fact that it accidentally switches its "current" variable for a "current_position" variable, and then oddly wants to use the current position to determine the probability of an item being selected.

As it stands, this code doesn't compile. "current_position" is not defined or declared. Still, perhaps the biggest caveat is that ChatGPT is not "writing" this code. It is not thinking through the problem and the challenges. It is rather appearing to do these things by comparing my requirements to the incredibly large dataset of similar code it has seen.

That's not to diminish what it is doing, though. After all, human programmers kind of do the same thing. More experienced programmers--like more experienced chess players--rely on patterns they have seen. The YouTube channel Veritasium has a great video about this.

It does suggest that its abilities to solve new problems is more limited. Still, if it can create solutions to problems that are just new combinations of smaller, known problems, then that's not a very big limitation. An unsettling amount of computer programming is exactly this.

So it's not surprising that one colleague's candid response to ChatGPT's programming ability was, "so that's like my whole job."

But...is it?

After ChatGPT provided the code snippet above, I asked it to rewrite the function without assuming the input linked list was well-formed. It modified the output by including this check at the beginning: `

if (head == NULL || n < 1) { return NULL; }

It then confidently told me:

This function now checks whether the input linked list is NULL or has fewer than n items, and returns NULL in those cases. It also checks whether n is a valid number (i.e. it is greater than 0) and returns NULL if it is not. This should make the function more robust and prevent it from crashing on invalid input.

The problem is that it isn't doing this. It is checking if the head is NULL, and if "n" is greater than 0, but it is not checking if the length of the linked list is sufficient to generate the desired number of items. There's actually not a way to do that without being given the size of the list, or traversing the list and counting.

To its credit, when I pointed this out, it admitted the mistake.

You are correct, the previous version of the function did not return NULL if the input linked list had fewer than n items. This was an oversight on my part, and the function has been updated to return NULL in that case.

It then added a manual count of the input list prior to constructing the output list, which is as good of a solution as I could provide myself.

There's a few other quibbles I could point out. For instance, it doesn't necessarily return a linked list of size n, just "close" to n. But with some more guidance, I'm sure it would get there.

What do these limitations mean?

So, is this type of oversight a deal-breaker? Does it expose a deep flaw in ChatGPT's abilities?

I don't think so. But neither do I think it should be ignored. In fact it's a good example of the inherent limitation in this kind of system that draws so heavily on the data its been trained on to generate "new" data.

It's a bit like reading a college student's paper that sounds clear and coherent, until you realize they are just copying and pasting various sources without understanding how the different ideas fit together. Still...if that's the case, this college student is really, really skilled at putting together plagiarized materials, and it usually seems capable of synthesizing their ideas, even if it's not actually doing so.

But more importantly, we can expect this model, and the ones to come after it, to improve. We can't simply say, "Aha! here is where this experiment fails. The jobs of human programmers are safe!"

In theology, there is a concept called, "the God of the gaps", which describes how people throughout history have simply used their deity to explain what they don't understand. Over time, as science expands and those gaps shrink, the role of their god decreases. This puts them in difficult, and hard to defend, position.

But serious theologians don't depend on the God of the gaps theory, and neither should modern programmers.

I'm hesitant to take the well-trodden position, "machines will never replace humans." It's tempting, and I can feel the strong psychological currents at play pulling me towards that. But I don't want to believe it out of hope alone.

AI-Assisted Programming

There was something almost satisfying about providing code feedback to the chatbot and having it adjust in response.

In reminded me of engineers on Star Trek collaboratively working with their computers. In one scene from The Next Generation, crew members who have been abducted and had their memories altered try to reconstruct the scene in the holodeck. They prompt the computer, it responds, they adjust the output, and repeat. Their AI abstracts the grunt work of describing what a table is, and lets them instead focus on what that table looked like.

It's a collaboration. The computer is, like ChatGPT, presumably pulling from its impressive database and running complicated algorithms to generate the output. The crew members direct, steer, and control that output towards their purposes.

A novice at programming might accept ChatGPT's initial code as complete and sufficient. But it takes actual understanding to look at the code, evaluate its strengths and weaknesses, and find where refinements are needed. (Or, depending on the context, where the refinements are not needed.)

What's more, real software is not just a bunch of code and algorithms placed side-by-side. Software architecture and system design are just as important and arguable more complicated. It takes a knowledgeable guiding hand to make it all make sense. After all, being a software engineer isn't just being a software mechanic.

(Incidentally, this LinkedIn comment proposing a reality show based on not having this kind of experience is funny and true.)

Ben Thompson wrote a great piece about ChatGPT and the future of AI-assisted homework. He argues that instead of fighting against students using AI, teachers should embrace it. He offers a great image for it as well:

one analogy for ChatGPT’s output is that sort of poster we are all familiar with who asserts things authoritatively regardless of whether or not they are true. Verifying and editing is an essential skillset right now for every individual.

He proposes giving students intentionally wrong output, and having them analyze the AI output for mistakes. A lot of what he says applies here, too, and that's almost exactly what I had to do in the code snippet above. It's a different skillset, but not an unfamiliar one: code reviews are an important part of modern software development, after all.

If computer programmers forego the task of writing each low-level function, and replace it with the role of guiding, correcting, and steering the AI that is writing them, I'm not sure much will have been lost. Optimistically, a lot will have been gained. Will we have less entry-level programmers and more mid-level programming "mentors", whether they are mentoring other humans or guiding an AI tool? Possibly. I'm not really sure.

In her book, "Hello World: Being Human in the Age of Algorithms", Hannah Fry argues that the best results come from humans and AI working together, not competing. She reaches this conclusion after looking at many different fields: transportation, medicine, and other life-or-death areas. The human component is not so easily replaced, but it doesn't have to be a "who does it better" question anyways. Perhaps ChatGPT, like GitHub Copilot before it, offers a taste of that future for programmers.

posts.title: Critiquing the Agile Principles
posts.excerpt: Agile software development is widely hailed as a philosophy of creating software that better responds to reality, better reflects human developers, and better meets changing business goals. The "agile manifesto" is short and simple: > We ar
posts.content:
Agile software development is widely hailed as a philosophy of creating software that better responds to reality, better reflects human developers, and better meets changing business goals. The "agile manifesto" is short and simple:

We are uncovering better ways of developing
software by doing it and helping others do it.
Through this work we have come to value:

Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Working software over comprehensive documentation
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
Responding to change over following a plan

That is, while there is value in the items on
the right, we value the items on the left more.

https://agilemanifesto.org/

Expanding on this, the authors made a list of a "agile principles". Below the principles are pasted, along with some thoughts and critiques of them I have. These are drawn from experience using scrum (an agile process) and leading a team of engineers that uses it.

While we definitely don't "do agile" perfectly, I do feel that we do it well enough that my critiques are fair -- or, at least, that they represent a fair assessment of how agile plays out in reality.

I greatly respect agile, and it is without a doubt the best software philosophy system I know. But pretending that it is perfect and not in need of reevaluation--maybe revision--would be self-contradictory. Can an agile system itself be rigid? I don't think so!

I also disagree with the notion I have come across that any critique of agile (or scrum, or any agile methodology) is simply an indicator that "you're doing it wrong". Agile was created by a group of intelligent humans, not delivered to humanity by God and inscribed on stone tablets. It's great, but it's not infallible.

So here are the principles, along with some changes I'd make.

Some Minor Critiques

Our highest priority is to satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery of valuable software.

My rewording of this would be, “Our highest priority is to create value for the customer, as quickly as is responsible.”

There are a couple of challenges here. The emphasis on early and continuous can lead to sacrificing quality, and developing for releasability is not always the right order.

There's also a hard lesson, that what customers want from software is not always what they need from software, especially over the long-term. True, the software exists to serve the end-user. But part of engineering is stepping back and looking at the big picture, and part of UI/UX is stepping back and looking at the user.

Delivering value instead of just quick satisfaction, and leaving a bit of breathing room for responsible development, pay off in the long run.

Welcome changing requirements, even late in development. Agile processes harness change for the customer's competitive advantage.

My only change here would be from "Welcome" to "Allow". We do not want to create patchwork features and incongruous software in our legitimate quest to respond to gradually refined requirements.

Deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference to the shorter timescale.

Teams and software stacks are different. What I've seen in practice is that shoehorning a project into a 2-week release cycle isn't always the best fit, and may even cause harm. I would write this as, "Deliver working software as frequently and responsibly as possible".

This also takes some of the burden of the initial development. Early on in the life of software, focusing strictly on releasability can be misguided.

Business people and developers must work together daily throughout the project.

Daily interaction is helpful in some regards, but doesn't have to always involve everyone, lest it interfere with development. I might just scratch the word "daily".

Build projects around motivated individuals. Give them the environment and support they need, and trust them to get the job done.

Yep.

The most efficient and effective method of conveying information to and within a development team is face-to-face conversation.

Face-to-face communication does not reflect the reality of distributed teams. Definitely, synchronous communication is vital. But quick voice calls can be very productive.

More important than this, though, is that different types of meetings have different needs. Unless meetings are moderated well, conversations often wander. They also have little staying power unless clear outputs are defined.

I'd reshape this whole point in that direction. "Conveying information requires a shared understanding of goals and clear action items. Synchronous communication is often the most efficient method."

Working software is the primary measure of progress.

Working is vague. “An increase in the software’s ability to provide value for the customer is the primary measure of progress.”

The Biggest Change

There's 5 more. I want to talk about one of them the most, so let's get the other 4 out of the way. These are pretty spot on;

Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility.

Simplicity--the art of maximizing the amount of work not done--is essential.

At regular intervals, the team reflects on how to become more effective, then tunes and adjusts its behavior accordingly.

More on this one below.

The best architectures, requirements, and designs
emerge from self-organizing teams.

Okay...this one does need a quick comment. Business requirements often emerge from outside the self-organizing team. So, there's that.

But more importantly:

Agile processes promote sustainable development. The sponsors, developers, and users should be able to maintain a constant pace indefinitely.

Humans are not machines. They cannot work indefinitely in a structure that does not allow for some flexibility or responsiveness to human nature. This is especially important as teams are made of more than one person. What works for some won't work for all, especially as the team dynamic evolves.

Even a structure that has a rhythm of work and tries to take human nature into account will itself eventually be restrictive. The context they work in will change, the people themselves will change.

We've seen more of an emphasis on mental health in the software world, and this should continue to be emphasized. Continuous work, even at a sustainable pace, can lead to burnout.

Absolutely we should strive to achieve a sustainable rhythm. But we should also recognize that the rhythm itself may need to evolve. Yes, agile allows for team reflection to be more efficient. But let's give ourselves the freedom to apply that same idea to the agile principles themselves.

posts.content:
Yesterday I shared the first of a 2-part series tackling noisy sensor readings. It set up the case study--monitoring the water depth and change of a municipal stormwater system--and used basic software techniques to look past the variations inherent to real-world sensor data.

In this 2nd part, we are approach the same problem using a Kalman Filter, a widely used approach to dealing with uncertainty in a probabilistically sound way. After setting up the filter and looking at the results, we compare its performance to the simpler techniques from part 1. We find they're both great at reducing noise, but one forms markedly better.

https://www.losant.com/blog/implementing-a-kalman-filter-for-better-noise-filtering

posts.title: Part 1: Sensor noise and straight-forward software techniques to reducing it

posts.content:
Imagine a municipal stormwater system, and you want to know the water depth. You add a floating depth sensor (not too different from a toilet tank..), but it's heavily affected by the churning water. You try an ultrasonic sensor that reflects sound waves off a wide area of the water, but find it's less accurate the lower the water depth is. When you look at a graph of the data from both sensors together, you get a fair idea of the water level...but the separate, erratic readings are hard to work with and it's difficult to see if the water level is rising, falling, or just turbulent.

This case study is explored in my 2 part series on reducing sensor noise with software techniques. Losant just published part 1 and part 2 comes tomorrow.

This first part walks through some simple approaches to smoothing out the unsteady sensor readings, and looks at deriving trends without getting misled by insignificant variations. The 2nd part will describe using Kalman filters to achieve the same goals and more, from a more probabilistic approach.

I hope you enjoy it!

https://www.losant.com/blog/sensor-noise-and-straight-forward-software-techniques-to-reduce-it

posts.title: A* Search with Landmarks (ATL) Simulator
posts.excerpt: In 2004 Andrew Goldberg and Chris Harrelson published a research paper entitled, "Computing the Shortest Path: A\* Search Meets Graph Theory" which you can access in full [online](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/
posts.content:
In 2004 Andrew Goldberg and Chris Harrelson published a research paper entitled, "Computing the Shortest Path: A* Search Meets Graph Theory" which you can access in full online. Their work proposed a new heuristic for A* search that relied on pre-calculating "landmarks" on a graph that could then be used with the triangle inequality to quickly find minimum distances. For this reason, they called it ATL, that is, the A*, Triangle Inequality, Landmarks method.

There's a bit of complexity in that idea, and while their technique has become very popular, there are not many resources that explain it in simpler, less research-papery terms. Since I used this technique in the Artificial Intelligence course I took at Georgia Tech, I thought it would be worthwhile to share how it works. I created a simulator for demonstrating the approach (link towards the bottom) and will use screenshots of the simulator to explain the concept.

In the end, landmarks are not nearly as complicated as they first seem. Yet they are extremely effective -- far more-so than the more common Euclidean distance approach (or it's planetary parallel, the Haversine distance algorithm). Using landmarks effectively led my implementation to be the 2nd fastest in a cohort of ~600 submissions, beaten only by a reach-based approach that could, theoretically, also be used with landmarks.

A* heuristic theory review

To understand landmark heuristics, you first have to understand A* search. There are many great resources on this, such as this one from brilliant.org. However, the basic idea is that as we are considering how to get from some starting point (S) to some target point (T) on a graph, for each step we keep track of both the cost of the path so far and the estimated cost yet to come.

In other words, for each step we are considering, we say, "I know it takes me 200 units of effort to get to this next point, because I've travelled this far and I'm next to it now. I think it will take about 100 more from there. So I will assign this step that I'm thinking about a cost of 300."

This is commonly written as f(n) = g(n) + h(n) where f(n) is the total cost, g(n) is the cost so far, and h(n) is the estimated cost forward.

Perhaps the most important thing to note is that in order for the a* algorithm to find the optimal path, the heuristic value must be optimistic. It's totally find to underestimate that "cost from here". It's not okay at all to overestimate it.

That's worth developing an intuition about, so consider: if a heuristic overestimates a cost, it can actually block an optimal path. You might never explore down the best path because you think it has too high of a cost, when in fact it doesn't.

A pessimistic estimate at Option A essentially blocks the A* algorithm from finding the shortest path that lies beyond.

But the flip-side is not too bad. If a heuristic is overly optimistic, your worst case is that you explore a path that doesn't contain the solution. You can't hide an optimal path behind a too-optimistic heuristic barrier. It just lets your algorithm waste time exploring something needlessly. You'll go down that path and not find the answer. Oh well.

An overly optimistic estimate just wastes time. When it learns the actual cost beyond B is 20, it will instead continue via Option A.

Looking at the f(n) = g(n) + h(n) formula, if you take it to the extreme and say "my heuristic is so optimistic that it always thinks the remaining cost is 0", then you'd get f(n) = g(n) + 0 which is exactly the same as uniform-cost search, the algorithm that just keeps track of the "cost so far". So it's fine, it doesn't break anything, but neither does such a heuristic help. The closer it is to the true value, the more it helps your algorithm.

Another way to think of it is that you don't want the heuristic (a guess) to outweigh the real costs. If the heuristic represents the "at least", then it can't outweigh the real costs.

So, you end up wanting your heuristic to be as close to the true value as possible, but without going over. Mathematically this is referred to as "tightening the bounds" of the heuristic value; specifically we are looking for a "lower bound", or an amount that it has to at least be. And the higher this "at least" value is, the more helpful the heuristic is.

That's why we relax the problem to find a heuristic, for instance, using euclidean distance for a maze. The path through the maze can't be better than a straight line (euclidean distance) so we can use that safely as an "at least" value. With that we know we are not overestimating, so we aren't blocking an optimal path behind a wrongly high heuristic.

Triangle Inequality

The other pre-requisite piece of knowledge is more simple. The triangle inequality states that when you add two sides of a triangle together, they must be longer than the third side by itself.

So, a + b > c. If this doesn't make intuitive sense, try to draw it out. The closest you can get is to have two sides (a and b) almost in a straight line, but not quite. To connect their ends the 3rd line can't quite be longer. So for instance if side a's length is 10, and side b's is 10, then about as long as you can get for side c would be something like 19.99.

As a and b approach a straight line, c gets longer, but it will never be longer than a + b.

Now imagine there is a city at each of the 3 dots in the image. You are trying to get from City 1 to City 2. But, let's pretend you don't know that distance yet.

You know City 2 to City 3 is 10 miles, and City 1 to City 3 is 19.99 miles. What the triangle inequality tells you is:

  • a + b > c
  • a + 10 > 19.99
  • a > 19.99 - 10
  • a > 9.99

So you know that side a is at least 9.99. As it happens, since we labeled it in the first image, you know that it is actually 10. But 9.99 is a really tight "lower bound" for what a has to be.

But wait...roads aren't straight like that

It is true that roads are almost never straight like this. So you might ask something like, "What if the road between cities 1 and 2 is very straight, but the roads between 1 and 3 is very curvy?". You know what though? It doesn't matter.

All we are claiming to deduce from the triangle inequality are lower bounds, i.e. "at least" values. Since the direct distance between two cities will always be shorter than the road distance, we can say that the direct distance is an "at least" value. It's an optimistic, "relaxed case" of the reality. Which, you know, is exactly what we need for a heuristic.

The ATL Method

This, then, is the how the ATL method works. We first select landmarks and pre-calculate their actual paths to every single other node. That's a lot of computation, and we haven't even started our actual search yet!

But this is pre-calculation that we do once, and then get to reuse as many times as we want for our actual searches. (Note: it would be prohibitively expensive in both memory and time to pre-calculate every node to every other node.)

These pre-calculation distances -- which are not euclidean or anything, they are actual costs of real paths -- give us 2 out of 3 sides of triangles between the landmark and any 2 other nodes.

At each step of the A* algorithm, we create abstract triangles between the node we are examining, the target node, and the landmarks we have pre-calculated.

Two sides of these triangles are already known, because the landmarks are completely pre-calculated to every other node, including the one we are examining and the target node we are trying to move towards. We use the triangle inequality to learn as much as we can about the third side. What is the largest "at least" length we can find? That's our heuristic value.

Let's look at an example using the well-known Romania graph:

When the algorithm explores 'f', it creates an abstract triangle.

Say the algorithm is looking for the shortest path between 'a' and 'b', and we have a single pre-calculated landmark at 'v'. When the algorithm explores 's', it looks at its neighbors to add them to the frontier of nodes it is able to explore, using the cost of `f(n) = g(n) + h(n) to determine the order of which nodes to explore. To estimate the cost remaining from 'f', the node it is considering in the image above, it creates an abstract triangle between 'f', 'b' (the target), and 'v' (the landmark).

It knows the edge between (f) and (v) is 438, and the edge between (b) and (v) is 227. For it to still be a triangle, the third edge has to at least be 211. So since the third edge of the triangle is at least 211, (f) is added to the frontier with a priority of 450 (239 cost so far + 211 heuristic).

While we are drawing the triangle abstractly, the known sides do not represent geometric distance. Looking at the side between 'v' and 'b', you can see that the length of 227 is the actual cost it would take to journey between them. This is essentially what makes landmarks so much more accurate -- they are encapsulating the actual topography of the graph as an estimate.

A more complex example

Now let's look at a more complex example from the simulator before I send you off to try it yourself. It uses a graph of about 3,000 major airports and the connections between them. (I created this sample by trimming and supplementing data originally provided by https://r.neo4j.com/airports.)

Let's say you are traveling from SAT (San Antonio, USA) to HYD (Hyderabad, India). Instead of a single landmark, we can select many (up to 10 in the simulator).

In the image below, the dark green dots are airports we have "explored", somewhat analogous to calling the airport and asking about their flights. The light green dots are the airports we've found a flight to, but haven't yet called (so we don't know what departing flights they might have) . In other words we have added them to what we call our "frontier", but we haven't wasted any real time with them yet. The purple dots are our landmarks, and of course the stars are the two airports we are traveling between.

Using the 9 landmarks, a path from San Antonio (SAT) to Hyderabad (HYD) is quickly found.

Compare that to the following image which just uses direct distance (haversine algorithm) as the heuristic:

The same path is found with a haversine algorithm, but many more airports are explored to find it.

This particular example may show landmarks to be more efficient, but there is a lot of variability depending on which landmarks you choose for a given source and target airports. More importantly, because airports' connections are not closely tied to their geographic distances, the nodes you'd expect to see explored aren't always the ones that are. In other words, keep in mind that this simulator is for teaching the concepts of landmarks, not to prove that landmarks are always better. I do think they generally perform better, but you won't always see it in a graph like this.

(An interesting aside: initially my dataset led to haversine outperforming landmarks every time. This was because I had also used haversine to generate the graph's distances between each airport, which wasn't provided in the neo4j data. So, haversine in effect knew the exact distance formula. To counteract this, a random factor was added to the dataset's distances. We'll call that a loose simulation of the many variables impacting flight time.)

With landmarks, just as before, at every step the triangle inequality is used to learn about the minimum path distance each neighboring airport must have to the target airport:

The actual running speed of the algorithm is much faster than this sample shows--this is generating an animation frame for each calculation.

The ATL method in short:

  • Ahead of time, select some "landmark" nodes
  • Still ahead of time, calculate the landmark nodes' distance to every other node in the whole network
  • When finding a path between any 2 nodes, use the A* algorithm
  • For the heuristic:
    • Create an imaginary, abstract triangle between the source node, target node, and the landmark
    • The pre-calculated landmark distances gives you 2 out of 3 of the triangle sides
    • The third side must be at least as long as the other two sides' difference
    • Do this for every landmark you pre-calculated
      • Each triangle inequality generates a truth, i.e. "the third side must be at least ___ long"
      • While they are all true, the longest "at least" value provides the tightest bounds and is the one we will use

Landmarks Simulator

Ready to try it out yourself? Visit the simulator and set the options you'd like to try at the bottom, including which algorithm to use. If you choose landmarks, you will choose which airports will serve as landmarks.

A note about speed: this simulator is primarily a teaching tool. For landmarks, it takes several additional steps to record what it is doing for you to review. As such, landmarks may appear to take more time in the simulator than haversine. Real applications do not exhibit this trait, so the metric to pay attention to is the number of explored nodes, which is generally the expensive part of graph search algorithms.

Goldberg and Harrelson suggest choosing landmarks along the outside perimeter of a graph, but the globe is a sphere so you may just want to space them around the Earth.

The simulator uses a Mercator projection, and it does not do anything fancy with the lines between airports. For example, the flight from Honolulu to Sydney does not go East as the line shows. These are really graph lines, not flight paths.

After you choose landmarks, you need to allow the simulator a little bit of time to pre-calculate their distances to every other node. Then you can calculate the route between two airports. Once you have calculated the route, you can either let it play through at different speeds, or step through it.

Access the simulator here (use a desktop/laptop, not a phone)

Perhaps the best way to develop an intuition on landmarks is to step slowly through a few landmark calculations, looking closely at the triangles overlaid on the map.

posts.title: You can't judge software engineering skills on a scale of 1-10
posts.excerpt: Okay, you "can". But you shouldn't ask job applicants to rate themselves on a scale of 1-10 in various languages, skills, and toolsets. It's ambiguous, subjective, and unfair. There's a better scale anyways: the competency scale. In additio
posts.content:
Okay, you "can". But you shouldn't ask job applicants to rate themselves on a scale of 1-10 in various languages, skills, and toolsets. It's ambiguous, subjective, and unfair. There's a better scale anyways: the competency scale.

In addition to evaluating candidates, a competency scale can also serve as an excellent career development planning tool. We'll go over both use-cases below, right after we look at the problems with the traditional 1-10 scale.

The Candidate's Conundrum

How often have you seen this kind of question on an interview assessment, or heard it asked in an interview?

I'm guilty of asking this of candidates, though I have the ulterior motive of assessing their humility. ("You're a 9 in JavaScript? That's fantastic. Let's talk prototypal inheritance.") Humility, as I've written before, is one of the key skills of a successful software engineer.

But if you've been asked this, you know the problem you face. Rate yourself too high, and they'll think you're arrogant or lying. Rate yourself too low, and you won't seem like you have what it takes for the job.

How can a broad, complex skill be reduced to a number anyways? I always want to ask, "What aggregation method am I supposed to use here?" Are you supposed to average out all the different elements that make up a skill, or go by the part you're best at?

In my experience, most people with solid ability in the skill will say 7 or 8. This tells the interviewer precious little.

Aside from the unfair guessing-game it places candidates in, it's entirely subjective. How is a 6 different from an 8? Am I a 7 if I can do it well, but still have to Google things (like most candidates). Whatever the answer is, do you expect the scale to stay consistent between candidates? Not likely!

Luckily, there's a better scale. A scale that is founded on solid psychological principles.

Hierarchy of Competence

The "Hierarchy of Competence" suggests there are 4 phases in learning a skill, and can be pictured as a pyramid:

From bottom to top, these levels represent our journey as we discover and master a skill:

  1. Unconscious incompetence: I'm not skilled at this, and I don't even realize how unskilled I am, or why it's worth learning to do it better.
  2. Conscious incompetence: I see that I'm unskilled, and the value in learning to do it better. I'll start trying, though I will make a lot of mistakes.
  3. Conscious competence: I am capable of doing this well, though it takes a good deal of effort on my part. I may have to slow down or retrace my steps at times.
  4. Unconscious competence: This comes naturally to me now. I can do this well, and can intuit the right way of doing it without having to think about it.

At first, we "don't know what we don't know". When we come to appreciate our inability, we can begin to improve. It takes great effort at first, and involves mistakes. But eventually, it becomes second-nature to us.

The final stage, "unconscious competence," does not mean that the skill takes no work at all. Some things will naturally remain complex. But we know what to do, and see naturally the best way to do it.

Translating to Levels

Those competency levels are a bit of a mouthful, and we aren't interviewing candidates to give them a psychology lesson. We can translate them into more user-friendly skill levels:

These levels ("Beginner," "Novice," "Practitioner," and "Expert") correspond to the stages above. The terms are familiar and friendly enough that most people can quickly grasp them.

More importantly, they correspond to how learning a software engineering skill (or any skill, really) actually works. We don't learn discretely on a scale of 1-10. You will not hear software engineers saying casually, "I was a 7 yesterday, but then I read this book on web assembly, and now I'm an 8!".

Scales like that are oversimplifications, because life is not a role-playing game. The truth is that with software engineering in particular, you're continually learning and improving.

But you do progress from knowing nothing about it ("Beginner"), to learning it a little but doing it poorly ("Novice"), to doing it competently, but with some effort, on a regular basis ("Practitioner"), to doing it well by second-nature ("Expert").

When I'm interviewing candidates, what I want to know is where they are on that journey for the different skills needed in the job.

By the way, even an Expert will still look things up. Googling things is a normal, healthy part of the job. (Frankly, I'd rather you look something up to make sure you're doing it right. Doctors do this, too.) But the intuition, the second-nature understanding of how a problem should be approached, can't be faked.

TaylorScript, an Example of Learning a Skill

These levels are also easy to apply to a technical skill, and most software engineers will relate to them from their own experience. Imagine a software engineer hears of a fictitious new, possibly revolutionary language, TaylorScript.

At first, they have no idea what it is, why it matters, how it's different, or why they should bother learning it. They may hear it mentioned in the break-room, see it mentioned on a blog, or read it on a job description. They are a Beginner.

Eventually, they run into this word enough times that they decide to do some research. They might discover TaylorScript is semantically brilliant, works flawlessly across browsers, and handles heavy computation tasks with ease. Excited, they read the "Getting Started" guide, download the test environment and begin playing with some tutorials. They are a Novice.

At this point, they will have a lot of misconceptions and false assumptions about TaylorScript. They will make mistakes, and not be able to see the better way of doing things. But they are learning, and they recognize that they are, in fact, making mistakes.

And as they iron out the wrinkles in their knowledge, they progress. They make fewer and fewer mistakes, though they have to think hard about how to do things the right way. They may have to rewrite sections of their code, and still make occasional mistakes. They are a Practitioner, able to do the work and do it well, though with a fair bit of effort.

After a great deal of experience, they do not have to struggle so much to use TaylorScript. They have a broad and deep knowledge of how it works, and why it's set up the way it is. When reviewing others' code, they see hidden anti-patterns and mistakes without even trying. They can predict what works fine now but will be a problem later. They are an Expert.

Since the scale relates to how we actually learn in real life, it's easy for candidates to apply to their own skills. They may not be able to tell the difference between a "6" or a "7", but they will be able to tell you whether they are a Novice or a Practitioner.

Candidate Assessments

Even with friendlier names, the levels still need some explanation when evaluating candidates. A short key can help keep everyone on the same page. For instance:

  1. BEGINNER - I haven't done this very much yet, or at all.
  2. NOVICE - I've started learning this, and can get by (slowly). I can't help others much except as a fellow learner.
  3. PRACTITIONER - I'm familiar with this and can do it well, but I have to concentrate to do it right. I can help others, but may have to look it up or try a few things.
  4. EXPERT - I'm very experienced with this, and it comes naturally to me now. I can definitely help others who have questions about this.

I like framing the descriptions with the team-oriented aspect of, "how much can I help others with this?" This reinforces a culture of collaboration, and helps candidates think about their skills from a different angle.

Their answers will be specific enough to tell you what you need to know, without getting bogged down in tiny differences.

Is it a skill central to the job? You're looking for at least a practitioner. A senior role that will be mentoring others in this skill? That's an expert. A tangential skill they can learn on the job? A novice in that is fine.

Career Development

I originally developed this model to help my employees identify areas they want to focus their professional development on. At Losant, each employee has a dedicated professional development fund and an expectation that half a day each week can be spent on side projects and learning. This year we started an annual career development planning process, and I wanted something to help the software engineers on my team think about their skills.

When used in this case, it's important to make it clear that this is a career tool, not a performance evaluation.

Drawing from resources like the Developer Roadmaps, I put together a spreadsheet of skills used in their role. I added one column for them to rate themselves in each skill, and another with a "target" rating. For fun, it creates a visual graph showing potential areas they could work on.

Competency Scale Summary

This kind of scale is the beginning of the conversation, not the end of it. You won't really know how a candidate's skills stack up until you've worked with them for several months.

The 1-10 scales are pretending to be more accurate than they really are! But the competency scale is honest in its breakdown, reflects how people actually progress, and tells you what you really need to know.

Precisely because it so closely relates to actual learning, it's also useful as a career development tool. An engineer can recognize where they are a novice or a beginner, and choose to work on those areas. They can feel confident that even though they haven't mastered every element of a skill or language, they can still be a solid practitioner of it. And when they call themselves an Expert at something, they know it's not presumption. They've simply honed their skill to the point they naturally do it well. That's a measurable, achievable, and worthy goal.

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: Comparing Arrays using .map (ReactJS)
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Comparing Arrays using .map (ReactJS)](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/65899043/comparing-arrays-using-map-reactjs) * * * ## My answer: You are correct in where the problem lies: `course.courseUrl === courseList.C
posts.content:
Original question: Comparing Arrays using .map (ReactJS)

My answer:

You are correct in where the problem lies: course.courseUrl === courseList.CourseCode In this case course is a single item from a list, with a property courseUrl. That's fine. But courseList is an array of items, each of which has a CourseCode property. The Array itself does not (although, interestingly, it could). It seems like what you are trying to do is pull the full course data (from courses) but filtered to only the ones the user has. In this case, you have to loop through one list, looking through the other list for each item. What you want is filter (or, more powerfully, reduce) but probably not map. const filteredCourses = availableCourses.filter( availableCourse => studentsCourses.some( studentsCourse => studentsCourse.id === availableCourse.id ) ); You'll notice I renamed the variables to make it clear which of the two lists is being used at each part. The outer function filter will return a new array containing only those items that return 'true' in the callback function. The inner callback function some loops through another array (the student's enrolled courses) and returns true if it finds any that match the given condition. So in English, "Filter this list of all the courses, giving me back only the courses that have a matching ID in the list of the student's enrolled courses."

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: Having null when trying to display single object using React hooks
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Having null when trying to display single object using React hooks](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/65877091/having-null-when-trying-to-display-single-object-using-react-hooks) * * * ## My answer: When axios gives
posts.content:
Original question: Having null when trying to display single object using React hooks

My answer:

When axios gives you a response to a GET request, the data returned from the server is in a data property. This is a bit confusing in your example, because the data returned from the server also has a data property. So, in effect, you need to access response.data.data. You might adjust when you set the course details to instead have setCourseDetails(response.data); However, you also have some mismatched types. Your coursedetails starts as an array, but you then set it to an axios response, which is an object. So you'll want to change that to useState({}) or something similar. Your JSX return value (at least, I presume it is. It's not wrapped in a return statement, but perhaps you deleted some for consciseness.) also presumes that there is always a data property on coursedetails, and a course_name property on that data property. This isn't true, for instance, at the beginning. You will want to adjust this to check for its presence, i.e. {coursedata.data && coursedata.data.course_name ? coursedata.data : ''} Finally, it is helpful to track the status of async requests like this. I often use a separate state for the status, i.e. const [status,setStatus] = useState('init'); Then right before the axios request is fired, setStatus('loading') and then right after it is successful, setStatus('success'). (And, if there's an error, setStatus('error'). This makes it easier to show different loading states to the user.

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: How can I fix the Axios get request and the React Hooks?
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [https://stackoverflow.com/questions/65870417/how-can-i-fix-the-axios-get-request-and-the-react-hooks/](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/65870417/how-can-i-fix-the-axios-get-request-and-the-react-hooks/) * * * ## My
posts.content:
Original question: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/65870417/how-can-i-fix-the-axios-get-request-and-the-react-hooks/

My answer:

I think your code is a little over-engineered, and doesn't properly handle the asynchronous nature of the request. What I typically do is return the fetch or axios object so that the calling component can wait for the response and handle it when it's ready. Forked example As you can see, I've removed a couple of pieces from your Container.jsx component (which might need a different name fwiw). Instead of setting a flag for the form being ready to submit, I just have the button directly calling the fetchNameData function. The checkGender function from your utilities function now directly returns the axios object, which is a promise. The fetchNameData function is async so it can wait for the results from this promise.

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: react library testing are not updating my screen
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [React Material-UI - styling displayed rows label in TablePagination component](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/65795991/react-material-ui-styling-displayed-rows-label-in-tablepagination-component) * * * ## My answ
posts.content:
Original question: React Material-UI - styling displayed rows label in TablePagination component

My answer:

This turns out to be mostly a CSS issue. The example in the Material-UI docs does not have this problem, because it is effectively aligning the table pagination to the right. Since the arrows have a consistent width (and there's nothing to their right) if you align the pagination to the right then they never move. What you have done in your example is override the spacer that is used to achieve this "right" alignment. The pagination component is set to display: flex and uses the default horizontal direction. The first element, the "spacer", is an empty element that comes with a default flex-grow property of "1", i.e. it will grow into any available extra space at a normal rate. It effectively "eats" the empty horizontal space in the footer, growing and thus pushing the other elements to the right. You have changed the spacer's flex-grow property to 0, so it does not eat up that extra space and the pagination components effectively align to the left, which means the pagination arrows' position depends on the widths of the components that come before it, which means that it can change depending on the page. (side note: they could have achieved almost the same effect by setting the flex container to justify-content: flex-end) If you do want the pagination on the left, you will need to make the items to the left of the pagination arrows a fixed with if you do not want the positions of the items to their right to adjust. For instance:

const StyledTablePagination = withStyles((theme) => ({
  spacer: {
    flex: "0 1 0%"
  },
  caption: {
    width: "75px"
  }
}))(TablePagination);

posts.title: Software engineering: it's how you work, not just what you do
posts.excerpt: Anyone who has interviewed and hired enough software engineers can tell you that technical skill is only one piece of the puzzle. For instance, I love coding challenges. (In fact, I am currently participating in the [Advent of Code 2020](ht
posts.content:
Anyone who has interviewed and hired enough software engineers can tell you that technical skill is only one piece of the puzzle.

For instance, I love coding challenges. (In fact, I am currently participating in the Advent of Code 2020). But your ability to quickly write an algorithm does not mean you can write software.

Other skills--like how you talk to people, manage your time, and follow through--are at least as important as your technical chops. And unlike learning a new programming language, they cannot be so easily taught.

However, you can work on them. Below I share a few of the most important traits that I've found make a huge difference in an engineer's success, and some questions to think about for each of them.

Humility

Humility doesn't just make you more pleasant to work with. It also affects the quality of your work.

If you actually think your work is always perfect, then you won't be open to improving it. And if your work from 3 months ago was also "perfect", then you haven't improved.

But perhaps thinking you're "the best" just means "better than everyone else" on the team. This, too, is toxic. You may get away with it on smaller teams and projects, but sooner or later the thinking will come back to bite you. Because, as a human, you will make mistakes.

I have seen people like this bend over backwards to explain why their mistakes weren't actually mistakes at all. They end up blaming their teammates, former employees, technology, clients--anything they can think of. This creates a judgmental, divisive, and highly negative culture for everyone.

Instead, recognize that you are continuously learning. Remember that even the best software in the world created by huge teams of experienced engineers has bugs. And take my word that the best and most talented software engineers I have known have been the ones quickest to admit they make mistakes.

A culture of humility is the strongest antidote to imposter syndrome. You're not a fraud just because you're not perfect. See? None of us are.

Initiative

At age 16, in my very first job as a theme park employee, I learned that I hate being micro-managed.

Now that I manage others, just about the very last thing I want to do is micro-manage. That's mostly because it's demeaning and I hate it myself, but also because I don't have the time.

(Note: it is absolutely my job to step in when needed. There should be no task a manager is "above" doing when needed.)

Too many developers view their tasks as a list of "inputs". They'll follow the steps, complete the tasks given, and generally do them well. But if something is missing, or if some of the "input" is "invalid", the train screeches to a halt.

But some are able to go a step further, zoom out, and ask, "What needs to be done here?"

Employees with initiative are ones to whom I can give a project and trust that they will do whatever is needed to get it done well. There may be missing information--they will figure out who to ask. Or perhaps there are vague, conflicting requirements from the client--they will work to refine them. Maybe they don't have experience with a key technology--they'll learn it.

Even projects that have stalled out in the hands of others begin moving again in their hands. And clients feel less like they're working with a call-center representative, and more like they're working with an experienced, devoted consultant.

Synthesis

A great engineer can synthesize complex parts into a cohesive whole.

This is hugely important for planning software architecture. Even a modest website relies on multiple layers of hardware, software, APIs, languages and network requests. It is relatively easy to make each layer "work". It is much harder to understand how they fit together.

This has grown even more important with the rise of cloud infrastructure. Cloud providers like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft ofter literally hundreds of services that can be interconnected to power an application. Having a clear vision about the whole allows you to plan robust, scalable, and secure systems. This "vision" is what software architecture diagrams attempt to elicit.

Even with existing software, synthesis is a big part of proper debugging. It is often important to step back from an immediate problem and contextualize it in its place in the broader system to determine the true cause of an issue.

But synthesis goes beyond technical vision. How does this project fit into our business objectives? How will this feature co-exist with the existing ones? What exactly is our client trying to accomplish with this new product? Even a single meeting must be synthesized properly if you want to avoid "missing the forest for the trees".

And Many More

There are of course many other traits that matter a lot. Communication, respect, a sense of team, drive, innovation, endurance...the list keeps going.

If there is a single lesson here, it is that how you work is just as important as what you do. Software engineering is much more than writing code. It's about what code to write, how to create software well, and how what you're doing fits into the bigger picture. That picture includes colleagues, legacy software, clients, business requirements, and so much more. Having technical skills alone just doesn't cut it.

While demeanor, natural talents, and personality play into these traits, they are mostly about attitude. We can reflect on how we view them, and, if necessary, how our view needs to shift.

Humility

  • Do I secretly think I'm better than everyone else on my team?
  • When others disagree with me, do I hear them out before assuming they're wrong?
  • When someone points out a mistake in my work, do I immediately defend it?
  • When someone else shines, do I celebrate their accomplishments?
  • When I don't know something, am I open to others about it?

Initiative

  • Do I take pride in my projects?
  • Do I skip over things I know "should" be done, because I haven't been asked to do them?
  • Do I step back to ask, "what needs to be done here?"
  • Have I considered the quality I would want if I were using the software?

Synthesis

  • Do I dive in and start working on a task without caring to understand how it fits in to the broader project?
  • Do I think about how my work fits into the work of my teammates?
  • Do I listen to coworkers, clients, and others for what their underlying concerns are?
  • Do I keep the 'big picture' in mind when I am working on a small piece of it?

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: react library testing are not updating my screen
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [react library testing are not updating my screen](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/65042912/react-library-testing-are-not-updating-my-screen/) * * * ## My answer: The warning from React, "Warning: An update to Poke
posts.content:
Original question: react library testing are not updating my screen

My answer:

The warning from React, "Warning: An update to Pokemon inside a test was not wrapped in act(...)" means that it has detected a change to your state that is not accounted for in your testing. In this case, this warning is wrapped inside of a more explanatory message saying that this problem occurred after your test. In your code, you have await waitFor(() => userEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button"))). However, waitFor is meant to be used with an assertion. In other words it is meant to wait until an expectation is true -- not until an event is fired, because the firing of an event like this isn't asynchronous (the processing of it may be, but not the firing of it.) Instead, you should just fire the event, and then waitFor something you can test that shows the process is finished. For instance, you said "they will be awarded 10 points and it will be logged on the screen". So after your event, do a waitFor that looks for the message showing that they answered it correctly, which you are already doing in the next line. So try:

userEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button"));
await waitFor(() => {
   expect(screen.getByText(/Score: 10/)).toBeInTheDocument();
});

Or, even simpler, since findBy* methods use waitFor inside:

userEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button"));
screen.findByText(/Score: 10/);

PS You can learn more about that error message and some different approaches to fix it by reading Kent Dodds article on it, Fix the "not wrapped in act() warning
