posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: CSS works for id, but not for class because of bootstrap
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [CSS works for id, but not for class because of bootstrap](http://StackOverflow.com/q/60028924) * * * ## My answer: How is bootstrap overriding you? The answer is likely selector specificity, which means it has a highe
posts.content:
Original question: CSS works for id, but not for class because of bootstrap

My answer:

How is bootstrap overriding you? The answer is likely selector specificity, which means it has a higher priority than your selector. But you can use the same trick and write a selector with a higher specificity than it. For the sake of demonstration:

 .search.search.search.search.search{ ... }

now has a specificity of 0 0 5 0 instead of 0 0 1 0. The first number is inline styles (i.e. style="..."), the second is id's (i.e. id=""), the third is class, and the fourth is element (i.e. div).

When your browser decides which CSS rule(s) to apply, if two rules conflict, it uses the one with more specificity. So an ID selector will always beat a class selector, for instance.

If you inspect the element in question and look at what other selectors are applying rules to it, you can figure out how much specificity you need to overrule it.

More about specificity

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: php echo a javascript variable to file.txt
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [php echo a javascript variable to file.txt](http://StackOverflow.com/q/60017947) * * * ## My answer: It seems like what you want is for PHP to write the file with the result of the timezone variable, i.e. that it woul
posts.content:
Original question: php echo a javascript variable to file.txt

My answer:

It seems like what you want is for PHP to write the file with the result of the timezone variable, i.e. that it would be a text file with the name of a timezone in it.

Probably what you are seeing is PHP writing that JavaScript line instead, i.e. <script>document.writeln(timezone);</script>

Right?

What's happening is PHP executes completely before JavaScript is run. Your first example is working because PHP executes, including the writing of a line of JavaScript, and then JavaScript executes, including that line, and you see the result.

What you are trying to do in the second example isn't possible. PHP is executing, including the writing of that line of JavaScript (to the file), and then JavaScript executes, but of course not in that text file.

Your two choices are to find a different way to get the timezone strictly in PHP, or else to get it with JavaScript and then use AJAX to trigger a later run of PHP, i.e. after JavaScript has run.

EDIT

Your JavaScript will fetch the timezone as before. Then it will send that to a separate file that outputs it:

var url = '..'; // url of a php file that JUST processes the file write
$.ajax({
  type: "POST",
  url: url,
  data: {
        'timezoneToPrint' : timezone
    }
});

And in your other PHP file, which you have just called, you can now print it to a file

if($_POST['timezoneToPrint']){
   // ..write the file here, the timezone is in $_POST['timezoneToPrint']
}

posts.content:
Original question: JavaScript - sort 2 object arrays on the same field

My answer:

const output = [];
sortedArray.forEach( sortedItem => {
    const matchingItem = unsortedArray.find( unsortedItem => unsortedItem.sortField === sortedItem.sortField );

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: Merge corresponding objects inside array JS
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Merge corresponding objects inside array JS](http://StackOverflow.com/q/59949470) * * * ## My answer: Here's another approach, which is not performance optimized and is less concise than the other answers, but breaks
posts.content:
Original question: Merge corresponding objects inside array JS

My answer:

Here's another approach, which is not performance optimized and is less concise than the other answers, but breaks the steps down to make clear what's happening.

const data1 = [{ id: 1, someKey1: 'someValue2'}, { id: 2, someKey2: 'someValue2' }, { id: 3, someKey3: 'someValue3' }]
const data2 = [{ uid: 1, someKey4: 'someValue4'}, { uid: 2, someKey5: 'someValue5' }]

function mergeProperties(set1, linkingProperty1, set2, linkingProperty2){

  const keys1 = set1.map( item => item[linkingProperty1] );
  const keys2 = set2.map( item => item[linkingProperty2] );
  const mergedKeys = keys1.concat(keys2);
  const filteredKeys = mergedKeys.filter( key => !!key || key === 0); //truthy or actually number 0
  const uniqueKeys = filteredKeys.filter((a, b) => filteredKeys.indexOf(a) === b);

  // now we have a complete list, with no duplicates, of all possible ids

  const mergedArray = uniqueKeys.reduce( (accumulator, key) => {
      const resultInSet1 = set1.find( item => item[linkingProperty1] === key );
      const resultInSet2 = set2.find( item => item[linkingProperty2] === key );
      let item = {};
      if(resultInSet1){
        delete resultInSet1[linkingProperty1];
        item = {...resultInSet1};
      }
      if(resultInSet2){
        delete resultInSet2[linkingProperty2];
        item = {...item, ...resultInSet2};
      }
      return [...accumulator, item];
  }, []);

  return mergedArray;
}

console.log( mergeProperties(data1,"id",data2,"uid") );

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: Is creating a table to store one single row sign of bad programming?
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Is creating a table to store one single row sign of bad programming?](http://StackOverflow.com/q/59939872) * * * ## My answer: If your question is really just, "is it a bad design practice to use a database (**edit**:
posts.content:
Original question: Is creating a table to store one single row sign of bad programming?

My answer:

If your question is really just, "is it a bad design practice to use a database (edit: or database table) to hold only one piece--or a few pieces--of data", I would say probably not. Databases are a place to hold data, and they very easily scale. You might at some point need to hold more data, and in the future a lot more data, and databases do that very efficiently.

Is it overkill for a single piece of data? Probably, but I doubt you'd end up just storing that one piece there. If it's just one user (you) you don't need a database, but rather secure credentials or an application that only you can access. But assuming it's not just for you, you'll probably find a lot of other things that are helpful to store there.

However, the question you didn't really ask but should be more interested in, is can you do this securely? The answer there is a lot more dubious. Even very well-designed, complex user access systems have vulnerabilities. It is difficult to account for all of the common vulnerabilities and design flaws. How will you handle password encryption? Brute force attack denial? Attacks that use the variance in the response time of your database to different passwords to hone in on the password?

I'm not a security expert, but I know enough to know that, and to leave security related systems to those who specialize in them. I suggest you do the same.

If you absolutely need to have a user-authentication process, use a system that already exists. It's not that hard, and a lot more secure, to tie into an authentication system. If you don't absolutely need to, and this is all just for you or one other user, just avoid the security problem and don't develop it as a public system that you log into over the application.

Edit: Rereading your question, you already have a database but are asking about an additional table in it. My answer holds -- it's not a bad practice, but storing of a password in it is still very risky if you don't know what you're doing.

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: Why is this throwing "Cannot read property 'length' of undefined"?
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Why is this throwing "Cannot read property 'length' of undefined"?](http://StackOverflow.com/q/59922867) * * * ## My answer: I believe the problem is in your clone function: ``` let selector = $closestOperation.clone(
posts.content:
Original question: Why is this throwing "Cannot read property 'length' of undefined"?

My answer:

I believe the problem is in your clone function:

let selector = $closestOperation.clone()
.insertAfter($closestOperation).attr("id", "operation-" + cloneIndex)
.find("*")
.each(function() {
  let id = this.id || "";
  let match = id.match(regex) || [];
  if (match.length == 3) {
    this.id = match[1] + '-' + (cloneIndex);
  }
});
// ...
bindToSelector(selector);

When you run the .find("*"), your selector is becoming a large array of 10 items. Each of these is then getting sent to your selector function and bound to the event handler.

When you change the value, these items are run through your buildSelect function, but don't match anything, since you were only expecting the select element to be sent through it. Thus the default value of {} gets returned. This empty object does NOT have the value "operationValues" which you try to access with result['operationValues'], so it is undefined and therefore has no length.

Original question: How to get code from another file and write everything to one file?

My answer:

The HTML <script src= is going to fetch a resource and run it, from wherever you have specified in the src attribute. It's expecting a URL.

The htmlspecialchars( function is expecting a string, and will return a string.

The way you have it right now, it will take the string "static/functions.js" and process it.

Your question suggests you want it to operate on the contenst of the file. This is techncially possible, but the file has to be fetched first.

htmlspecialchars( file_get_contents(__DIR__ . 'static/functions.js') )

But that still seems odd. You want to convert all the encoded special characters in your JavaScript file to their HTML entities? Like < to <? That's almost surely going to make the JavaScript invalid.

Even if it didn't ruin your JavaScript, you'd still be trying to take the contents of that file and putting them in the src property of the script tag, which is expecting a URL.

Overall this seems like you need to step back and think about what exactly you're trying to accomplish.

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: After adding a hook in functions.php, limit login plugin doesn't display value
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [After adding a hook in functions.php, limit login plugin doesn't display value](http://StackOverflow.com/q/59929802) * * * ## My answer: First, the `create_function()` function is deprecated. You could try it like thi
posts.content:
Original question: After adding a hook in functions.php, limit login plugin doesn't display value

My answer:

First, the create_function() function is deprecated. You could try it like this:

function my_login_errors_function(){
    return 'Error: Wrong Username or Password';
}
add_filter('login_errors', 'my_login_errors_function');

However, this doesn't fix the main problem, which is that your function will change every login error text to the string we are returning.

Filters are like machines on a conveyor belt, receiving something and passing something along to the next step. But the way your function is written, it's a machine that completely disregards what comes in, and always spits out the same thing.

If you want to only replace a particular login error message, you would first have to check the existing text (the input to your filter machine) to see if it matched the one you want to replace, and then and only then would you return something else (otherwise returning the original argument's value).

function my_login_errors_function( $error ){
    if( $error === 'The error message I want to replace' ){
         return 'Error: Wrong Username or Password';
    }
    return $error;
}
add_filter( 'login_errors', 'my_login_errors_function' );

Likely what's happening is that plugin is using a login error to display the count, but since your function is overwriting every error message, that count is getting overwritten.

posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Wordpress custom menu for each user?](http://StackOverflow.com/q/59908758) * * * ## My answer: This is not a built-in feature, but yes, this would be possible on a custom WordPress site (i.e. WordPress.org, not WordPr
posts.content:
Original question: Wordpress custom menu for each user?

My answer:

This is not a built-in feature, but yes, this would be possible on a custom WordPress site (i.e. WordPress.org, not WordPress.com), and there are a lot of different ways you could structure it.

It would not be trivial to implement, however.

My initial approach would be to have an actual WordPress menu hold all possible items, and then store user preferences as to which of the items are shown or hidden. On their user profile edit page, you could output the menu items as a checkbox list, and then store their selection as a user option. On the rest of the site, when you output the menu, you'd first pull that user option, then output the menu items manually one at a time if they have the option for that item checked.

There are of course other ways, but they would be similarly complex -- well beyond copying and pasting a code snippet, or me typing up a solution for you here.

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: React Native: How to render muliple images dynamically after fetching from multiple rest api's
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [React Native: How to render muliple images dynamically after fetching from multiple rest api's](http://StackOverflow.com/q/59908834) * * * ## My answer: The way to think about the render() method is that it may run re
posts.content:
Original question: React Native: How to render muliple images dynamically after fetching from multiple rest api's

My answer:

The way to think about the render() method is that it may run repeatedly. In most cases it is re-run every time there's a change that affects its output.

The way you have it structured, your render() function calls {this.displayProductSection()} which calls this.getLineItems() which calls this.getProductPrimaryImage(item.product_id) which makes the AJAX request to the WordPress API.

Since render can (and likely will) be run repeatedly, this means your request for the image is being created repeatedly.

Running an AJAX request is not like displaying an image, where you put the src URL in the tag and the browser loads it once. HTML is parsed and run once, this is requesting it repeatedly.

A better pattern would be:

  • In state, track whether the remote data has been requested yet. You could do a status property with init, loading, success, error as possible strings.
  • In your componentDidMount, request the data. Change the status from init to loading.
  • When the data comes in, change the status from loading to succcess (or error, depending on the result) and store the result in state.
  • In your render function, do a conditional based on that status property. If it is loading, show a loader. If it is success, output the image based on the state you stored above.

Sometimes you aren't quite ready to fetch the remote data when the component mounts. Maybe it depends on some user input first. In that case, you could instead hook into componentDidUpdate. Check for your condition there, but since this function call also run repeatedly, also check the status and only request it if it hasn't been requested yet.

In either case, notice the separation of concerns. Your render() function is doing one thing -- displaying. It's not kicking off network requests or triggering side effects. Your lifecycle methods (or functions that respond to user input) handle that stuff.

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: Cloning Rows of a table
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Cloning Rows of a table](http://StackOverflow.com/q/59894862) * * * ## My answer: A ` ` with no type= property specified is by default a "submit" type button. That's why you'll often see the odd-looking ` `. This is l
posts.content:
Original question: Cloning Rows of a table

My answer:

A <button> with no type= property specified is by default a "submit" type button. That's why you'll often see the odd-looking <button type="button">. This is likely why your page is refreshing, although you usually see that behavior when the button is inside of a form. Perhaps that form tag is just not visible in your HTML excerpt.

As @Rory McCrossan mentioned, you have one event handler, presumably tied to a high level item in your HTML (DOM), and then inside of it you are using a switch statement to determine what was actually clicked. If you don't have a good reason for this, it makes more sense to tie the event handlers to the specific elements they relate to. The way you have it may work but you're making but it's a lot less clean, more error-prone, and harder to work with this way.

If it were me, I'd set it up like this for your DOM:

 <th><button type="button" class="js-add-row">Add Row</button></th>

Then in your JS:

var rowCount = 1;
$( '.js-add-row' ).on('click', function(){
    const template = `<tr class="row-${rowCount}"> ... </tr>`;
    $( this ).closest( 'table' ).find( 'tbody' ).append(template);
    rowCount++;
});

Obviously you'd want to put in your whole template there. Instead of storing the template in JS, you could just clone the row that's out there, but that only works if you don't want to let the user delete all the rows. Or, sometimes people will store this template in the DOM but hidden so that it's not a real row. Or as a data- element on one of the table elements. The best practice may depend on your use-case.

The $( this ).closest( 'table' ).find( 'tbody' ) part allows this to be more reusable. It's literally saying, from where this button was clicked, find the table it's inside of, then grab the tbody tag. You could have multiple tables with their own add buttons, and this would still work (in that case, the template would either need to be the same, or cloned from that first row).

You can see the advantage here of isolating this event handler. You have a clean function for doing this one thing. It's easy to find, easy to modify, easy to expand and copy.

Demo: JSFiddle

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: Why reorder not working after button click?
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Why reorder not working after button click?](http://StackOverflow.com/q/59858965) * * * ## My answer: Your parent file (App.js) has the menu data and passes it along to the child file (Header.js). What is sent, howeve
posts.content:
Original question: Why reorder not working after button click?

My answer:

Your parent file (App.js) has the menu data and passes it along to the child file (Header.js). What is sent, however, is not the original menu data, but a copy of it.

Your child file (Header.js) tries to change its value, but the original is not changed. The way React works is to continuously re-render every time there is a likely change in what would be displayed. So your change to the copy of the 'open' property is lost, because a new copy is made and sent down.

What you need to do is allow the parent's copy to be modified. Generally you would do this by tracking the modifiable data in state, not as a const.

In the fork I made of your code, I kept the const but added id's to each menu item so that they can be targetted. Then I added state (useState hook) to create state based off of your const, with ability for it to be modified.

  const [menu, setMenu] = useState(TASK_LIST_HEADER);
  const toggleMenu = id => {
    const newMenuState = menu.map(menuItem => {
      if (menuItem.id === id) {
        menuItem.menu.open = !menuItem.menu.open;
      }
      return menuItem;
    });
    setMenu(newMenuState);
  };

The toggleMenu function takes as a parameter an id, i.e. which menu item do we want to update? Then it uses the setMenu part of the state hook to update the menu in state with the newly opened (or closed) menu item.

The toggleMenu function is then passed down to the child (Header) so that it can be called from there.

Working fork: https://codesandbox.io/s/dazzling-lichterman-rgdfy

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: Twitter API tells me " media type unrecognized." for images that always worked
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Twitter API tells me " media type unrecognized." for images that always worked](http://StackOverflow.com/q/59858831) * * * ## My answer: Twitter's documentation states: > Ensure the POST is a multipart/form-data reque
posts.content:
Original question: Twitter API tells me " media type unrecognized." for images that always worked

My answer:

Twitter's documentation states:

Ensure the POST is a multipart/form-data request. Either upload the raw binary (media parameter) of the file, or its base64-encoded contents (media_data parameter). Use raw binary when possible, because base64 encoding results in larger file sizes

However it looks like you are uploading base64-encoded contents, while using the media parameter. Try changing the media parameter to media_data.

It's likely a recent change or one that is only recently enforced, hence it working before for you.

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: currentValue.indexOf is not a function at getValueForCheckbox in Formik
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [currentValue.indexOf is not a function at getValueForCheckbox in Formik](http://StackOverflow.com/q/59859300) * * * ## My answer: We can't see your "data", which would be helpful, but in short, the library you are usi
posts.content:
Original question: currentValue.indexOf is not a function at getValueForCheckbox in Formik

My answer:

We can't see your "data", which would be helpful, but in short, the library you are using for your form is expecting indexOf() to work on the value of the checkbox, but it is not.

Your code is written to suggest "data" has a day_of_week array and a periods array, and that the periods array items are themselves iterable (i.e. arrays, strings, etc.) with at least one value each. When you write the [0] in there, you are making a promise that it has at least one value. And the form library you are using is also expecting that the value will have an indexOf property, which it would automatically if it were a string or array.

I suspect that time, which is pointing at each item in your periods array, is undefined, or an empty array or string, or it is of some type where saying [0] on it doesn't make sense. And if it does make sense, whatever it has there (at time[0]) is probably undefined.

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: access to the endpoints wp api rest title post rendered inreact app
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [access to the endpoints wp api rest title post rendered inreact app](http://StackOverflow.com/q/59850755) * * * ## My answer: In principle, what you have shown should work. The response of that WP API endpoint does in
posts.content:
Original question: access to the endpoints wp api rest title post rendered inreact app

My answer:

In principle, what you have shown should work. The response of that WP API endpoint does include:

"title": {
    "rendered": "Your post's title"
},

This is backed up by your console.log output.

You haven't shown your default state, where your console.log output is written, or where you are trying to access the full path (i.e. {this.state.item.title.rendered}), but it sounds like you are doing at least the full path part in the render function.

Assuming so, I believe what you have is a timing issue. The render function may run as many times as it needs to (i.e. when the component updates). The first time it runs, your state does not have the title property yet, as your HTTP request is not yet complete. It's undefined, and when you try to access a child property of undefined, you get that error.

The difference with your earlier console statement is you aren't trying to access a property of undefined. You are just outputting the state's value itself (i.e., undefined). And one very tricky thing about the console is that it's not a historical record. A value that a console.log shows can change...say from 'undefined' to the value that gets set there later, title property and all. It all happens so fast that you don't see this.

It's best to keep in mind that the render() function may run over and over again, and your JSX needs to be written in such a way that it accounts for the possible states you expect. Here, you can expect that initially your state for "item" does not have all the properties that it will have later.

You could instead write something like,

{this.state.item.title ? this.state.item.title.rendered : 'Loading...'}

Or whatever else you'd like to write there (or leave it blank, etc.). So you are first checking to see if title has a truthy value (not undefined), and if so, accessing the child's property. A common pattern is to use this form:

{this.state.item.title && (<h1>{this.state.item.title.rendered}</h1>)}

Here the difference is we are relying on JavaScript's return value for &&, which will be the second item's value. If the first item is falsy, it doesn't even look at the second part, so it doesn't complain.

Or, you may try to take a step back and track a separate variable in state for your loading process. Something like dataReady, which you would set to true once you receive the HTTP request back. Then, your render code looks a bit cleaner:

{this.state.dataReady && (
    <h1>{this.state.item.title.rendered}</h1>
    <h2>(some other stuff</h2>
)}

For more information, I recommend you read about conditional rendering.

posts.title: Focusing in on JavaScript's Filter, Map, and Reduce
posts.excerpt: Creating applications frequently involves lists, or collections of data that we want to present to a user. For instance, I spent years making websites for property management companies. Each site was a list of pages, created by a list of us
posts.content:
Creating applications frequently involves lists, or collections of data that we want to present to a user.

For instance, I spent years making websites for property management companies. Each site was a list of pages, created by a list of users, frequently showing a list of cities, each with a list of properties, with their own lists of amenities, available units, rental dates...and so on.

Coders typically start out learning simple loops, like "for" and "while", to process and manipulate these lists. But modern JavaScript provides several great functions that are more powerful. Once you understand them, they're easier, too.

Filter

When you filter a list, you are trying to eliminate items that you don't want.

[code language="javascript"] var myArray = [{ "id": "3401341", "category": "blue", ”¦ },{ "id": "3354541", "category": "red", ”¦ },{ "id": "4401341", "category": "blue", ”¦ }]; var resultArray = myArray.filter( function myCallback(item) { return item.category === 'blue'; });[/code]

So we've started with an array of 3 items, each with an id, a category, and some other properties not shown.

Filter hands each of these items in turn to the function you provide, and your function returns either true (keep this item) or false (chuck it).

More concisely, using ES6 syntax, we could write the filter line:

[code language="javascript"]const resultArray = myArray.filter( item => item.category === 'blue' );[/code]

That uses an arrow function for brevity, and the shortcut of automatically returning the single line's result. I've also switched it to const instead of var, since we don't want it to ever be reassigned to something else.

Map

When you use map on a list, you're transforming each element, but keeping all of them.

[code language="javascript"]var myArray = [{ "id": "3401341", "category": "blue", ”¦ },{ "id": "3354541", "category": "red", ”¦ },{ "id": "4401341", "category": "blue", ”¦ }]; var resultArray = myArray.map( function myCallback(item) { item.orderProcessed = true; return item; });[/code]

Similar to before, we have the same starting array and we write a callback function that gets used for every item in the list.

Here, we're adding an "orderProcessed" property to each item. I don't even know what this sample list is anymore. Apparently it's orders? Anyways...

Written more concisely, the last line could be:

[code language="javascript"]const resultArray = myArray.map( item => { return {”¦item,orderProcessed:true}; });[/code]

Here we're using the spread (...) operator, which just takes each of the properties of the object out. We shove them right back into a new object we're creating, along with the added orderProcessed property. If we accidentally wrote: return {item, orderProcessed:true} without the ..., then our final items would look like this:

[code language="javascript"]{ { "id": "3401341", "color": "blue", ”¦ }, "orderProcessed" : true }[/code]

So we don't want that nesting, we just want orderProcessed to be right alongside the other properties. The spread operator (...) strips the original properties out, and then we put them all back in together.

Reduce

My personal favorite is the hardest to understand. Reduce is confusing, but also the most powerful.

Reduce loops through each item in the array as well. But as it does so, it passes along a value. That value can be anything, even another array or object. Each item in the original array gets sent to the function you write, along with this pass-along object. It can add to the pass-along object, modify it, add itself to it, etc. When its turn is over, it hands off the pass-along object to the next item in the array.

Most basic examples of reduce are around pulling some combined value out of the objects. Like this:

[code language="javascript"] var myArray = [{ "id": "3401341", "category": "blue", "value": 3, ”¦ },{ "id": "3354541", "category": "red", "value": 2, ”¦ } ,{ "id": "4401341", "category": "blue", "value": 5 ”¦ }]; var result = myArray.reduce( function myCallback(accumulator,item) { return accumulator + item.value; }, 0);[/code]

This time our callback function gets 2 arguments, the accumulator (pass-along object), and then each item like before. There's also an easy-to-miss 2nd argument for the whole reduce function. See the 0 right at the end? That's the starting value for the pass-along object.

So now, our callback function's responsibility is to return the pass-along object. It can be a new one, the same one, a modified one, whatever.

The value of "result" above would be 10.

Deeper Reduce

That example's great and all. I use reduce functions like that. But I more commonly use them to combine map and filter functionalities into a single loop.

See, if I want to filter an array, but I'm not really interested in the original objects, I have to go through the array twice. First to filter out the unwanted items, then to process (or extract something from) the wanted items.

Here's an example. Using the above array, what if I want a list of all the ids with a category of blue?

I can first filter out the non-blues:

[code language="javascript"]const filteredArray = myArray.filter( item => item.category=== 'blue');[/code]

Then I can make a new array of just the id's:

[code language="javascript"]const filteredIds = filteredArray.map( item => item.id; );[/code]

This will give me an array like this:

[code language="javascript"]["3401341","3354541","4401341"][/code]

That's okay. But with an array of 1,000's of items, I've now looped through them twice (or most of them, at least).

Reduce can do this job better! We just use a pass-along object that is, itself, an array.

[code language="javascript"]const filteredIds = myArray.reduce( (accumulator, item) => { if ( item.category=== 'blue' ){ return [”¦accumulator, item.id]; } return accumulator; }, []);[/code]

Same resulting array!

We've given our reduce a starting, empty array ([]). Then this pass-along object gets sent to our function, along with each item in turn.

Our function asks, "Is this item's color blue?" If so, it adds its id to the pass-along object and then sends the pass-along object to the next item.

If not, it just sends the pass-along object it received, without adding its id to it.

Reduce can take two other arguments (for a total of 4). The third is the index of the current item, and the fourth is the array itself.

There's also a complentary reduceRight which just works the array over backwards.

Pure Functions and Reduce

I keep referring to the item as a "pass-along" object, because that helps conceptually understand what's happening. But a big caveat here is that it's not actually the same object passed along. In fact, it should be a new one each time if you need to modify it in any way.

In this example, we don't just do accumulator.push(item.id) and then return the modified accumulator. Unless we aren't changing it at all, we make a copy of the accumulator, and then pass that copy along. This is to keep our function "pure", meaning it's not changing anything outside of its own scope. If it changed the same accumulator it received, then it is affecting something it received.

Non-pure functions are a lot harder to debug and reason about, at least once you get used to writing them pure. Plus, reducer functions are supposed to be pure, so just do it that way to save yourself future headaches.

This makes the spread operator super useful, as it makes creating a copy of the accumulator trivial at each iteration.

JS Array Functions

Each of these functions is powerful when used appropriately. I said Reduce is my favorite, because it is the most powerful. But it's overkill if all you need to do is filter, or map, an array.

I've also seen some arguments that a typical for loop can be faster, so some of it depends on the scale you're working with. I tend to think of for loops as faster in one particular case: when you know you'll sometimes "exit early" out of the loop. All of the array functions I've discussed on this page run through the entire array every time. But a for loop, or a while loop, can be broken out of at will (i.e. "break;"). This can save some processing time if you're just looking for a particular value, for instance.

Reduce in particular is hard to understand. It's weird to get an "accumulator" along with your item. But once you get used to it, it's equally hard to go back to not using it. So, it's absolutely worth your time!

posts.title: Revisiting React, now with Hooks--and experience
posts.excerpt: I first learned React in 2015, when it had been out in the Open Source world for just a couple of years. My first experience was...rocky, to say the least. It was the first full JavaScript framework I learned, which itself requires a major
posts.content:
I first learned React in 2015, when it had been out in the Open Source world for just a couple of years. My first experience was...rocky, to say the least. It was the first full JavaScript framework I learned, which itself requires a major thought process shift. (Far more powerful, but far easier to make mistakes.) JSX was very off-putting to me, as well. It seemed like an additional burden, and I didn't really get the benefits. (I do now--JavaScript passing around DOM code like a native object? Cool!)

Plus, Redux was confusing. It felt like an advanced topic you had to learn while standing upside-down on your head. "The...reducers...are pure functions...that define and then redefine the state and are always run for any update...because..."

I made a few demos and small projects with it, but shifted to Angular for heavy client projects and eventually Vue for lighter client projects.

And yet Gutenberg is written in React, and a few small contributions I wanted to make required me to delve back into it. Plus, the top WordPress folks were advising that the future of WordPress required developers to be JavaScript experts. So, to React I returned.

Aside: What I wanted to contribute to Gutenberg

I had been advocating for a container block, along with many, many others, and when it came out in beta I found a few things a little clunky. I submitted a humble patch for the odd behavior of "single-child" blocks not having drag handles, which you wouldn't need in a top-level context--if it's the only block, where else can you drag it? But as it turns out, drag handles are necessary when it has a parent, because you might want to drag the child out of the parent.

My "big" change was from:

[code language="js"] if ( isLocked || ( isFirst && isLast ) ) { [/code]

to:

[code language="js"] if ( isLocked || ( isFirst && isLast && ! rootClientId ) ) { [/code]

Which is admittedly minor, but reflected a lot of research and trial and error. But I found I was so rusty with React that I needed a lot of hand-holding, and so I decided I would eventually need to dive back in to better understand it.

"We do a lot of React here at Losant"

In May, I accepted a new position with a really cool IoT platform called Losant. It was the final nail in the coffin for deciding to relearn React, because a lot of their client projects, I was told, were written with it. They were using the classic React + Redux paradigm, plus a lot of the newer features.

A whole new React with Hooks

So I jumped back in, determined to give React another chance. And I was surprised to find that, in the 3-4 years since I had last used React, it had changed a lot. Okay, maybe it's not an entirely new framework, and to be honest there's still a lot more that's the same. But I could simply not believe how much it had grown.

Hooks are, I think it's safe to say, a game-changer with React. When these new features were announced at React Conf 2018, they described their apt naming. Hooks were about giving developers access to features that were there all along, but that were previously tightly controlled under the hood.

Dan Abramov's presentation really does a fantastic job of highlighting these amazing new features:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dpw9EHDh2bM&t=685

In the small time I've been working with the very talented folks at Losant, I've seen some amazing things done with these hooks. It's amazing how useState, useEffect, and useContext in particular literally supercharge functional components.

A Great React Course

I've also had the opportunity of working with the more traditional React + Redux model, which I will say I am much more comfortable with after completing Stephen Grider's Modern React with Redux course, which has also been updated with (brief) introductions to the hooks. Stephen has a great way of predicting what questions will come into your head while you're learning (or re-learning) React.

A Revised Opinion

The changes to React in the last couple of years are amazing. With the addition of hooks, which really are a gamechanger, a lot of the complexities in mastering the framework are removed. My opinion on the framework is much, much brighter.

But to be honest, it was my own inexperience that colored my opinion of it in the first place.

It's probably not fair to judge a framework you don't fully understand. With a few more years of web development experience, and a great deal of more hands-on experience with the framework in particular, I now look on React with different eyes.

I enjoy developing with it, and am more than excited that it has such a bright future, with web applications, WordPress, and beyond.

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: PHP code in page template vs functions
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [PHP code in page template vs functions](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/308372) * * * ## My answer: In spite of no 'official' answers, this question is still rather popular, so a year later I will post my solidif
posts.content:
Original question: PHP code in page template vs functions

My answer:

In spite of no 'official' answers, this question is still rather popular, so a year later I will post my solidified thoughts on this.

What led to this question is the experience of code working in some places, and not in others. For instance, why was I having to wrap code within a function in functions.php instead of just putting it there loosely, while I was able to keep it loose in a template file? It felt as if there was some fundamental difference in how WordPress treats the code in different places.

But of course, that's not accurate. PHP is PHP, and WordPress is just chugging along merrily on its way, line by line.

The main difference, as I wrote in my original question and as Krzysiek and others affirmed, is the loading order. But the loading order in WordPress is everything.

A theme's functions.php is loaded, relatively speaking, very early on. It's still very much in a preparatory phase. WordPress's key functions are ready, such as add_action(), as are plugins and globals. But it's not ready for you to start doing things yet. The page output isn't being written yet, the main loop isn't running, etc.

So if you put a loose line of code to do something "now" in functions.php, it's probably too early. Instead, the loose lines of code here should be preparatory in nature, i.e. "Do this later," or "Here's a constant for later," or, as the name of the file suggests, "Here's a function to run later."

Template files, on the other hand, are run relatively late. WordPress is so far along in the process of loading that it has enough information to choose the correct template file for the user's request. Almost any loose code makes sense here, because we're nearing the end of the cycle. Everything else is set up and we're already building our output.

With all this in mind, things start to come into focus. Why does a syntax error in functions.php cause a white screen of death, but a syntax error in a template file just break the page halfway through? Because functions.php is running before any output, so an error breaks things before there's anything to show, but a template file could be halfway through output.

So it does come down to sequence, but in a more profound way than I originally thought.

p.s. What has helped me understand this better over the last year are (a) a better understanding of the loading order gained from stepping through the loading sequence with xDebug, literally watching how things unfold, and (b) a deeper understanding of hooks. Since loading order is so important in WordPress, the hooks system is critical. It's like time travel for your code.

posts.title: The Right Perspective for Contributing to WordPress
posts.excerpt: ## Who is "they"? I've been using WordPress for 8 years, and developing custom themes and plugins for 3. In that time I've come to greatly appreciate the versatility and growth of the platform, which is not only being updated but evolving.
posts.content:
Who is "they"?

I've been using WordPress for 8 years, and developing custom themes and plugins for 3. In that time I've come to greatly appreciate the versatility and growth of the platform, which is not only being updated but evolving. When I deliver a WordPress-based project to a client, we talk about how to make changes to their site and the importance of keeping their site up to date. I found myself referring to an ambiguous "they" in these discussions; i.e. "they release frequent security patches" or "they are encouraging the best practice of X here." But who is the they? I've known for years that it was an open source community of volunteers, but it wasn't until recently that I grew determined to overcome the hurdles and actually contribute.

The main hurdle is self-inflicted

The hurdles are more process and social oriented than technical. In fact you can contribute to WordPress without writing a single line of code. But in spite of the extensive contributing handbook and guides, learning the ropes still takes time. It's easy to make a faux pas by, say, making a joke in the wrong Slack channel (which I've *cough* never done). The first time I tried to contribute was by suggesting a fix for a very old (8+ years) annoyance that the current version number is not shown when WordPress suggests an update to X.XX version. I thought this would be a simple, good first bug. But the process went like this:

  1. Research issue
  2. Create a ticket
  3. Find out a ticket already existed and that mine was being merged into it
  4. See past potential solutions and that the issue is quite old
  5. Write a proposed code change
  6. Attend a meeting on Slack and try to get some attention for the issue
  7. Be told it would be reviewed but that unless it captured the interest of one of the core maintainers it wouldnt be touched.
  8. Try to get it more attention, but grow frustrated that it didn't seem important to others

Those last items, which were told directly to me, were honest but discouraging. What was the point of trying to help if my work would sit on the shelf growing dusty? It led me to stop trying to contribute for a year, and I do still see it as a entry barrier. But while it's frustrating from the perspective of, "how can I get this particular issue fixed," it makes sense from the perspective of the WordPress project as a whole. What gets changed should be partially determined by a stable group of dedicated people. If you can't make a good and broad enough case that what you want to see changed should get changed in the way you want, then it's not worth it for "all of WordPress" to change in that way.

The better perspective

Instead of, "how can I get the WordPress community to change X," I'd suggest the stereotypical question reversal: "what does the WordPress contributing team need from me?" In other words, what work that already has the attention and support of the decision makers can I help with? Contributing to WordPress isn't about getting your pet issue fixed. It's about helping make the software you use better for everyone. When you view it that way, the major hurdle of trying to wedge yourself into the mix disappears. You're filling a gap, and there's no need to push yourself in. You're needed. The new steps, nearly a year after I first attempted to "contribute," were far more successful.

  1. Check out the tickets marked for the next release, and choose one that still needed testing
  2. Research the issue and try to replicate and/or solve it
  3. Post my results on the issue

That's it. Contributed. And since my results were enough to lead to discovering a new but related bug, I had my next way to contribute. I created a new ticket for it, did more research, and kept following the trail. Since the new bug I discovered was related to a feature being rolled out, it got attention on its own merits. I didn't have to try to fight for attention. Instead, I watched the ticket for any discussion, asked for feedback, and got assistance in helping steer it through the development cycle. After two weeks, I had written a fix (actually 2) for the bug as well as a unit test (again, 2 versions), and the change had been discussed, approved, and committed. It felt like a real contribution. It was. I'm still learning some of the best ways to "grease the wheels", but I'm not trying to steer the cart anymore. Already I've made connections, and more importantly, been able to make a real contribution by applying my skills of research, debugging and troubleshooting potential solutions. It wasn't my 'pet issue' that got fixed, but it was a real one, and it was one that I was able to resolve for every user of WordPress everywhere. Each of those millions of sites will have 4 lines of my code. That feels awesome.

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: Problem adding sidebar to Underscores theme
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Problem adding sidebar to Underscores theme](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/334684) * * * ## My answer: Template files are _included_, not called like a function. Even though you called `get_sidebar()`, behind t
posts.content:
Original question: Problem adding sidebar to Underscores theme

My answer:

Template files are included, not called like a function. Even though you called get_sidebar(), behind the scenes that is eventually calling include. So in other words, your template pages (like footer.php, page.php, and sidebar.php) are not directly within a function, so you cannot 'return' out of them, as you are attempting to do in sidebar.php.

So WordPress is progressing past that point, and then running dynamic_sidebar( 'sidebar-1' );. Now here's where someone else will have to jump in and tell you why it's loading the wrong widgets. I didn't think it would fallback to an active sidebar, but at least based on your code it seems to be. WordPress definitely does that with menus unless you specifically tell it not to.

But in any case, I think if you just modify your code you'll avoid the behavior entirely:

if ( is_active_sidebar( 'sidebar-1' ) ) :
?>

<aside id="secondary" class="widget-area">
    <?php dynamic_sidebar( 'sidebar-1' ); ?>
</aside><!-- #secondary -->

<?php endif; ?>

So all I did is use flip the check (removing the !) and then wrap the entire dynamic_sidebar section with it (using the alternate PHP format of : and endif;)

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: remove slider mobile not via css
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [remove slider mobile not via css](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/333714) * * * ## My answer: This is one of those problems that seems like it should have a simple solution, but really doesn't. There are options,
posts.content:
Original question: remove slider mobile not via css

My answer:

This is one of those problems that seems like it should have a simple solution, but really doesn't. There are options, they're just not easy.

At least, from what I can see.

CSS is the best approach to detecting browser width IMO. In fact, you really can't detect browser width from PHP. You can with JavaScript but that's where the complexities come in.

Even if you could detect browser width in PHP, you wouldn't want to. What if they made their browser bigger (i.e. rotated their device)? PHP is gone by that point, and can't add it back anymore.

There is a clever technique I read about where you use the new HTML5 image srcset to still serve an image at mobile resolution, but a very small one. However since you're using a slider, which I presume means a plug-in, you probably don't have that flexibility.

That leaves you with JavaScript. You could remove the images if the browser width is small, but you'd need to keep watching the viewport width in case it changed, and be ready to put them back. Probably better, only load them when needed (i.e. lazy load). It's possible your slider, or an alternative, would just natively give you that functionality.

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: How to make an embeded a Youtube video from custom field text responsive to screen size?
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [How to make an embeded a Youtube video from custom field text responsive to screen size?](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/333448) * * * ## My answer: Welcome to WordPress StackExchange. This is really an HTML/CSS
posts.content:
Original question: How to make an embeded a Youtube video from custom field text responsive to screen size?

My answer:

Welcome to WordPress StackExchange.

This is really an HTML/CSS question rather than a WordPress specific one, so you will have better luck getting a quick answer in the future by posting to another StackExchange site, such as Stack Overflow.

However, your issue should be fixed if you set a percent as the width, rather than hard coding in a value like the 500 shown in your snippet.

For instance,

<iframe width="100%" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/yHfLyMAHrQE" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture" allowfullscreen></iframe>

Result: https://jsfiddle.net/qj6o4t23/

However, that will always fill 100% wide, so a better approach might be to have a max-width on it as well, which would mean using CSS rules instead of HTML attributes.

<iframe style="width:100%; max-width: 500px; height: 315px" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/yHfLyMAHrQE" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture" allowfullscreen></iframe>

Result: https://jsfiddle.net/qj6o4t23/1/

With multiple rules like this, you're better off following the best practice of defining the styles in a CSS separately.

posts.title: Sanitizing inputs and escaping outputs: it's not just about security
posts.excerpt: WordPress, now representing 33%+ of the top websites in the world, is a constant target for hackers and other malicious folk. The WordPress community does a great job of pushing updates to the core code, and even taking proactive steps to p
posts.content:
WordPress, now representing 33%+ of the top websites in the world, is a constant target for hackers and other malicious folk. The WordPress community does a great job of pushing updates to the core code, and even taking proactive steps to push its users towards safer server practices. But security in WordPress is only as strong as your site's weakest link. If a theme or plugin creates a vulnerability, and a bad guy is able to exploit it, chances are your entire site will be compromised.

But sanitation and escaping are not only about preventing attacks. More on that later.

I have been refocusing myself on applying recommended WordPress best practices for dealing with "untrusted" data. Let's first review the basics:

Sanitizing input

Sanitizing data is about cleaning data before we accept it. Whenever we accept input, we have to be careful that it is sanitized. This means the content we are accepting will not mess up our existing data or open up a security hole. After all, we're allowing something in through the perimeter of our security.

https://xkcd.com/327/

Sanitizing our inputs means that the data will first be filtered to prevent unwanted elements, such as injection attacks that intentionally misuse our database. WordPress provides a bunch of great, built-in sanitation functions. Among the simplest to use are:

  • sanitize_email()
  • sanitize_file_name()
  • sanitize_html_class()
  • sanitize_key()
  • sanitize_meta()
  • sanitize_mime_type()
  • sanitize_option()
  • sanitize_sql_orderby()
  • sanitize_text_field()
  • sanitize_textarea_field()
  • sanitize_title()
  • sanitize_title_for_query()
  • sanitize_title_with_dashes()
  • sanitize_user()

(We can also use a few heavier functions, such as wp_kses, to control input. WP_KSES filters out specific unwanted HTML elements, so it's really less focused on safeguarding our database and more about looking ahead to when it will be output again. It tends to happen before hand though, since it's so expensive a process to run and we'd rather just do it once prior to saving it. Which leads us to...)

Escaping output

Whereas sanitizing takes place before we accept data, escaping takes place when we use it. We have to escape all untrusted data in our themes, plugins, and other code. Data is not trusted when you can't completely account for its origin, such as user input, translation files, and even the WordPress database. (Another plugin might have an unpatched security hole, for instance.)

Escaping again filters out certain elements that can interfere and cause problems. This includes certain attacks that take place on the front end of a site, such as session hijacking of our users. Escaping is best done right at the point of output, so you can more easily tell if data has already been escaped or not (double escaping can mess up your data). As with sanitation, we have some great escaping functions:

  • esc_html() 
  • esc_url() 
  • esc_js() 
  • esc_attr() 
  • esc_textarea()

 

And, there are even combination functions that combine some of these with the translation functions.

For instance, if we have this code pulling data from an Advanced Custom Field and that data has an apostrophe in it, we're in for some trouble:

[code language="php"]$title = get_field( 'element_title' ); //Mary's Recipe echo "";[/code]

But if we just add the proper escaping function, we're all set!

[code language="php"]$title = esc_attr( get_field( 'element_title' ) ); //Mary's Recipe echo "";[/code]

It's not all about security

That last example brings up an important point. I had been implementing the above elements for a long time under the impression that it was all about security. Get off my site! and all that. But one day it occurred to me that I didn't understand something.

You see, many of WordPress' built-in functions are pre-escaped; the_title, for instance. But digging through the code, I noticed the_content() isn't. I thought I must be missing it, but I wasn't. the_content() isn't escaped.

Surely WordPress wasn't being hypocritical, telling me to escape "all the things" but leaving escaping out of arguably its most important output function. Worse, I couldn't easily escape it without resorting to wp_kses, which is a resource expensive function.

It led me to ask this question on WordPress Stack Exchange, which I phrased as, "Why escape if the_content isn't?" I wanted to know why the rest of my output should be escaped if WordPress' own function wasn't. Once a hacker exploited something (say, an XSS attack), would it matter that my other code was safe? They'd be in the perimeter and could unlock the front door It didn't seem safe to me.

There was a great discussion in several great answers to my question, and the gist of it is that it's not all about security. It's about data conforming to our expectations. Data being used in an attribute should not break attributes. Data being used as a URL should work like a URL.

It reminds me a little of setting field restrictions for users, something I do often for custom fields. "This must be a number between 0 and 100, because I'm using it as a percentage, and I don't want you to break the code I'm writing for you." With escaping, I get to say things like, "This must not contain something that behaves like an HTML tag, and if you do, I'mma gonna take it out."

Doing this is helpful from a security standpoint, but it is not the one-and-only defense. It's a piece of the security puzzle, but it's also about writing more robust, reliable code.

And, as some users pointed out, there are also several situations when a malicious user may have access to some things (like a translation file) but not all things (like the posts table).

And it's not hard, anyways

WordPress makes sanitizing and escaping easy. It makes code dealing with un-trusted input safer and more reliable. Sanitizing and escaping becomes a habit, and when you look at code that isn't processed correctly, it just starts to look wrong, like code that isn't indented. It just matters a whole lot more than that.

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: Why is an action callback function from an instance of a class always invoking the same function from an instance?
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Why is an action callback function from an instance of a class always invoking the same function from an instance?](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/333166) * * * ## My answer: It's possible I'm misunderstanding y
posts.content:
Original question: Why is an action callback function from an instance of a class always invoking the same function from an instance?

My answer:

It's possible I'm misunderstanding your question, but the way it is written it seems as though every instance of your FilterBuilder class will always get called.

Each instance of your class has in its constructor:

add_action('wp_ajax_myfilter', array($this, 'filter_function'));

(as well as the non-logged-in-user version)

There is no conditional here telling it when to run based on which "content type" or class instance you have. WordPress is literally being told, "Every time you get an ajax request for 'myfilter', run this instance's filter_function function." And since there are 2 instances in your example, and thus 2 constructors, WordPress is being told that twice (once for each).

WP AJAX functions are generally written to return data and die. (Grim maybe, but true :) So if your's is written as such, only the first registered action will run.

So, in short, it is true that each of your registered hooks is tied to its respective object ($this), and that their similar names is not a hindrance. However, you haven't given WordPress or your AJAX workflow anything to know which instance it should load.

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: How to Parse an Array of Elements in Gutenberg Block
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [How to Parse an Array of Elements in Gutenberg Block](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/333016) * * * ## My answer: When you set the attribute's source to children, it gives you DOM elements, i.e. including the wra
posts.content:
Original question: How to Parse an Array of Elements in Gutenberg Block

My answer:

When you set the attribute's source to children, it gives you DOM elements, i.e. including the wrapping HTML and not just the inner text.

So the behavior you're seeing, which you probably already know, is the HTML elements getting nested inside of themselves. You're wrapping the contents in <li>, which gets wrapped in <li>, which could get wrapped in <li> again, and so on.

That part I'm pretty sure about. The solution below is my understanding of how to do it, but having not yet done this type of attribute selector, I haven't fully tested this. That being said, I think what you are looking for is closer to:

attributes: {
  tabs: { 
    type: 'array',
    source: 'query',
    selector: 'ul.tabs',
    default: [],
    query: {
      val: {
        type: 'string',
        selector: 'li',
        source: 'text',
    },
  }
}

So we're creating an array of objects with one property, which comes from each children's text. Then in your save function, you have to specifically pull that new val property we just specified as coming from the inner text of the li selector:

save({attributes, className}) {
  const { tabs, newTab, content } = attributes;

  return (
    <div className={className}>
      <span className="data-drop" newtab={newTab}></span>
      <ul className="tabs">
      {tabs.map(tab => {
            return <li className="tab">{tab.val}</li>;
        })}
      </ul>          
    </div>
  );
}

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: Deleling wordpress posts permanently still have IDs
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Deleling wordpress posts permanently still have IDs](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/333023) * * * ## My answer: Even if you find a way to reset the post and pretend it didn't happen, you **shouldn't**. WordPress
posts.content:
Original question: Deleling wordpress posts permanently still have IDs

My answer:

Even if you find a way to reset the post and pretend it didn't happen, you shouldn't.

WordPress uses a relational database structure. In short, a bunch of different tables in the database point to and rely on each other. The ID value of each row, such as the post ID for posts, is particularly important for linking different rows in different tables.

For instance, the "posts" table stores basic information about each post, including the post ID. The "post_meta" table stores additional information about posts, linked to that post ID. The "comments" table stores comments, also cross-referenced to those post IDs. The list goes on and on.

Even within that same table ("posts"), other entries such as revisions refer back to the original post ID!

So as you can see, it's a complicated web of relationships. If WordPress was designed to go back and scrub all of these links when you trash a post, then I suppose it would work. It would still be confusing and a bad user experience, like how @Loren Rosen mentioned, which is one reason WordPress doesn't do it that way.

But the fact is, WordPress will not do all that for you when you trash a post. Some of the data is, I believe, removed when the post is permanently deleted. But a lot of those other records would be not just broken, but wrong.

So in summary, it's not a good idea. The post IDs are usually hidden from users, unless you aren't using permalinks, so what exactly are you trying to accomplish?

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: Show post updated date instead of published
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Show post updated date instead of published](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/332781) * * * ## My answer: get\_the\_modified\_date should do what you're looking for. I am guessing that perhaps you are struggling a
posts.content:
Original question: Show post updated date instead of published

My answer:

get_the_modified_date should do what you're looking for. I am guessing that perhaps you are struggling a bit with the sprintf syntax.

 $date = sprintf( '<span>' . __( 'Posted', 'theme' ) . ' <a href="%3$s"><time class="entry-date" datetime="%1$s">%2$s</time></a></span>',
    esc_attr( get_the_date( 'c' ) ),
    esc_html( time_ago() ),
    esc_html( get_day_link( get_the_date('Y'), get_the_date('m'), get_the_date('d') ) )
  );

Let's break it down:

sprintf argument 1 - the string with placeholders

sprintf( '<span>' . __( 'Posted', 'theme' ) . ' <a href="%3$s"><time class="entry-date" datetime="%1$s">%2$s</time></a></span>',

This is the main string that will be built. It has 3 placeholders. However, they are in a non-traditional order.

  1. The link (<a href=%3$s) has a placeholder for variable #3, a string.
  2. The datetime attribute (datetime=%1$s), which is part of the HTML time element that makes the time machine-readable (useful for advanced features, and if the time element contains more than just the actual time), has a placeholder for variable #1, a string.
  3. And finally the displayed time (>%2$s</time>) is looking for variable #2, a string.

sprintf arguments 2,3, and 4 - the values

Those 3 variables are provided in the following function arguments (again, not in the order they are used):

esc_attr( get_the_date( 'c' ) ),
esc_html( time_ago() ),
esc_html( get_day_link( get_the_date('Y'), get_the_date('m'), get_the_date('d') ) )

The first, which is feeding into that datetime= attribute, is getting the post's published date and outputting it in the 'c' format, which is a standard date format that looks like 20019-03-27T15:19:21+00:00.

The second, which is the displayed time, is referencing a function I don't recognized, called time_ago().

The third, which is being used for the link href=, is generating the link based off of the post's published date.

So, to properly change the date and still use that function, we should adjust all 3 parameters.

$date = sprintf( '<span>' . __( 'Posted', 'theme' ) . ' <a href="%3$s"><time class="entry-date" datetime="%1$s">%2$s</time></a></span>',
    esc_attr( get_the_modified_date( 'c' ) ),
    esc_html( get_the_modified_date(),
    esc_url( get_day_link( get_the_modified_date('Y'), get_the_modified_date('m'), get_the_modified_date('d') ) )
  );

Note I changed the 3rd parameter to esc_url since it is a URL that is being generated, and that the display of the output date can be adjusted by passing in PHP date formatting options, such as get_the_modified_date( 'm-d-Y' )

Finally, all of this is getting stored in your $date variable as HTML, so make sure to actually echo it to the page before you're done.

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: How publish post from pending status
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [How publish post from pending status](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/332785) * * * ## My answer: When WordPress gives you errors such as that the post needs an author and permalink, it is best to figure out a wa
posts.content:
Original question: How publish post from pending status

My answer:

When WordPress gives you errors such as that the post needs an author and permalink, it is best to figure out a way to provide these. Otherwise you are asking for trouble further down the line. You might find a way to force it, but it would be an uphill battle. WordPress is like a spiderweb of connections, and you would be severing several strands.

Your question sounds like it might be better directed at the creators of User Frontend Pro, as they are the ones who will be familiar with how the posts are being created and how that result is intended to fit into a workflow.

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: Write to / remove from default .htaccess file from plugin?
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Write to / remove from default .htaccess file from plugin?](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/332675) * * * ## My answer: Almost all of your code is correct. I didn't even know about the insert\_with\_markers funct
posts.content:
Original question: Write to / remove from default .htaccess file from plugin?

My answer:

Almost all of your code is correct. I didn't even know about the insert_with_markers function, and now I do, so thank you.

In return, I believe I have your solution.

get_home_path() is not defined when any of the hooks (init,wp, etc.) you mentioned are triggered. That function is defined in the admin-side "file.php", which as part of the admin dashboard side of things, has not yet loaded.

The hook admin_init, however, should serve you well, presuming you are making those .htaccess changes on the admin side. If not, you could either include wp-admin/includes/file.php manually, or use an alternate way of finding .htaccess, such as the constant ABSPATH (although they are not equivalent).

Using the admin_init hook on the first function you provided, I found the rules written to my .htaccess file the next time I loaded a page on the admin side.

By the way, you might want to do a check for current_user_can( 'edit_files' ) before allowing that code to run.

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: Why escape if the_content isnt?
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Why escape if the\_content isnt?](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/332740) * * * ## My answer: The built in function `the_content` runs through several filters, but does not escape output. It would be difficult fo
posts.content:
Original question: Why escape if the_content isnt?

My answer:

The built in function the_content runs through several filters, but does not escape output. It would be difficult for it to do so, as HTML and even some scripts must be allowed through.

When outputting, the_content seems to run through these filters (as of 5.0):

add_filter( 'the_content', 'do_blocks', 9 );
add_filter( 'the_content', 'wptexturize' );
add_filter( 'the_content', 'convert_smilies', 20 );
add_filter( 'the_content', 'wpautop' );
add_filter( 'the_content', 'shortcode_unautop' );
add_filter( 'the_content', 'prepend_attachment' );
add_filter( 'the_content', 'wp_make_content_images_responsive' );

(and)

add_filter( 'the_content', 'capital_P_dangit' );
add_filter( 'the_content', 'do_shortcode' );

It also does a simple string replace:

$content = str_replace( ']]>', ']]>', $content );

And then get_the_content does a tiny bit of processing related to the "more" link and a bug with foreign languages.

None of those prevent XSS script injection, right?

When saving, the data is sanitized through wp_kses_post. But as this is an expensive process, I understand why it's not used on output.

The rule of thumb for WordPress escaping is that everything needs to be escaped, regardless of input sanitation, and as lately as possible. I've read several articles saying this, because the database is not to be considered a trusted source.

But for the reasons above, the_content doesn't follow that. Nor do the core themes (i.e. TwentyNineteen) add additional escaping on output.

So...why is it helping anything to escape elsewhere? If I were a hacker with access to the database, wouldn't I just add my code to a post's content?
