TL;DR remove those images from your site.

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: Adding HTML to the end of every post with the Block Editor
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Adding HTML to the end of every post with the Block Editor](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/328018) * * * ## My answer: So from a WordPress conceptual point of view, I like the idea of it being a block better. Wi
posts.content:
Original question: Adding HTML to the end of every post with the Block Editor

My answer:

So from a WordPress conceptual point of view, I like the idea of it being a block better. Without it being a block you have some of a post's content in the database, and some being injected here. It sounds fine for this case but would be prone to cause you headaches later down if some of your requirements changed.

That being said, I think you could do this just by looking for the last html tag in the_content and injecting your icon's HTML in front of it. So it's a little more complicated than just appending it like you were.

To show the concept:

$text = "<div><p><div>text</div></p><p>text 2</p></div>";

//Find the position in the string of the last closing HTML tag, i.e. </ 
$last_tag = strrpos( $text, "</" );

//Insert your HTML at that position, with an extra argument of 0 indicating you don't want to replace any of the original, just insert
echo substr_replace( $text, '<span class="icon"></span>', $last_tag, 0 );

//Results in <div><p><div>text</div></p><p>text 2</p><span class="icon"></span></div>

In your case the $text variable would instead be passed into the function:

// Add Signature Image at End of Posts
add_filter('the_content','td_add_signature', 1);
function td_add_signature($text) {
  global $post;
  if(($post->post_type == 'post')) {
      $last_tag = strrpos( $text, "</" );
      $text = substr_replace( $text, '<span class="icon"></span>', $last_tag, 0 );
  }
  return $text;
}

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: Group posts by custom field
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Group posts by custom field](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/327830) * * * ## My answer: You're close. You have: ``` foreach (get_child_pages(wp_get_post_parent_id(get_the_ID())) as $s) { echo ' ID) . '">' . get_
posts.content:
Original question: Group posts by custom field

My answer:

You're close. You have:

foreach (get_child_pages(wp_get_post_parent_id(get_the_ID())) as $s) {
  echo '<li><a href="' . get_the_permalink($s->ID) . '">' . get_the_title($s->ID) . '</a></li>';
}

We need to add a layer above that to show the two lists. However we can't assume that the posts of one type will all come out together (i.e. all of one category, then all of the next). That means we can't just spit it all out in the order it comes in.

Here's a way utilizing a holding object to first group the posts by their value of that field:

//this will hold the post IDs sorted by outer groups
$list_groups = array(); 

foreach (get_child_pages(wp_get_post_parent_id(get_the_ID())) as $s) {

    //get the category of this post
    $list_category = get_post_meta( $s->ID, "type", true );

    //if this is the first post of that category, initialize the array
    if ( ! isset( $list_groups[ $list_category ] ) ){
        $list_groups[ $list_category ] = array();
    }

    //add this post ID to that category in our holding array
    $list_groups[ $list_category ][] = $s->ID;

}

//at this point we have an array ($list_groups) that has an inner array of post IDs for each category

foreach ( $list_groups as $category_name => $category_posts ){

    echo "<div class='category-group'><h2>$category_name</h2><ul>";

    foreach ( $category_posts as $category_post_id ){

        $p_permalink = get_the_permalink( $category_post_id );
        $p_title = get_the_title( $category_post_id );

        echo "<li><a href='$p_permalink'>$p_title</a></li>";

    }

    echo "</ul></div>";

}

So what we've done is first created a holding array that ends up looking like this:

$list_groups
---Product
   ---10
   ---15
   ---33
---About
   ---5
   ---12
   ---55

It's just an array holding arrays for each type, and in those arrays are the IDs of the posts that belong there.

Then we loop through that holding array and spit them out by category.

Sidenote: your wp_query looks to be limiting the results to just one of the two categories. I could be misreading that but if you only get one category out check it.

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: How to align full div
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [How to align full div](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/326169) * * * ## My answer: The main issue you are running into is that you are targeting the wrong element. The parent of .un-post-scoller is what has a lim
posts.content:
Original question: How to align full div

My answer:

The main issue you are running into is that you are targeting the wrong element. The parent of .un-post-scoller is what has a limited width aligned to the left, so you won't escape that easily.

Instead, target its parent. Unfortunately there is not a particularly clean candidate here since the parent is a generic grid system class (col-md-5). Usually you want to use the grid system's class to move things over -- in the case of Bootstrap, that would be offset-md-7 (or slightly different depending on your version and which grid system you use).

That requires modifying the actual HTML. Since you asked specifically for how to do it with CSS, you might try something like:

.header-overlay-scroller .col-md-5 {
    float: right;
}

The header-overlay-scroller is just there so that not all .col-md-5 classes are targeted.

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: Blogs got Deleted automatically
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Blogs got Deleted automatically](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/326059) * * * ## My answer: I assume you mean blog _posts_ and not blogs which usually refers to all posts together. Anyways, it sounds like a data
posts.content:
Original question: Blogs got Deleted automatically

My answer:

I assume you mean blog posts and not blogs which usually refers to all posts together.

Anyways, it sounds like a database issue, not a WordPress issue. WordPress will not automatically delete posts.

You either have some bad acting code on your site (like a plugin that's doing far too much), or much more likely, your site's database (or the posts table) was restored to an earlier date or emptied entirely.

Since you are still able to log in, we can rule out that your database is gone or that the entire database is reset. It may still be the wp_posts table which holds your posts.

You should restore your most recent database backup and go from there. If you are not making database/site backups, you (a) need to start and (b) should contact your host, because many (most?) web hosts make automatic backups and may be able to retrieve a recent one for you.

Do that today -- time is of the essence -- because generally automatic backups are only kept for a limited amount of time.

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: Setup a multisite to a running website
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Setup a multisite to a running website](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/325930) * * * ## My answer: > I enabled the multisite network on my main website ([http://example.com](http://example.com)) added subdomain
posts.content:
Original question: Setup a multisite to a running website

My answer:

I enabled the multisite network on my main website (http://example.com) added subdomain (http://pt.example.com) pointing to another directory. I got confused after this step. I installed a new wordpress on this directory with new database

A multisite WordPress installation shares a single copy of the WordPress files, and a single database. Each site within the network gets a separate set of tables in the database, but it's the same WordPress installation.

You should not create a separate folder and reinstall WordPress as you did. You should create the new "site" on the main WordPress installation and configure it (as it sounds like you did), then point your DNS for the subdomain to the same host (or virtual host) as your main WordPress installation.

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: Custom Archive Template for Multiple Categories
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Custom Archive Template for Multiple Categories](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/326012) * * * ## My answer: The simplest way I can think of would be to have the two categories you want to display together groupe
posts.content:
Original question: Custom Archive Template for Multiple Categories

My answer:

The simplest way I can think of would be to have the two categories you want to display together grouped under a parent category.

Parent Category
|----Child Category A
|----Child Category B

The file category-parent-category.php would by default show posts from both. The file category-child-category-a.php would only show from a. The file category-child-category-b.php would only show from b. The file category.php would show from all categories.

Would that do what you want?

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: Set og:image programmatically in custom single post with external images
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Set og:image programmatically in custom single post with external images](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/325449) * * * ## My answer: You could eventually get what you said to happen but it wouldn't **work** reli
posts.content:
Original question: Set og:image programmatically in custom single post with external images

My answer:

You could eventually get what you said to happen but it wouldn't work reliably.

In other words, you could replace the tag in the header with one of your images. But by that point most scrapers (social media scrapers, and anything interested in og: tags) will have already come and gone.

So, you have to replace it before those tags get written. The good news is you can! You just have to do with PHP instead of with AJAX. The bad news is it can quickly grow complex.

So, before WordPress has written the section, you need to have already fetched your first image URL with PHP and told WordPress you would like to add something there -- your og: meta tag. Whatever you were loading with AJAX (a list of image URLs filtered by a parameter?) you'll replicate with PHP -- just whatever you need to get that first image URL. Then you write it to the header.

For example, assuming a remote source that returns a JSON array of images might look like this:

function so325454_add_meta_tag(){

    $images = file_get_contents('...');
    if ( !$images ){ return; } //in case file fails

    $list_of_images = @json_decode( $images );
    if ( is_null( $list_of_images ) 
    || !is_array( $list_of_images ) 
    || count( $list_of_images ) < 1 ){ return; } //no content or bad JSON or empty array

    $image = $list_of_images[0]; 
    echo "<meta property='og:image' content='$image' />";
}
add_action( 'wp_head', 'so325454_add_meta_tag' );

Sadly you may have to be cautious of other plugins writing og tags, even the same og tags. In other words writing your tag there isn't stopping any others.

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: How to use innerHeight for div on both window load & resize?
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [How to use innerHeight for div on both window load & resize?](http://StackOverflow.com/q/54168155) * * * ## My answer: It's a little unclear exactly how you want the items aligned, but based on what you said it seems
posts.content:
Original question: How to use innerHeight for div on both window load & resize?

My answer:

It's a little unclear exactly how you want the items aligned, but based on what you said it seems like you want the .content and the .character to be vertically center aligned with each other.

In your snippet you have both of them absolutely positioned. If that's the way you want to go, you can just ignore their margins and JavaScript in general with this little vertical centering trick applied to both:

top: 50%;
transform: translateY( -50% );

The first line says "Put the top of this element 50% of the way down the element that it's positioned based on." Since it goes by the top, the second line says "Scoot me back up 50% of my height." That's just the way those CSS properties work -- the "top" % is about its parent, and the translateY % is about itself.

Since both of your elements would be vertically centered in their parent, they'd be aligned.

https://jsfiddle.net/qowxezpy/

HOWEVER if you don't need the elements to overlap like they do in this example (which I think looks nice and modern) there's a much easier way, using flex.

The parent would get:

display: flex;
align-items: center;

And the two children get:

flex-basis: 50%; //just to give them some width, since one is empty

posts.title: Wordpress Answer: Correct way to make static pages editable in wordpress
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Correct way to make static pages editable in wordpress](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/324865) * * * ## My answer: This is a little bit of a "finding the right balance" kind of question. You are struggling with
posts.content:
Original question: Correct way to make static pages editable in wordpress

My answer:

This is a little bit of a "finding the right balance" kind of question. You are struggling with the balance that all custom theme developers must work with.

At the one end of the spectrum your content area just spits out the_content() and all of the content formatting and control is up to the user (or you, on the backend, if you are doing it for them). You put a ton of burden on the little WYSIWYG editor in WordPress (TinyMCE).

At the other end is keeping the content area HTML in your template and just letting them put in specific pieces of information on the editor.

From your question, I think you are maybe missing just that last bit. How do you let them put in the content while controlling the HTML in the page template?

There's no single right answer, but a lot of developers use post meta data to do it. So if you're doing a "Meet the Staff" page with name, title, photo, and a short bio for all of the staff members, you'd set up specific custom meta fields to track just those pieces of data.

Then, in your page template, you inject that meta data into the right places within your HTML structure, using PHP to create loops (i.e. you repeat the HTML for each staff member).

There are some extremely helpful plugins to do that approach. Advanced Custom Fields is maybe the most common -- you define which fields go where, and accessing them on your page template is as easy as get_field('____'). The PRO version is the best deal in WordPress - $100 for all your sites, for life.

In our example, we'd create a field group that looks like this:

  • Staff Member (Repeater Field)
    • Name (Text field)
    • Title (Text field)
    • Photo (Photo field, set to return ID)
    • Bio (Textarea field)

(Field group assigned to pages that have the template, "Meet the Team".)

When editing the meet the team page, you'd see those 4 fields, and since it's a repeater you can duplicate them as many times as you want.

In your page template file (i.e. page-meet-the-team.php), you'd loop through that data.

//do we have any staff members?
if ( have_rows( 'staff_member' ) ):

    //loop through each staff member
    while ( have_rows( 'staff_member' ) ) : the_row();

        //pull the fields for each iteration of the loop
        $staff_name = get_sub_field( 'name' );
        $staff_title = get_sub_field( 'title' );
        $staff_photo_id = get_sub_field( 'photo' );
        $staff_bio = get_sub_field( 'bio' );

        //set up the photo if it was set
        $staff_photo = $staff_photo_id ? wp_get_attachment_img( $staff_photo_id, 'medium' ) : '';

        echo "<div class='staff-member'>";
        echo "<h3 class='staff-member__name'>$staff_name</h3>";
        echo "<h4 class='staff-member__title'>$staff_title</h4>";
        if( $staff_photo ){
            echo "<div class='staff-member__photo-container'>$staff_photo</div>";
        }
        echo "<p class='staff-member__bio'>$staff_bio</p>";
        echo "</div><!-- /.staff-member -->";

    endwhile;

endif;

So we've set up custom fields with ACF, used them to put in dynamic content on a page, and then looped through that data and spit it out on our page template. The end user doesn't see almost any of that -- they just open the page, and type in their content. You do the heavy lifting for them, as you should.

So all of that might be taking what you thought was a small job (throwing some HTML into a WordPress theme) and turning it into a complex one (defining fields, creating templates, etc.). You may decide it's not worth that and just keep the site more static like one of the ways you've tried. There's nothing wrong with that.

To be honest, your question is a huge part of the reason that Gutenberg was created. It gives the backend editor a ton of more flexibility for defining the content area. It might not be quite so helpful for your specific situation, because you are converting an existing static site that wasn't built around blocks like Gutenberg's.

posts.title: Wordpress" Answer: How can I call an api before user login
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [How can I call an api before user login](http://Wordpress.StackExchange.com/q/324764) * * * ## My answer: I think this is just a slight mistake on your "if" condition ``` $result = preg_split('///','domain.com/api/use
posts.content:
Original question: How can I call an api before user login

My answer:

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: Vue.http.get w/ authorization - makes 2 requests and fails on iOS only
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Vue.http.get w/ authorization - makes 2 requests and fails on iOS only](http://StackOverflow.com/q/53545354) * * * ## My answer: I have to make an authenticated HTTP request using a bearer token. This works flawlessly
posts.content:
Original question: Vue.http.get w/ authorization - makes 2 requests and fails on iOS only

My answer:

I have to make an authenticated HTTP request using a bearer token. This works flawlessly on everything I've tested...except some iOS devices.

  fetchWithToken : function( endpoint, token ){
    return Vue.http.get( urlBase + endpoint, {
      headers : {
        Authorization : 'Bearer ' + token
      }
    });
  },

From what I can tell, the request is being sent twice. Note this function only gets called once (verified by debugging) but the server receives 2 requests. The first request contains the token and authorizes successfully. The second has no token and fails, returning that failure to the rest of my app.

The two HTTP requests from one call makes me think CORS preflight requests. However it is the same domain and the urlBase variable in that function above is a relative address ('/api/'), not a full URL.

Is iOS forcing CORS? And if so, why is the second request sent without the authorization header instead of the preflight request?

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: Multiple functions returning promises
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Multiple functions returning promises](http://StackOverflow.com/q/53120080) * * * ## My answer: I have an HTTP helper that returns a promise for each request. Sometimes those requests depend on each other. I am confus
posts.content:
Original question: Multiple functions returning promises

My answer:

I have an HTTP helper that returns a promise for each request. Sometimes those requests depend on each other. I am confusing myself into coding what I think are anti-patterns for this.

Normally when chaining promises you use .then()

function giveMeASimplePromise(){
     return new Promise( function(resolve, reject){
          setTimeout( function(){
               console.log("I'm finishing a promise.");
               resolve();
          }, 3000 );
     });
}

giveMeASimplePromise().then( giveMeASimplePromise ).then( giveMeASimplePromise );

//prints 'I'm finishing a promise' 3 times spaced 3 seconds apart

But I am getting confused if there is a promise within one of those promises that needs to be part of the chain.

This is coming up for me because I have an HTTP helper function that returns a promise with each request. A couple of those requests depend on each other. And the whole process needs to return a promise to keep everything async.

function login( credentials ){
    //outer promise that's returned and either needs to resolve or reject based
    // on complete login cycle
    return new Promise( function(resolve, reject){
        //inner promise checking for username/password match. can be rejected 
        // for several reasons.
        var checkCredentials = httpHelper.checkCredentials( credentials );
        checkCredentials.then( function(result){
            if ( result.credentialsMatch ){
                //another inner promise checking for privilege levels. never rejects.
                var checkPrivileges = httpHelper.getPrivileges( result.userID ); 
                getPrivileges.then( function(result) ){
                    if( result.privilege > 0 ){
                        //want this to resolve the entire chain
                        resolve();
                    }else{
                        //want this to reject the entire chain
                        reject('You do not have sufficient privileges.');
                    }
                }
            }else{
                reject('Incorrect username and/or password.');
            }
        }).catch( function(reason){
            reject( reason );
        });
    });
}

var credentials = { ... };
var loginResult = login( credentials ).then( function(value){
    console.log('Logged in successfully.');
}).catch( function(reason){
    console.log('Could not log in: ', reason);
})

That's an anti-pattern, right? It feels wrong.

posts.title: Stop using is_page to conditionally enqueue in WordPress. There's a better way!
posts.excerpt: Trivia question: What is the best way to enqueue a script or a stylesheet on a specific page in WordPress? 1. Add the assets directly into header.php or footer.php 2. Add the assets directly via the HTML of the page template 3. Enqueue the
posts.content:
Trivia question: What is the best way to enqueue a script or a stylesheet on a specific page in WordPress?

  1. Add the assets directly into header.php or footer.php
  2. Add the assets directly via the HTML of the page template
  3. Enqueue the assets with wp_enqueue_script / wp_enqueue_style in functions.php
  4. Enqueue the assets as in C, but add conditions so that it only happens on certain pages
  5. Use the better, more WordPress-y way

Yes, there is a better way. A way that you will not turn back from once you understand the power of its pattern. But first, what's wrong with options A-D?

A. Add the assets directly into header.php or footer.php

This is the easiest, but the least efficient. If you add a <script ... or <link ... tag into the header or footer file, it will load on every page. The same script may load more than once if a plugin uses the same file. You cannot not load it on a specific page without using a separate header or footer file.

B. Add the assets directly via the HTML of the page template

Similar to A, with one slight advantage. It will only load on the page it's used for. Unfortunately it's not going to load in an optimal place (CSS should be loaded in header, most JavaScript should be loaded towards the end of the page to not block rendering). You still risk double-loading, and you cannot not load it in some cases if you need to, at least without bending over backwards.

C. Enqueue the assets with wp_enqueue_script / wp_enqueue_style in functions.php

Now we're getting somewhere! The WordPress way is to let WordPress handle enqueing scripts and stylesheets. You get automatic versioning, and an alias with which you can un-register an asset or specify dependencies. The best approach is to first register a script and then enqueue it when necessary, but that's not the point I'm making with this article. Simply enqueuing is worlds above directly importing the assets in the page templates. In its natural form, you're still loading the asset on every page. Which leads us to...

D. Enqueue the assets as in C, but add conditions so that it only happens on certain pages

This is by far the most common solution I see posted on the Internet. You mitigate the disadvantage of C and avoid loading it on every page by adding conditions in PHP where you enqueue the file. [code language="php"] if( is_front_page() || is_page( 35 ) || is_page_template( 'page-contact-us.php' ) ){ wp_enqueue_script( 'form-validator' ); } [/code] The problem here is that it starts off simple, but quickly grows more complex. Another page needs that asset? Modify the conditional statement. Duplicate the page it so that it gets a new ID? I hope you wrote your conditionals flexibly. Don't get me wrong -- this is an appropriate solution in a lot of cases. But it doesn't have to be this messy!

E. Use the better, more WordPress-y way

What's the better, more WordPress-y way to conditionally enqueue? Hooks! Your own hooks! The easiest hooks! Don't be afraid of hooks! This pattern is the way to go. There are two pieces to it:

1. In your page template (or widget, plugin, etc.  -- wherever you want to use the assets ) add a do_action line. Seriously, just throw it in there.

[code language="php"]do_action( 'application_assets' ); [/code]

2. In your functions.php file, tie into the hook you just created to enqueue the assets

[code language="php"]add_action( 'application_assets', 'enqueue_application_assets' ); function enqueue_application_assets(){ wp_enqueue_script( 'form-validator', ..... wp_enqueue_style( 'form-style', ..... wp_enqueue_script( 'masked-input', .... }[/code] What are doing here is simple, Whenever we want these assets to be used, we're telling WordPress, "Hey, right here, if anybody has any 'application_assets' code they want to run, please do it.". What 'application_assets' code did we tell WordPress we wanted to run? The enqueue-ing of those assets. (It technically happens in the reverse order -- first WordPress add_actions the actions, then it do_actions them.) Edit: It's actually nearly as good to use a function call here, something like enqueue_application_assets() which you would define in your functions.php file. You know, like the name suggests. However, I tend to use the hooks pattern instead, because that way other code in other places can also tie into this action. There's not a ton of difference with the exception that a function can only live in one place, and that one place therefore must control whatever happens, whereas a hook can have unlimited functions tied to it. Either way is fine. Let's compare it to our earlier methods:

  • Does it run on every page?
    • No, it runs specifically on the pages we want it.
  • Can it accidentally be loaded more than once?
    • No, WordPress only enqueues once per file, even if called twice.
  • Can we choose to not load it?
    • Yes, we can hook into the same action later and un-enqueue it.
  • Can we load it in the proper places?
    • Yes, we can load scripts in the footer and stylesheets in the header, because we're using WordPress's enqueue functions.
  • Does it tolerate changes to the pages its used on?
    • Yes, since the "condition" to have it loaded is the presence of the do_action, it doesn't rely on the page id, page slug, template file name, or anything else like that that might change. It's simply in the code, or not.
  • Will the conditionality grow more complex the more places we use it?
    • No -- each place we want to use it just gets the add_action line. If a page doesn't use it, it doesn't get the line. If it does, it does.
  • What if I REALLY want to add in a conditional statement?
    • You still can! Right in the enqueue function we wrote.

I use this pattern all the time now, and I wish someone had shown it to me earlier. Instead I had to work it out over time, but I'm sure I'm not the only one who has. It's the kind of elegantly simple solution that is so obvious once you begin using it, you can't believe you didn't think of it before. P.S. This doesn't just apply to enqueuing assets, although that's my most common usage. You can use it for any block of code that needs to run on specific pages only.

posts.title: Clear code boundaries and event buses in JavaScript
posts.excerpt: Writing an application so that every piece of code can affect every other piece is like the wild west. You may be able to "do more" but lawlessness will result. Code written like this is difficult to debug, almost impossible to extend, and
posts.content:
Writing an application so that every piece of code can affect every other piece is like the wild west. You may be able to "do more" but lawlessness will result. Code written like this is difficult to debug, almost impossible to extend, and almost always buggy.

As code grows more complex, it becomes more critical to maintain clear boundaries between components. If your app is a chess game, then a "knight" class should not be able to stop the game timer even if it puts the opposing king in check mate. Instead, it should complete its move, the game logic controller should do a check for game ending scenarios, and then the game itself should stop the clock.

Bad

  • Knight: Moving to E4 is a legal move for me. 
  • Knight: I move to E4.
  • Knight: Looking at all the other pieces, I see I just check-mated the king. I rock thee!
  • Knight: Stop the timer. Announce the game is over. Lock all the other pieces. The war is over!

Good

  • Knight: Yes, moving to E4 is a legal move for me.
  • Game Logic: Okay, go ahead and move to E4.
  • Knight: I move to E4.
  • Game Logic: Looking at all the pieces, the other player is now in check mate.
  • Game Logic: Stop the timer. Announce the game is over. Lock all the pieces.

The need for boundaries

Hopefully it is obvious why the second situation is better. In the first, you might end up repeating code. (Does every piece need to know how to check for check mate?) You also have a bunch of independent actors. (What if another piece is doing something while the knight is checking for mate?). It's also incredibly difficult to debug this. (When you run into a bug where check mate is being erroneously declared, how will you know where to look? Answer: You'll look over your entire application's code, because you can't be sure.)

Using Object Oriented Programming (OOP) principles helps establish the desired separation. It's kind of obvious a Game should have Players, Players should have Pieces, Pieces should have piece logic. And in a multi-file compiled JavaScript app, like a full-fledged framework project (i.e. Angular, React, Vue, etc.), this compartmentalization is hinted at by the very file structure.

Defining boundaries is a little less obvious for isolated JavaScript code, like the little 1-200 lines you might write to power the UI of a web page. However even here the principle can be very helpful.

Event Buses

One helpful tool in creating boundaries in simple projects is the "event bus". An event bus is a central communications hub that processes events. It's like a bulletin board for different pieces of your code.

  • Components can "post" a message to it (i.e. "I have new data," "I was clicked," etc.)
  • Components can "subscribe" to messages (i.e. "Let me know when there's new data.").
  • Posts can also pass along payloads (i.e. "Here is my new data", "Here is my button ID") and subscriptions can receive and process that data.

That's really all there is to it, but they are wildly useful. Their functionality is especially helpful when asynchronous operations are involved, as you can't just program sequentially. 

An Example Event Bus Implementation in English

Let's use as an example a search results page for flights with filters that update the results on the fly with AJAX.

  • Central Data Repository: Hey Event Bus, if you receive any "New Results Fetched" messages, pass that along to me so I can update.
  • Search Results View: Hey Event Bus, I don't care if results are fetched, but when they're completely processed I do. So if you receive any "Results Ready" messages, let me know. Oh, also I need to know when new results are being loaded so I can tell the user, so let me know if you receive any "Updating Results" messages as well.
  • AJAX Data Fetcher Utility: Hey Event Bus, if you receive any "Search Filter Changed" messages, please let me know so I can go get new data based on it.

(some time passes, then the user adjusts a search filter)

  • Max Price Slider: Hey Event Bus, I have a "Search Filter Changed" message for you because the user just updated me. My name is "Max Price" and my new value is $800.
  • Event Bus: Attention! New "Search Filter Changed" message. "Max Price" was changed to "$800".
  • AJAX Data Fetcher Utility: Thanks, Event Bus! I'm going to get new data based on that change. In the meantime, I have a "Updating Results" message for you.
  • Event Bus: Attention! New "Updating Results" message. No payload.
  • Search Results View: Thanks, Event Bus! I'm going to replace the results shown to the user with a "Loading..." message.

(the new results are fetched with AJAX, a hundred milliseconds or so pass)

  • AJAX Data Fetcher Utility: I have my new results ready. Event Bus, please post, "New Results Fetched" with data {...}.
  • Event Bus: Attention! New "New Results Fetched" message. Payload is {...}
  • Central Data Repository: Thanks! Let me process those for a second here....and....we're good! Event Bus, please post, "Results Ready" with this processed data {...}.
  • Event Bus: Attention! New "Results Ready" message. Payload is {...}.
  • Search Results View: Thanks! Let me hide the "Loading..." message and display the new results.

So on the one hand, it looks more complex because there is more "talking" between components. But this is handling a complex process that involves asynchronous data, and the different parts of our app are not tripping over each other anymore. They are respectfully handling their own business and keeping each other in the loop. 

A Simple Event Bus Class

This helpful little utility class handles all the dirty work of an event bus. You simply have to use it! Credit goes to Pierfrancesco Soffritti 

[code language="javascript"] function EventBus() { const eventCallbacksPairs = []; this.subscribe = function( eventType, callback ) { const eventCallbacksPair = findEventCallbacksPair(eventType); if(eventCallbacksPair) eventCallbacksPair.callbacks.push(callback); else eventCallbacksPairs.push( new EventCallbacksPair(eventType, callback) ); } this.post = function( eventType, args ) { const eventCallbacksPair = findEventCallbacksPair(eventType); if(!eventCallbacksPair) { console.error("no subscribers for event " +eventType); return; } eventCallbacksPair.callbacks.forEach( callback => callback(args) ); } function findEventCallbacksPair(eventType) { return eventCallbacksPairs.find( eventObject => eventObject.eventType === eventType ); } function EventCallbacksPair( eventType, callback ) { this.eventType = eventType; this.callbacks = [callback]; } }[/code]

posts.title: A Vue.js powered, headless WordPress Progressive Web App
posts.excerpt: It consistently blows my mind how much web developers are continually learning. It's actually one of the things I love about the field, because if I had to always do the same thing the same way, I'd get bored fast. There's always something
posts.content:
It consistently blows my mind how much web developers are continually learning. It's actually one of the things I love about the field, because if I had to always do the same thing the same way, I'd get bored fast. There's always something new to learn, and to learn to do better. 

If you're always doing your best work, then that means a project from 2 years ago is 2 years short of your best work. I respect the people who say that if you're not disgusted by your work from 6 months ago then you aren't improving fast enough. It's a little harsh, but I get it.

The custom WordPress theme I had created for my own site served me well, but it was time to go. I had patched it with some better practices and design changes every few months, but I wanted to do something exciting, something that pushed the edge a little bit.

I eventually settled on doing a Vue.js powered headless WordPress Progressive Web App, served through Amazon Web Services and sporting a fresh design.

...a Vue.js powered...

I've made a couple of personal React projects (like this Game of Life simulator) and some Angular powered Single Page Apps for clients at work. But Vue.js, so simple and lightweight to get up and running, has recently been my choice for throwing together quick demos and micro-apps. 

But I hadn't done a full-scale app with it, and my blog was a perfect opportunity. With very little work, it can be set up to handle routing (i.e. for blog posts), make http requests, and use a centralized data store (Vuex).

About halfway through I really started missing Angular's Observers, particularly the BehaviorSubject I had come to rely on. At first I tried bending promises into the same pattern (you can make an externally-resolvable promise if you try hard enough), but it's really about a pattern shift and eventually the Vue.js way came together. 

It was a lot of fun, and I haven't lost any respect for Vue.js. The source of my app is available on GitHub.

...headless WordPress implementation...

I decided to do a headless WordPress implementation, meaning WordPress would continue to power the backend of my site but would only be served to visitors through the awesome WordPress REST API. 

This went hand-in-hand with my desire to use Vue.js, as I wanted the framework to power my site, not just be incorporated into it. 

The single greatest lesson I learned here is how much I take WordPress for granted. It takes care of so much for you. This was driven home when creating the post archive page. "Oh of course...I can't use posts_nav_link()..."

On the bright side, it is so frickin easy to create custom API endpoints. I had to create one to serve a list of all my posts (with only the minimal information needed) since the main posts query, initially limited to 100 posts, gets large well before that.

...Progressive Web App...

Google spells out minimum and exemplary requirements for a Progressive Web App, but one thing I learned is that it's less of a certification and more of a goal, something like Calculus limits. (The limit of a project as it approaches perfection from the left is a progressive web app?)

The main goals here are to provide mobile users with an installable, user-friendly experience that is so slick it feels like an installed app. It definitely must work even when offline (achieved through Service Workers), be served over SSL, utilize history-based page routing, and have near-instant page loads and navigation.

Luckily, the VUE-CLI provides a starter for the service worker. In its current version it utilizes Google Workbox, which generates the actual service worker for you. The documentation on this implementation was extremely sparse.

I can't get over how fun it is to browse my site while offline.

...served through Amazon Web Services...

I don't think you really 'get' Amazon Web Services (AWS) until you start using it. Wow, there's a lot there. 

I was hosting my site before on a cheap monthly shared host (NameCheap), and while the limits and uptime were fine, the speed was so-so and it got more and more constricting as I tried to do more with it. I barely managed to get a Let's Encrypt SSL cert installed on it.

For my app to meet Progressive Web App speed requirements, I needed to move up a tier. Moving to AWS was more like shifting harbors, with a whole new world of tiers.

The site is now hosted on an EC2 instance (virtual machine). I started with a Bitnami WordPress setup, which preconfigured the server for powering WordPress. Best practices, especially relating to server settings and file ownership and permissions, are set up out of the box. 

Since both WordPress and my headless WordPress app were going to live on the same server, there was a lot of server configuration necessary for routing the right requests to the right places. Enabling the right Apache modules to optimize my app was also a new experience for me. 

After getting everything set up and running on AWS, I will simply say this: I have never appreciated the Systems folks at my day-job as much as I should have been. They've been handling so much for me. 

...and sporting a fresh design.

My previous custom theme featured a large hero image and strongly delineated sections. It originally featured separate sections for project and portfolio pieces, and the blog was only a piece of the whole picture. As time went on I realized the blogging was at the heart of what I'm doing here, so I wanted my design to really emphasize that.

Starting with mobile, I designed a minimalist home page with subtle UI animations, post prev/next buttons tied right into the main navigation of the site, and layouts and typography reminiscent of a magazine. Progressive Web Apps are meant to have simple, intuitive UI components similar to that of an app, so the main menu at the top would be fixed and simple.

Moving from the mobile to the desktop was relatively simple. The menu moves to the left, the prev/nexzt buttons move to either side of the screen, and the article has a little more breathing room. Continuing the magazine theme, the article page features a bold title area with a prominent feature image.

Bring it all together

I'm obviously a bit proud of how all the pieces came together. The result is clean and simple, but also powerful under the hood. There is still some room for improvements and enhancements, and I'm planning some more posts on handling a few of the challenges that came up in the process. In particular, I would like to bring commenting and taxonomy navigation back in. But in the meantime the site is running great so far -- the featured image of this post is a screenshot of the latest Lighthouse audits I ran. The results were 98 for Performance, 100 for Progressive Web App, 100 for Accessibility, 100 for Best Practices, and 90 for SEO. That's way better than my old blog's results. 

Have you created a WordPress powered PWA? I'd love to hear about it!

posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Parametized getter in Vuex - trigger udpate](http://StackOverflow.com/q/52148561) * * * ## My answer: My Vuex store has a collection of data, say 1,000 records. There is a getter with a parameter, getItem, taking an I
posts.content:
Original question: Parametized getter in Vuex - trigger udpate

My answer:

My Vuex store has a collection of data, say 1,000 records. There is a getter with a parameter, getItem, taking an ID and returning the correct record.

I need components accessing that getter to know when the data is ready (when the asynchronous fetching of all the records is done).

However since it's a parametized getter, Vue isn't watching the state it depends on to know when to update it. What should I do?

I keep wanting to revert to a BehaviorSubject pattern I used in Angular a lot, but Vuex + rxJS seems heavy for this, right?

I feel I need to somehow emit a trigger for the getter to recalculate.

store.js

import Vue from 'vue'
import Vuex from 'vuex'
import VueResource from 'vue-resource'

Vue.use(VueResource);

Vue.use(Vuex)

export default new Vuex.Store({
  state: {
    numberOfPosts : -1,
    posts : {}, //dictionary keyed on slug
    postsLoaded : false,
  },
  getters : {
    postsLoaded : function(state){
      return state.postsLoaded;
    },
    totalPosts : function(state){
      return state.numberOfPosts;
    },
    post: function( state ){
      return function(slug){
        if( state.posts.hasOwnProperty( slug ) ){
          return state.posts.slug;
        }else{
          return null;
        }
      }
    }
  },
  mutations: {
    storePosts : function(state, payload){
      state.numberOfPosts = payload.length;
      for( var post of payload ){
        state.posts[ post.slug ] = post;
      }
      state.postsLoaded = true;
    }
  },
  actions: {
    fetchPosts(context) {
      return new Promise((resolve) => {
        Vue.http.get(' {url redacted} ').then((response) => {
          context.commit('storePosts', response.body);
          resolve();
        });
      });
    }
  }
})

Post.vue

        <div v-if="postNotFound">No matching post was found.</div>
        <div v-if="postsLoaded && !postNotFound" class="post-area">
          {{ this.postData.title.rendered }}
        </div>

<script>
import { mapGetters } from 'vuex'

      this.postNotFound = true;
    }
  },
  computed : mapGetters([
    'postsLoaded',
    'post'
  ])
}
</script>

As it stands, it shows the "post not found" message because when it accesses the getter, the data isn't ready yet. If a post isn't found, I need to distinguish between (a) the data is loaded and there isn't a post that matches, and (b) the data isn't loaded so wait

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: JavaScript Stopwatch - Trouble Displaying a Leading Digit
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [JavaScript Stopwatch - Trouble Displaying a Leading Digit](http://StackOverflow.com/q/52085830) * * * ## My answer: When you do "0" + minutes (and seconds, and hours) those variables get automatically converted into a
posts.content:
Original question: JavaScript Stopwatch - Trouble Displaying a Leading Digit

My answer:

When you do "0" + minutes (and seconds, and hours) those variables get automatically converted into a string, consisting of two characters, a zero and something else.

Since the variables carry through each iteration, the next time you are adding another "0" character to the beginning of the string, and so-on.

The reason it's not happening to seconds is because you are converting seconds BACK to an int at the beginning of the loop when you do seconds++. So it becomes a string, then an int, then a string, etc.

To see this in action, try this snippet:

var test = 1;
console.log( typeof test );  //outputs "number"
test = "0" + test;
console.log( typeof test ); //outputs "string"
test++;
console.log( typeof test); //outputs number

My suggestion would be to separate counting units from display units. See if minutes is less than 10, and if so set outputMinutes to "0" + minutes. Do the same for seconds and hours. Then you just change the outputMinutes, outputSeconds, and outputHours each time, while the actual minutes, seconds, and hours variables remain as integers.

posts.title: Dungeon Generation with Binary Space Partitioning
posts.excerpt: Old 80's games like Rogue and Adventure saw players exploring top-down dungeons, moving from room to room, fighting monsters, and collecting treasure. The games were brutally hard, and I'm not the only one who felt the difficulty made you w
posts.content:
Old 80's games like Rogue and Adventure saw players exploring top-down dungeons, moving from room to room, fighting monsters, and collecting treasure. The games were brutally hard, and I'm not the only one who felt the difficulty made you want to play them all the more. "I'm better than this game, damnit!"

Rogue and Adventure were different and led to many spinoffs, with Rogue itself lending its name to a genre of what are now called Roguelike games. These games are turnlike in that each player move triggers the next 'tick' in the game (progressing the game one step, allowing all the monsters to move, etc.) They featured permadeath, meaning there were no save points or extra lives. And they used procedurally generated maps, meaning the levels were never the same twice.

The map generation is awesome. There are a lot of approaches to generating a map, most of which feature recursion, but the most common is called a Binary Space Partion. It's a little tricky the first time you hear it, but is also beautifully simple. I wish I could have been there when those early 80's game designers were figuring out how to apply these mathematical concepts to their unorthodox cause of programming kickass games.

Binary Space Partition

The method results in a 2d map of rooms linked together with passages. None of the rooms should overlap, and there should be at least one passage into each room.

Let's say you were going to draw out your map in sand with a long stick.

  1. You mark out the outer boundary of the map as a rectangle.
  2. Randomly, you draw out a line to divide it into 2 sections (doesn't matter if horizontally or vertically)
  3. Randomly, you divide each of those 2 sections.
  4. Randomly, you divide each of those 4 sections

...and so on until you have a bunch of random little rectangles. These are not your dungeon rooms. They are the maximum possible borders for each of the rooms' walls. Now you take your shovel and carve out the actual rooms within those borders.

  1. Randomly, you take your stick and draw a smaller complete rectangle inside each room border.
  2. Now you take your shovel and dig out each actual room.

We now how have a bunch of separated little rectangles. Any kid knows the next step is to dig tunnels between them. Randomly? That could work, but you might end up with some left-out rooms. We can do better than that.

As we were dividing the map, making it smaller and smaller, we were basically creatin

  1. Entire Map
    1. Huge Area A
      1. Big Area A
        1. Medium Area A
          1. Small Area A
          2. Small Area B
        2. Medium Area B
          1. Small Area A
          2. Small Area B
      2. Big Area B
        1. Medium Area A
          1. Small Area A
          2. Small Area B
        2. Medium Area B
          1. Small Area A
          2. Small Area B
    2. Huge Area B
      1. Big Area A
        1. Medium Area A
          1. Small Area A
          2. Small Area B
        2. Medium Area B
          1. Small Area A
          2. Small Area B
      2. Big Area B
        1. Medium Area A
          1. Small Area A
          2. Small Area B
        2. Medium Area B
          1. Small Area A
          2. Small Area B

In other words, we have recursively partitioned out our spaces by dividing it into 2's (binary). A binary space partitioning. Within each of those Small Areas, we've now carved out an actual Room. To connect the rooms, we work our way back up the hierarchy, connecting each "sibling" with a random passage. 

  1. Dig out a tunnel between a room in each Small Area A and Small Area B
  2. Dig out a tunnel between a room in each Medium Area A and Medium Area B
  3. Dig out a tunnel between a room in each Big Area A and Big Area B
  4. Dig out a tunnel between a room in each Huge Area A and Huge Area B

And..that's it! There's now a network of rooms and passages. 

Coding out a BSP Dungeon

After you get the concept, coding it out is the real challenge. There is a lot of abstract geometry math to do, and humans think more linearly than recursively.

I found it supremely helpful to do the abstract map generation with Object Oriented Programming, generally separately from any game logic or display. My MapNode class represents a conceptual area and it's inner room, holds all of it's children nodes, and is aware of what other nodes it has connections to. This makes it easier to traverse down and up the hierarchy without losing your place, and it would be very easy to extend with further helper functions.

[code language="JavaScript"] export class MapNode{ constructor( x1, y1, x2, y2, parent ){ this.x1 = x1; this.y1 = y1; this.x2 = x2; this.y2 = y2; this.innerX1; this.innerY1; this.innerX2; this.innerY2; this.children = []; this.connections = []; this.parent = parent; } } //Carve out an inner room MapNode.prototype.carveInner = function( minRoomDimension ){ let deltaY = this.y2 - this.y1; let deltaX = this.x2 - this.x1; if ( deltaY < minRoomDimension + 4 ){ this.innerY1 = this.y1; this.innerY2 = this.y2; }else{ this.innerY1 = randInt( this.y1, this.y1 + ( .3 * deltaY ) ); this.innerY2 = randInt( this.y2 - ( .3 * deltaY ), this.y2 ); } if ( deltaX < minRoomDimension + 4 ){ this.innerX1 = this.x1; this.innerX2 = this.x2; }else{ this.innerX1 = randInt( this.x1, this.x1 + ( .3 * deltaX ) ); this.innerX2 = randInt( this.x2 - ( .3 * deltaX ), this.x2 ); } } //Establish connection to siblings. We ask our parent who our siblings are. MapNode.prototype.connect = function(){ if( this.parent != null ){ let thisNode = this; let nodes = this.parent.children.filter( function(i){ //filter out this child, can't compare memory due to filter copy return !( i.x1 == thisNode.x1 && i.x2 == thisNode.x2 && i.y1 == thisNode.y1 && i.y2 == thisNode.y2 ); } ); this.connectToNodes( nodes ); } } //Establish a connection MapNode.prototype.connectToNodes = function( nodes ){ for( let node of nodes ){ if( !this.hasConnection( node ) ){ this.connections.push( node ); } } } //Is node connected to given node? MapNode.prototype.hasConnection = function( node ){ for( let connection of this.connections ){ if ( connection == node ){ return true; } } return false; } //Split this node into two smaller nodes (if there is room) MapNode.prototype.split = function( horizontal, minRoomDimension, current, max ){ horizontal = horizontal || false; minRoomDimension = minRoomDimension || 10; current = current || { number : 0 }; max = max || 25; let dim = horizontal ? 'x' : 'y'; let alt = horizontal ? 'y' : 'x'; let axis = randInt( this[ dim + '1' ] + minRoomDimension, this[ dim + '2' ] - minRoomDimension - 1 ); //split if enough room on either side (happens until limits overlap) if( this[ dim + '1' ] + minRoomDimension <= axis && this[ dim + '2' ] - minRoomDimension - 1 >= axis && current.number + 1 < max ){ //Can't use direct constructor as we don't know if primary dimension is x or y //This is also a little helpful for visualizing let first = new MapNode( null, null, null, null, this ); let second = new MapNode( null, null, null, null, this ); first[ dim + '1' ] = this[ dim + '1' ]; first[ alt + '1' ] = this[ alt + '1' ]; first[ dim + '2' ] = axis; first[ alt + '2' ] = this[ alt + '2' ]; second[ dim + '1' ] = axis + 1; second[ alt + '1' ] = this[ alt + '1' ]; second[ dim + '2' ] = this[ dim + '2' ]; second[ alt + '2' ] = this[ alt + '2' ]; this.children.push( first ); this.children.push( second ); current.number++; first.split( !horizontal, minRoomDimension, current, max ); second.split( !horizontal, minRoomDimension, current, max ); this.connect(); }else{ this.carveInner( minRoomDimension ); this.connect(); } } //I'm a sucker for little helper functions function randInt(min,max){ let r = Math.floor(Math.random()*(max-min+1)+min); return r; }[/code]

Splitting Rooms

This isn't terribly hard. You have to pick if each split is horizontal is vertical, and then pick where within the area's boundaries to draw the line. If there is going to be a minimum area size, you have to be that far away from the walls or you shouldn't split.

After splitting, you have two new areas, each of which also need to be split, so on and so on until you reach the minimum specified room size or the max number of rooms. 

Take a look in the split function above. It's basically doing what I just said -- choosing an orientation (not randomly here; instead the opposite of the node's parent's split direction), picking an axis position respecting the minimum room sizes given and the maximum number of rooms, and then splitting down to create two new nodes.

This leaves us with an abstract representation of our dungeon, but hasn't printed anything to the screen. Our game will need to use this class to set up the actual view, then tie in the game logic (rules, players, monsters, etc.) to interact with it. But as far as Binary Space Partitioning, this is it!

posts.title: Unit Testing and Test Driven Development (TDD)
posts.excerpt: Unit Testing allows developers to efficiently--and thoroughly--test individual pieces of their code to make sure it behaves correctly. Since most functions and snippets are written for a specific purpose, it is far too easy and tempting to
posts.content:
Unit Testing allows developers to efficiently--and thoroughly--test individual pieces of their code to make sure it behaves correctly. Since most functions and snippets are written for a specific purpose, it is far too easy and tempting to write it "until it works" and then move along. But unless the code is tightly controlled, with varying data this isn't really good enough.

With unit testing, we subject our code to a wide gamut of possible conditions to make sure it always does just what we expect, everything we expect, and nothing but what we expect.

Test Driven Development (TDD) employs this outlook from the very beginning. Rather than taking an existing function and trying to come up with tests to see if it "holds up", we write the code iteratively, specifically to solve each of our tests. The development of a function, isNumberPrime( num ), might look like this:

//Test 1 - isNumberPrime should return a boolean value

function isNumberPrime( num ){      return true; }

So our first test passes, and we move on by adding other tests that break our code, fixing it as we go.

//Test 1 - isNumberPrime should return a boolean value
//Test 2 - 3 should return true and 4 should return false

function isNumberPrime( num ){      for( var i = num - 1; i > 1; i-- ){           if ( num % i == 0 ){                return false;           }      }      return true; }

This works for basic cases, but there are some obvious ones where it will completely break (i.e. negative numbers will be an infinite loop). Let's add a few more tests

//Test 1 - isNumberPrime should return a boolean value
//Test 2 - 3 should return true and 4 should return false
//Test 3 - negative numbers should not cause an infinite loop
//Test 4 - 0 should return false, 1 should return true

function isNumberPrime( num ){      if ( num < 1 ) return false;      if ( num == 1 ) return true;      for( var i = num - 1; i > 1; i-- ){           if ( num % i == 0 ){                return false;           }      }      return true; }

I added test 4 above so that our for-loop, which starts out with i at 1 less than our number, will never start out too low. That covers all integers. What about floats?

//Test 1 - isNumberPrime should return a boolean value
//Test 2 - 3 should return true and 4 should return false
//Test 3 - negative numbers should not cause an infinite loop
//Test 4 - 0 should return false, 1 should return true
//Test 5 - 3.5 should return false

function isNumberPrime( num ){      if ( !Number.isInteger( num ) ){           return false;      }      if ( num < 1 ) return false;      if ( num == 1 ) return true;      for( var i = num - 1; i > 1; i-- ){           if ( num % i == 0 ){                return false;           }      }      return true; }

I honestly thought it would already return false, but 3.5 returned true. This is because our code basically says, "For the number you gave me, keep subtracting 1, and see if that new number divides evenly into it. If you never find one that does, it is a prime number." Since none of a float's would, the code thought it was prime. We can just make sure our input is an integer.

That's a great example of what I mentioned before. I assumed my code would already work for non-integers, but it didn't. It gave a bad result, and now my code is better because I'm letting my tests drive my development.

Coming up with the tests is, of course, the challenge. You have to think of different inputs, especially inputs at the fringes, and throw everything you can at it. Here's my test suite after a bunch of other tests, none of which ended up breaking the function.

//Test 6 - 6 should return false
//Test 7 - 200 should return false
//Test 8 - 25 should return false
//Test 9 - 17 should return true
//Test 10 - 199 should return true

Everything's looking great. Now, prime numbers get really huge really fast, and I know my function is not going to handle everything. But I also know it could be a lot more efficient. Take the input, 100,000,000. My code will do hundreds of thousands of division operations to test this out. Eventually it will figure it out when it gets down to 100,000,000 / 50,000,000 and finds an even division.  Yikes. I can tell you right away it's not prime, because it's an even number!

So the second great thing about unit testing is once you have your code stable, you can begin optimizing it, a.k.a. refactoring.

//Test 11 - 100000000 should return false

function isNumberPrime( num ){      if ( !Number.isInteger( num ) ){           return false;      }      if ( num < 1 ) return false;      if ( num == 1 ) return true;      if ( num % 2 == 0 ) return false;      for( var i = num - 1; i > 1; i-- ){           if ( num % i == 0 ){                return false;           }      }      return true; }

The total time it took my unit tests to run went from 0.7 seconds down to .001 seconds. Testing 1 billion, the change took us from 6.5 seconds down to .001 seconds. Way better, and because all of our other tests are still in place, we know we haven't messed anything up!

We could continue optimizing our code. Seeing how much a difference the i % 2 == 0 test made, I am curious about doing the same thing for odd numbers. Maybe counting UP instead of counting down will let us hit a 'fail' condition sooner. I can try out this idea, and plenty of others, without worrying about my code because at each step, I know that I haven't lost any progress.
