posts.title: CSS, The Confusing Bits ”” Part 3: Positioning
posts.excerpt: [Part 1 - Series Introduction](https://tmdesigned.com/post/css-the-confusing-bits-part-1-introduction/) [Part 2 - Z-Index](https://tmdesigned.com/post/css-the-confusing-bits-part-2-z-index/) Part 3 - Positioning Part 4 - Height and Width *
posts.content:
Part 1 - Series Introduction
Part 2 - Z-Index
Part 3 - Positioning
Part 4 - Height and Width

Positioning is actually not terribly complicated once you read the specs. The problem is that most people don't, because it usually works just like you'd expect. When people need to deviate from normal, it's often a limited case and they can fiddle enough to get it to work. That's the trick with CSS--moving beyond individual use cases to a true understanding isn't immediately necessary, but is eventually important. Otherwise you end up scratching your head and blaming the browser.

Positioning Modes

  • Static - This is the default mode. It means that the element will be positioned normally as it falls in the box-model. More on that below.
  • Relative - Starts with static, but you can adjust it from that point.
  • Absolute - Taken out of the normal flow of the page, and is instead attached to a parent's box-model positioning. More below.
  • Fixed - Taken out of the normal flow, but is attached to the viewport itself, meaning it won't even scroll up and down.
  • Sticky - Not in use yet.

The Box Model

We really can't dissect those positioning modes any further without understanding the box model. Here's some sample code for our discussion:

Hello, world!

What a great example!

*{ border: 1px dotted rgba(255,0,0,.5); }

.fancy-text{ color: green; text-decoration: green wavy underline; }

As the browser gets ready to display the page, it goes through several steps. First it parses the HTML and the CSS. That's exactly what it sounds like, so we're going to skip it.

Then, it creates the Render Tree: "Here's every item I need to actually show the user, how all of those items relate to each other, and what CSS rules will apply to them." At this point the browser knows, for instance, that the h2 and the div.child are children of div.parent, and that they each have some style rules.

At this point, it does not know where each item will go, or how much space each item will take. That's the next phase, reflow. Here, it uses everything it learned to create the box-model.

Now it determines where every item will go, and how much space it will take.

Note the orange above, representing the default top and bottom margin on an h2 tag. It affects the spacing of other items, so it's figured out now.

Also note that the divs and h2 tag all get the full width of the rectangle, while the span only gets the width it needs. That's display: block vs display: inline at work, but the point here is the browser is already figuring how much space they'll need.

No images here, but if there were, their width and height would be blocked out as well, but not filled in with the actual image.

There are no visible styles ready other than what affects the sizing, like font-size. This is called the box-model, obviously, because it's an arrangement of boxes.

After the box model is done, the browser is ready to paint. This is an application of visual styles, and also the rendering of any raster content like images:

The dotted red lines are actually a part of our CSS, included to keep the box model apparent for us. So the main difference from before are the red lines, and the font styling on the word, "example!".

Positioning and the Box-Model

So let's return to positioning, which is really about the 2nd phase, the box-model. Positioning answers the question, how should items be positioned in the box-model?

Position: Static

Position static is the default mode. It means that when the browser figures out the box-model, it should just leave everything as it is.

Position: Relative

First the browser calculates how the element would flow within the box-model, then other CSS rules can alter it. If there aren't any other positioning rules, there won't be a visible difference. (Although, there are a few differences.)

So if you have:

.child{ position: relative; left: 10px; }

It will place the item in the box model, just skooched 10px over from the left.

Position: absolute and Position: fixed

Absolute and fixed positioning work nearly the same way. The big change here is that they are removed from the main box-model. They no longer have a place in it, and they don't affect the other items in it. That's a huge change!

Stop. Let's be clear about one thing. I said they don't affect the other items in the box-model. But they do maintain their place in the hierarchy of the DOM. They just don't affect the positioning of the other elements.

For instance, normally the height of an element is determined by how much room its content needs. But if that content is positioned absolutely, the element ignores them. So they still have a parent-child relationship, but the parent doesn't care about the child's size.

Okay. So where in the layout of the page are they placed? Well, they're moved onto a sort of "pseudo layer." They get pushed on top (by default) of the other elements, and they can't push things around there. It's like a higher level of consciousness. And while they're there, they can be moved around.

Here's the tricky bit. With relative positioning, "top," "bottom," "left," and "right" refers to adjusting the element itself. You read "left: 20px" as, "Move this item 20px over from the left of where it was." This is called box-positioning because we are adjusting a box within the box-model.

With absolute positioning, we have the same properties (top, bottom, left, and right) but they refer to what the element is attached to, not the element itself. "Left: 20px" means, "Put this element 20px from the left edge of what it's attached to." This is called cartesian-positioning because its more like specifying coordinates. You may remember "Cartesian" from geometry. It's the name for those (x,y) graphs you used to draw curves on.

Now, where the element goes depends on what it attaches to. In geometry we set a (0,0) point and that becomes the center of our graph. But what will this element's center be?

Well, since it's a box, it's actually easier to think about it's corners. So instead let's ask, "Where will this element's top left corner be?" We can figure out the other 3 corners using this first one and the width and height. Enter the "positioning context", aka, "the thing my element is getting attached to."

Fixed is the easiest: it attaches to the viewport, and it doesn't move. This is how we often create sticky headers, since no matter how far down the page we scroll the viewport--and anything attached to it--stays still.

.element{ position:fixed; top:0; left:0; width:100%; height:80px; }

This creates an 80px tall bar at the top of the browser window, which will always be there regardless of scrolling. Again, the top and left properties are saying, "Put this element 0px from the top edge, and 0px from the left edge, of what it's attached to (its positioning context)."

Interestingly, we can also "stretch" elements with those properties:

.element{ position:fixed; top:0; left:0; right:0; height:80px; }

See the difference? If the element is 0px from the left edge of it's positioning context, AND 0px from the right edge, then by definition it's stretching across.

Absolute doesn't attach to the viewport. It attaches by default to the html element, the root of the page. (Since the html element usually spans the height of all the page's context, you couldn't do the sticky-bar trick like above. It will scroll right along with the html element!)

However, unlike with fixed positioning, which always anchors to the viewport, the positioning context of absolute positioning can be changed. How? By giving one of it's ancestors position: relative. You do this even if you aren't relatively adjusting that parent's position.

Put another way, an absolutely positioned element looks up through it's ancestors and attaches itself to the first position: relative element it finds.

I used to think this was arbitrary, as if setting position: relative on a parent was just a wink and a nod to the browser that we want absolute items anchored on it. But it really makes sense when you think of positioning contexts. Remember, relative positioning was saying "Figure out where this would normally go, and then adjust it." If we adjusted it 300 pixels to the right, all of it's children are adjusted as well -- or you might say, they're within it's positioning context.

So the children of a relatively positioned element, including its absolutely positioned children, get adjusted as well. This is a fairly common design pattern. Want something to be absolutely positioned? Set it to absolute, and set its parent to relative.

A final warning

With good, responsive web design, the goal is not so much to get it to "look right" but rather to know how the elements will interact--with different content, at different sizes, on different setups, etc.

One danger, for instance, is with absolutely positioned elements in particular. You have deliberately taken them out of the flow of the standard box model. That means the box model can't adjust to accommodate them. If the absolutely positioned element gets bigger than you expected, it may begin to cover up content.

Keeping the mechanisms of the box model in mind helps you recognize dangers like this. But it also helps you unlock positioning's power. Dangerous doesn't necessarily mean bad, after all.

posts.title: DRY WordPress Theme Development
posts.excerpt: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) code is a fundamental concept that encourages developers to...well, to not repeat themselves. If two chunks of code do the same thing, it should be abstracted into one chunk of code used twice. The benefits are o
posts.content:
DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) code is a fundamental concept that encourages developers to...well, to not repeat themselves. If two chunks of code do the same thing, it should be abstracted into one chunk of code used twice. The benefits are obvious -- aside from saved time, you also reduce any future changes and also eliminate a lot of complexity. With WordPress theme development, writing DRY code is partially just about a mindset. Are two page templates doing almost the exact same thing? Maybe they can be pulled together and you can use post meta (or an ACF field) to distinguish them. That's a simple shift, but makes a big difference. But truly writing DRY code in WordPress themes takes more than just a willingness to reduce duplication. You also have to know of a few techniques, and be willing to roll your own when necessary.

Template Parts

At its core, template parts are just about separating out your code into separate files and then including them in an outer page. So for instance, you might have: [code language="php"]//Header and wrapping classes and such up above ... get_template_part( 'template-parts/title' ); get_template_part( 'template-parts/meta-box' ); get_template_part( 'template-parts/article', 'blog' ); get_template_part( 'template-parts/comments' ); get_template_part( 'template-parts/call-to-action' ); ... //End wrapping classes and footer and such down below[/code] There are some bonus features that come with get_template_part. First, it works great with child themes. It will look for the file first in the child (in case it overrides the parent), and then in the parent if not present. The third item above shows a second bonus that I have yet to find particularly helpful. It will look first for article-blog.php, but if it can't find it, it will use article.php instead. (More specifically, the order it looks for the files would be article-blog.php (child), article-blog.php (parent), article.php (child), article.php (parent).) I don't always find that helpful -- I already know what files are going to be there, except for child themes. So that's helpful if I I want to allow child themes to be more specific than I am in my parent theme.

Native include

Instead of get_template_part, you can instead opt for PHP's built-in include() function. You lose the built in parent/child theme handling, but you gain something else. Specifically, access to the outer context's scope. With get_template_part, the included partial template is isolated. Consider: [code language="php"]//page-staff.php ... while ( $staff_query->have_posts() ) : $staff_query->the_post(); $last_name = get_field( 'last_name' ); get_template_part( 'template-parts/staff-bio' ); endwhile; ...[/code] [code language="php"]//template-parts/staff-bio.php ... echo "My name is: $last_name."; ...[/code] This doesn't work. $last_name is not defined in the partial's context. Instead you would access what you need in the template part itself: [code language="php"]//page-staff.php ... while ( $staff_query->have_posts() ) : $staff_query->the_post(); get_template_part( 'template-parts/staff-bio' ); endwhile; ...[/code] [code language="php"]//template-parts/staff-bio.php ... echo "My name is: " . get_field( 'last_name' ); ...[/code] Even though variable scope doesn't cross the get_template_part boundary, the current post and/or row does, so we just access what we need from within the template part. If that's not possible, you can use include instead: [code language="php"]include( 'template-parts/staff-bio.php' );[/code] then it would work.

Sometimes there's a better way!

At least in this case, avoiding the get_template_part didn't make sense. True the variable couldn't cross the scope boundaries, but it really didn't have to. Again, that same call to get_field() -- or anything else that directly accesses data about the current loop item -- should just happen inside of the partial. That won't solve every case. If you have a reusable item, say, a callout box, then the template part has to get it's dynamic data from different places. But how is to know, "Okay, this time I get the title from X, that other time I got it from Y."? You either have to use a lot of conditionals, or create different copies of the template part that do almost the same thing. But you don't want to create multiple copies of that partial, since that flies right in the face of DRY principles. So in that case, it would make more sense to pull the data in the outer template file, and then include the reusable module: [code language="php"]//page-about.php ... $callout_title = 'Mission Statement'; $callout_text = get_field( 'mission_statement' ); include( 'template-parts/callout.php' ); ... $callout_title = 'Our Founder'; $callout_text = get_field( 'owner_biography' ); include( 'template-parts/callout.php' ); ...[/code] Then, of course, template-parts/callout.php just uses the current value of those two variables. It's not terribly hard to recreate the child-theme handling around this, either, so it's not the end of the world. I sometimes make a function called 'super_get_template_part()' that let's me add in extra features like this but preserves the child-theme handling.

Wrapped Content

All of the above techniques really revolve around inserted data. [code language="php"]... get_template_part( 'template-parts/inner' ); ...[/code] What if you want elements wrapped around these? Sometimes that's a simple, single div. Other times it's much more complex. So where should you put the wrapping code, in the outer template file, or the inner? If it's in the outer, then each time you want to use that inner file you have to repeat the wrapping code around it. That's not very DRY. If it's in the inner, then for any variations on the wrapping elements (say, the wrapping element sometimes needs a different class or includes a menu, but sometimes doesn't) you'll require a whole new template part. Well, that's not technically true. Like I mentioned earlier, you can use conditional statements inside of there, but that road has its limits. You can only conditionally find your way out of so many corners. You probably do not want to split up your template part files into multiple sections, i.e. template-parts/inner-top, template-parts/inner-content and template-parts/inner-bottom. This works, but quickly leads to overwhelming numbers of files. A better solution is to treat the problem like you would adding a shortcode. When creating a WordPress shortcode, you can either have it operate as a command: [code language="php"][call_to_action][/code] Or, as a tag pair (enclosing content): [code language="php"][call_to_action] Get in touch today! [/call_to_action][/code] The second case is what we want to look at. How do we implement that with code? [code language="php"]function tm_call_to_action($atts = [], $content = null) {     $output = "

";     $output .=  do_shortcode( $content ); $output .= "

";     return $output; } add_shortcode('call_to_action', 'tm_call_to_action');[/code]

We take the content the user has enclosed, wrap it up, and return it. That's exactly what we want to do, but with template parts on the backend.

So in short...we add a function that takes the content, wraps it up, and outputs it.

[code language="php"]function callout_box( $title, $text ){      echo "

";      echo "

$title

"; echo "

$text

";      echo "

"; }[/code]

Our earlier example would look a fair bit cleaner, too:

[code language="php"]//page-about.php ... callout_box( 'Mission Statement', get_field( 'mission_statement' ) ); ... callout_box( 'Our Founder', get_field( 'owner_biography' ) ); ...[/code]

Summary

When to use each of these techniques is the piece that comes with experience. Truth be told, there isn't always one right answer. The principle of DRY code is less a pass/fail standard and more an ideal to approach. In general, I find my themes using more and more template parts, with as much dynamic data as is possible and reasonable pulled from post meta. Have a neat DRY trick? Let me know!

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: Javascript - Lists created through user input with a sort button
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Javascript - Lists created through user input with a sort button](http://StackOverflow.com/q/49026667) * * * ## My answer: You just need to insert it into both lists as each word is added, i.e. where you have: ``` doc
posts.content:
Original question: Javascript - Lists created through user input with a sort button

My answer:

You just need to insert it into both lists as each word is added, i.e. where you have:

document.getElementById("sortedUL").appendChild(li);

you should add a second line like this:

document.getElementById("unsortedUL").appendChild(li.cloneNode(true));

The node cloning might be what you were missing if you tried it before, otherwise it would move the same element and it ends up in only one list. The 'true' argument makes a deep copy so that the text node underneath it is copied as well.

Incidentally, this whole operation would be a lot easier with jQuery, it's the kind of DOM manipulation that the library was meant for. However people jump to jQuery so quickly and it's good that you are doing it with vanilla JavaScript.

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: How do I create a hyperlink inside an input text field in html?
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [How do I create a hyperlink inside an input text field in html?](http://StackOverflow.com/q/49018512) * * * ## My answer: An input field's value is stored as plain text, therefore you cannot include HTML (i.e. a link)
posts.content:
Original question: How do I create a hyperlink inside an input text field in html?

My answer:

An input field's value is stored as plain text, therefore you cannot include HTML (i.e. a link) and expect the HTML to be parsed and functioning.

You could simulate this behavior with JavaScript, however I would recommend against it. (You would add a click listener, your function would pull the value of the field, see if it is a valid URL, and then open up the location.)

I'm not going to write the code for this because it would be a terrible user experience. The standard behavior for an input field is that you click on it to edit the text. This is an assumption your users have, and they would therefore (a) not think to click on it because they don't expect it to be a link, and (b) click in it if they wanted to edit the text, only to be redirected and unable to edit the text.

Alternatively, you could add a small button next to the input, i.e. 'Open' or 'Test' or an external link icon.

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: Stuck on 5.3.4 codeHS program (JavaScript)
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Stuck on 5.3.4 codeHS program (JavaScript)](http://StackOverflow.com/q/48712657) * * * ## My answer: Yes, automated code checkers depend on things like your function being set up just as specified. It is likely expect
posts.content:
Original question: Stuck on 5.3.4 codeHS program (JavaScript)

My answer:

Yes, automated code checkers depend on things like your function being set up just as specified. It is likely expecting your function to take 2 parameters, but yours wants 4, so when it sends in the values they are not getting assigned to the right variables.

Look at the values you have in your start function calls to horizontalLine. Do you notice that of the 4 given, 2 are always the same each time? Your 2nd and 4th argument are always the same, because, as the exercise prompt explains, flat lines have the same y value. So you don't need to pass them in separately because they are the same. You'll just pass it in once, but use it twice.

The prompt also specifies that the x value will always start at 0. Yet, you are passing it in every time (notice that your first parameter is always 0?). So again, you don't need to pass that in, just use it.

That's the concept, now for the implementation.

The first two lines of your function are actually doing, more or less, what they need to do. They are setting up the variables that DON'T need to be passed in. So, why are you passing them in? Just change your function definition to only send in the two parameters you're actually using!

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: Scrollable Flex-box Child issue in IE11/Edge
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Scrollable Flex-box Child issue in IE11/Edge](http://StackOverflow.com/q/48709343) * * * ## My answer: There is a known bug in IE where it gets confused about heights of flex items. Basically, the flex-item can't acce
posts.content:
Original question: Scrollable Flex-box Child issue in IE11/Edge

My answer:

There is a known bug in IE where it gets confused about heights of flex items. Basically, the flex-item can't access the parent's height to know how high to make itself. Oddly, it CAN access the height of a grand-parent. It is essentially the same as flex-bug #3 on this commonly used list, although your specifics are slightly different.

The easiest workaround, in my opinion, is to add:

display:flex;
flex-direction:column;

To a div wrapped around your flex-container (in your case, around the

element).

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: Are there other options besides "text-align:center;" for centering things in a DIV?
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Are there other options besides "text-align:center;" for centering things in a DIV?](http://StackOverflow.com/q/48673757) * * * ## My answer: Text-align:center works on elements that are "inline" or "inline-block". Th
posts.content:
Original question: Are there other options besides "text-align:center;" for centering things in a DIV?

My answer:

Text-align:center works on elements that are "inline" or "inline-block". That means text, images, links, etc. that don't ask to take up as much width as they can, only what they need. Their "display" property is set to inline, and they can be centered like text would be -- hence the name, text-align.

If you want to center a non-inline element, most often 'block', now you're talking about elements that naturally want as much width as they can get. So centering them doesn't mean much, because they fill the whole thing. In this case you can do so either by setting its left and right margins to 'auto' and specifying a width, or by using a different display mode on the parent like flex.

It looks like you are part of the way towards implementing the second option. On your parent element, you DO have display flex. But flex is like a wild stallion that must be tamed. It takes some getting used to. For instance, it doesn't care much about text-align:center.

Making your parent element flex (without any other specifications) is basically saying, "Hey parent element, fit in all of your children in a row." In your case you have two children, both of which are div's, so they will go side by side.

Flex has a primary axis (by default, horizontal) and to center the items within that axis you'd use justify-content: center. Adding that to your CSS for #loginArea puts all of the children in one row, but centered.

That may be what you want. If instead you wanted the loginInstructions div to be on it's own line, you could also add: flex-wrap:wrap; to the parent, allowing it to create additional rows, and flex-basis:100% to loginInstructions, telling it to take up 100% of a flex-row.

posts.title: Fun with recursive functions
posts.excerpt: Most repetitive code is written iteratively, with a relatively linear and stable flow to the code. Have a huge list of data? Let's go through it one item at a time. It's linear in that it's very easy to follow it from round A, to round B, t
posts.content:
Most repetitive code is written iteratively, with a relatively linear and stable flow to the code. Have a huge list of data? Let's go through it one item at a time. It's linear in that it's very easy to follow it from round A, to round B, to round C. And it's stable in that not much changes from round to round. [code language="javascript"]var characters = ['Harry','Ron','Hermione']; for ( var i = 0; i < characters.length; i++ ){ console.log( characters[ i ] ); } //Console output: //Harry //Ron //Hermione[/code] The code loops through the array, spitting out each one in turn, and then looks to the next item. When it runs out, it stops. Nothing changes each time except the counter we are using ( i ). Recursive code is usually more compact, more elegant, and WAY cooler. Simply put, it is a function (or any looping process) that calls itself. It's also hard to wrap your mind around, and has some pros and cons. Let's do the same thing as above but recursively. [code language="javascript"]var characters = ['Harry','Ron','Hermione']; logArray( characters ); function logArray( array ){ if ( array.length == 0 ) return; console.log( array.shift() ); logArray( array ); } //Console output: //Harry //Ron //Hermione[/code] Since this is a teaching example, our recursive function is actually not more concise. But, this does the exact same thing as our earlier function, with one additional minor difference. Can you spot it? It empties the original array! That's probably a bad thing. We'll talk about that in a moment, but first let's make sure we understand what's happening. [code language="javascript"]var characters = ['Harry','Ron','Hermione']; logArray( characters );[/code] First, we abstracted the loop into a separate function, then called the function. Good so far? [code language="javascript"]function logArray( array ){ if ( array.length == 0 ) return; console.log( array.shift() ); logArray( array ); }[/code] The function takes an array, and then let's skip over its first line for a moment. array.shift() pops off the first element of an array and returns it. Wrapped around this we are console.logging the output, so that same first item. In line 3 the function calls itself again, and we are officially recursive. The difference of course is that now our array is one item shorter because of the array.shift() call. So then we loop through the function again, this time without Harry. The check on line 1 fails a second time, because the array isn't empty. Ron gets logged, the function is called again, Hermione gets logged. After Hermione, the function is called again, but the check on line 1 passes. The array is empty, so that function ends. This null return statement echoes back through all the previous iterations, and we're done. So line 1 here is our 'base' case, and it's one of two key recursive needs. To not run indefinitely, recursive functions need to:

  1. Have data that changes in some way each time
  2. Have a base case that ends the process

What about that side effect?

Remember, this function wiped out our original array. When we passed it to the function, we sent our original (really, a direct reference to it, but still). It was emptied one item at a time, and now there's nothing left. This is almost certainly an unwanted side effect. How can we avoid it? First, we can use a time-tested trick: [code language="javascript"]var copy = JSON.parse( JSON.stringify( source ) );[/code] We first turn our object into JSON, which is just a string of text. Then we decode that text back into an object. A new one. That's right, we're Star Trek teleporting our object into a new copy. JSON.stringify decomposes the original Shatner, and JSON.parse builds a new copy from the blueprint. The original Kirk is dead, sad to say. Or, we can use a newer method: [code language="javascript"]var copy = Object.create( source ); [/code] The nice thing about this approach is that the source is actually a 'prototype' child of the original. We're not using that here, but it comes in handy in more advanced cases. So, we could create our copy before calling the function and or just build it into the function. The latter option is actually a bit complicated, because our recursive function depends on something changing from time to time, and if we're just passing copies around nothing's going to get done. [code language="javascript"]var characters = ['Harry','Ron','Hermione']; logArray( characters ); console.log( 'There are', characters.length, 'items left in the array.' ); function logArray( array ){ if ( array.length == 0 ) return; var copy = Object.create( array ); console.log( copy.shift() ); logArray( copy ); } //Console output: //Harry //Ron //Hermione //There are 3 items left in the array.[/code] So we create a copy each time and then shift the item off of it instead. The bad news here is we have now created tons of extra copies. Each time we loop through the array we've made a whole new object. So now we're a bit worse off than our original, iterative approach, from a memory management perspective. The good news is that the latest JavaScript is smart enough to ditch these objects ASAP if we do things right. Prior to ES6, JavaScript couldn't handle tail calling correctly at all. With ES6, it can, but only in 'strict' mode and only when certain conditions are met. Which brings us to a final warning about recursive functions.

Tail Considerations

As the function calls itself, we can think of it as building out a nested tree. logArray() // first time, outputs Harry ---logArray() //second time, outputs Ron ------logArray() // third time, outputs Hermione ---------logArray() // fourth time, outputs nothing ------------returns null; ---------returns that same null; ------returns still that same null; ---returns null, the original; returns once more, the same null; Null is nothing, so 'the same' null is just a concept we're using to demonstrate that the final return value is echo-ing back through up the chain. As you can see, once the function calls itself that iteration is pretty much done. It doesn't have anything left to do except return, so anything inside of it can be trashed. But JavaScript won't do this for us unless we set it up correctly. Specifically, the return statement has to be the last command of the function, and it can't depend on anything else. So with recursive functions, it's important to make sure that your recursive calls are clean. In JavaScript, this is called "proper tail calling." Even something like this: [code language="javascript"]function factorial ( n ){ use 'strict'; if ( n == 0 ) return 1; return n * factorial( n - 1 ); } console.log( factorial( 5 ) ); //120[/code] ...which is the most common recursive example, factorials ( i.e. factorial(5) = 5*4*3*2*1 ), means that each iteration has to stay alive, because it has to do that n * step AFTER all the iterations are set up. The loop here would look like: factorial( 5 ) ---factorial( 4 ) ------factorial( 3 ) ---------factorial( 2 ) ------------factorial( 1 ) ---------------factorial( 0 ) ------------------return 1; ---------------return 1 * 1; ------------return 2 * 1; ---------return 3 * 2; ------return 4 * 6; ---return 5 * 24; In this case it's not a problem, because we are creating almost no memory each time. But if we were copying a huge object each time, we might run into problems. We could instead rewrite the factorial function to have two arguments, the running total and the next integer, so that each return statement only has to do one thing: return a value. The rule of thumb is that if a return statement has to 'do' anything other than returning, it's not a 'proper tail call' and can't be optimized.

Advantages

The conciseness of recursive code is probably outweighed by the difficulty in understanding it. However, there are a few cases where it really makes the most sense. The factorials example above is a common one, as is 'tree' exploration. By tree I mean the association of items into parent and children branches, whether files on a hard drive or even the DOM of a web page. Your function can explore the whole tree by repeatedly calling itself at each level. Our Harry Potter is not, alas, a good recursive candidate. The iterative version is easier to understand, faster to code, and probably faster to run. At the end of the day, recursive functions:

  1. Are hard to write and understand
  2. Come with risks
  3. Offer a few niche capabilities,
  4. But are VERY fun to write :)

posts.title: How Git Works
posts.excerpt: In preparing a training series on git, I previewed 6 different video courses to try and identify the best approach to understanding git. I did this in an effort to spare others from the learning pains that are so common when diving into ver
posts.content: In preparing a training series on git, I previewed 6 different video courses to try and identify the best approach to understanding git. I did this in an effort to spare others from the learning pains that are so common when diving into version control. You can read about commits, merges, rebasing, pulls, and so forth a hundred times but until you start messing with it, until you get it wrong a bunch of times, it doesn't start to click. I found the available courses lacking, because they are taught from the perspective of someone who (naturally) already understands git. They struggled to find a balance between explaining how git "thinks" and using git as a black-box. The closest courses to successfully explaining git and providing the right foundation are by Paola Perrotta: How Git Works and Mastering Git. How Git Works is fascinating, because he peels back the layers of the onion that is git, explaining each component bit by bit. He starts with the SHA algorithm, which is a truly fascinating topic. In developing my own learning resources, I created an approach based on Perrotta's. Say you had two cloth bags, full of dozens of items and quite bulky and heavy. How could you tell if the two bags contained the same contents? The obvious answer is to take the contents out and compare them. How laborious! What if you didn't have to be certain, just reasonably confident? Would there be a faster way? Sure -- you could compare the shape of the bags, and more importantly their weight. If they were exactly, down to 1/10th of a gram, the same weight, you might say you were reasonably confident the contents were the same. Of course, different things can weigh the same. But what if they couldn't? That's the advantage behind SHA. It's a way for the computer to very quickly get the 'shape' of a file. But unlike weight, no two things will have the same SHA. So now we have a way for a computer to (a) see if a file has changed, and even (b) see if two different files have the same exact contents. This is really the root of all of git. Without SHA, if you had 1,000 revisions of a project, the computer would store a copy of each file for each revision. Many of the files in those 1,000 revisions would be exactly the same, but the computer wouldn't know. But with SHA, it only has to track unique files. Perrotta wisely expands out from this core point, explaining how directories also have a SHA "hash", as does each commit. He rips the veil off of the .git directory, showing what it actually is -- a collection of file content objects ("blobs") and of other objects showing their relationship -- both to each other, and across time. True, knowing how git works does not tell one how to use it. But it does set the proper foundation. It means that from then on in your training whenever you use words like "commit" and "hash" you can have a realistic mental image of what they are. Perrotta's approach is the winner, and I hope my own training resources I develop from this approach build on his work in the same clear, helpful manner.

posts.title: CSS, The Confusing Bits -- Part 2: Z-Index
posts.excerpt: [Part 1 - Series Introduction](https://tmdesigned.com/post/css-the-confusing-bits-part-1-introduction/) Part 2 - Z-Index [Part 3 - Positioning](https://www.tmdesigned.com/css-the-confusing-bits-part-3-positioning/) Part 4 - Height and Width
posts.content:
Part 1 - Series Introduction
Part 2 - Z-Index
Part 3 - Positioning
Part 4 - Height and Width

Z-Index is more complicated than it at first seems. "Oh, they're layers," you say. "Higher numbers go on top of lower ones." Like so many other things, you test it out in a limited context, it seems to work as you expect, and you go about your merry way with a completely wrong understanding.

Until it doesn't work anymore.

Well, to be fair, that definition isn't wrong per se, it's just incomplete. Very incomplete. So what are we missing?

Here is the technical definition of how your browser is supposed to layer elements. I've put it in a scroll-box so you don't have to read it all, just skim it. I mean seriously, the actual title of this spec is "Elaborate description of Stacking Contexts". When a technical document refers to it's description as elaborate, buckle your seatbelt.

  1. If the element is a root element:

    1. background color of element over the entire canvas.
    2. background image of element, over the entire canvas, anchored at the origin that would be used if it was painted for the root element.

  2. If the element is a block, list-item, or other block equivalent:

    1. background color of element unless it is the root element.
    2. background image of element unless it is the root element.
    3. border of element.

    Otherwise, if the element is a block level table:

    1. table backgrounds (color then image) unless it is the root element.
    2. column group backgrounds (color then image).
    3. column backgrounds (color then image).
    4. row group backgrounds (color then image).
    5. row backgrounds (color then image).
    6. cell backgrounds (color then image).
    7. all table borders (in tree order for separated borders).

  3. Stacking contexts formed by positioned descendants with negative z-indices (excluding 0) in z-index order (most negative first) then tree order.

  4. For all its in-flow, non-positioned, block-level descendants in tree order: If the element is a block, list-item, or other block equivalent:

    1. background color of element.
    2. background image of element.
    3. border of element.

    Otherwise, the element is a table:

    1. table backgrounds (color then image).
    2. column group backgrounds (color then image).
    3. column backgrounds (color then image).
    4. row group backgrounds (color then image).
    5. row backgrounds (color then image).
    6. cell backgrounds (color then image).
    7. all table borders (in tree order for separated borders).

  5. All non-positioned floating descendants, in tree order. For each one of these, treat the element as if it created a new stacking context, but any positioned descendants and descendants which actually create a new stacking context should be considered part of the parent stacking context, not this new one.

  6. If the element is an inline element that generates a stacking context, then:

    1. For each line box that the element is in:
      1. Jump to 7.2.1 for the box(es) of the element in that line box (in tree order).

  7. Otherwise: first for the element, then for all its in-flow, non-positioned, block-level descendants in tree order:

    1. If the element is a block-level replaced element, then: the replaced content, atomically.
    2. Otherwise, for each line box of that element:

      1. For each box that is a child of that element, in that line box, in tree order:

        1. background color of element.

        2. background image of element.

        3. border of element.

        4. For inline elements:

          1. For all the element's in-flow, non-positioned, inline-level children that are in this line box, and all runs of text inside the element that is on this line box, in tree order:
            1. If this is a run of text, then:
              1. any underlining affecting the text of the element, in tree order of the elements applying the underlining (such that the deepest element's underlining, if any, is painted topmost and the root element's underlining, if any, is drawn bottommost).
              2. any overlining affecting the text of the element, in tree order of the elements applying the overlining (such that the deepest element's overlining, if any, is painted topmost and the root element's overlining, if any, is drawn bottommost).
              3. the text.
              4. any line-through affecting the text of the element, in tree order of the elements applying the line-through (such that the deepest element's line-through, if any, is painted topmost and the root element's line-through, if any, is drawn bottommost).
            2. Otherwise, jump to 7.2.1 for that element.

          For inline-block and inline-table elements:

          1. For each one of these, treat the element as if it created a new stacking context, but any positioned descendants and descendants which actually create a new stacking context should be considered part of the parent stacking context, not this new one.

          For inline-level replaced elements:

          1. the replaced content, atomically.

        Some of the boxes may have been generated by line splitting or the Unicode bidirectional algorithm.

      2. Optionally, the outline of the element (see 10 below).

    3. Optionally, if the element is block-level, the outline of the element (see 10 below).

  8. All positioned descendants with 'z-index: auto' or 'z-index: 0', in tree order. For those with 'z-index: auto', treat the element as if it created a new stacking context, but any positioned descendants and descendants which actually create a new stacking context should be considered part of the parent stacking context, not this new one. For those with 'z-index: 0', treat the stacking context generated atomically.

  9. Stacking contexts formed by positioned descendants with z-indices greater than or equal to 1 in z-index order (smallest first) then tree order.

  10. Finally, implementations that do not draw outlines in steps above must draw outlines from this stacking context at this stage. (It is recommended to draw outlines in this step and not in the steps above.)https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS21/zindex.html

You don't need to go through that (I did mention that, didn't I?) There's probably just one key concept you've been missing, and I won't drag it out. There is one key element of z-indices that trips people up: stacking contexts.

Stacking Contexts

Think of stacking contexts like groups that move up and down together. Other elements from outside the group can be below the group, or above the group, but not in-between the group--you can't be "in-between" a single thing, after all.

Z-Index stacking contexts work the same way. Each stacking context is a group, and its elements are layered in a certain order. Then, the group as a whole is layered in a certain order with other stacking contexts, and so on.

So if your page header is a stacking context (group), and your footer is a stacking context, either one or the other will be on top. You couldn't interleave elements of the footer and the header. (This does come up, by the way, especially with sticky items.)

What creates a stacking context? Turns out there are a lot of causes, which does not help confusion on the matter. The main ones are:

  1. The HTML element automatically creates one. Because of course.
  2. If an element is positioned absolute, positioned relative, or is a flex-item, AND has a specified z-index.
  3. If an element is positioned fixed.
  4. If an element is partially transparent, or has transform, filter, perspective, clip-path, or mask.

That last one often surprises people, but it makes sense. The browser has to render it off screen and it's not going to put up with z-index on top of that. (On top of that. Yep.)

Z-Index Strategies

First, if you know you are going to be dealing with z-indices (i.e. you are going to have a fixed menu, modal boxes, overlays, etc.) then it's worth the time to plan it out before structuring the DOM.  You don't have to know everything, just think out the groups.

Your diagram doesn't have to be as slipshod as mine, and you don't even have to draw it at all. Just give some thought to which layers need to be on top of which other ones, and cross-reference that in your mind with how you're structuring your DOM.

Second, if nothing else, when z-indices don't behave as you think they should, think back to stacking contexts. If you can identify which elements are creating them, you'll likely be close to your solution.

Finally, there is a handy little Chrome extension called z-context, which simply tells you whether a selected element creates a stacking context, and if so, why. It can be useful for debugging, although you'll start to identify the causes yourself once you start paying attention.

posts.title: What I wish I had known about Angular
posts.excerpt: Making the jump from vanilla JavaScript to a library like jQuery is _refreshing_. "You mean I don't have to \_\_\_\_ anymore ??" These libraries are really meant to help and smooth over some coding rough edges. Frameworks like Angular are
posts.content:
Making the jump from vanilla JavaScript to a library like jQuery is refreshing. "You mean I don't have to ____ anymore ??" These libraries are really meant to help and smooth over some coding rough edges. Frameworks like Angular are nothing like that. At all. They aren't meant to smooth over rough edges, they're meant to expand the capability of the language. That's the practical way of looking at it. The technical way of looking at it is, "Everything Angular accomplishes it does through JavaScript, and it's really opening up a very advanced usage of what's already there, smoothing over the rough edges of getting to that level." But again, for the average JavaScript programmer, switching to Angular (or React or similar) is not about making things easier, it's about making things better and more advanced. Having spent the last month or two diving into Angular for a few real-world apps, here is what I wish I had known going in. Perhaps this will be helpful to some other "JavaScript ninjas" who are making the transition to the full framework of Angular.

  • Angular is not AngularJS. AngularJS was the first version, and was used more or less like any other library. You included the whole library, wrote your "angular" code as part of your output files, and when the user visited it "sort of" compiled your code on the fly. Angular 2 (and 3,4 etc.) is usually precompiled. You have a whole project full of files, and you compile them down into an output JavaScript file. I think there are two advantages here. First, you get a better framework for advanced developing, separating your project out into appropriate pieces and keeping a helpful file structure. Second, the Angular compiler doesn't have to run every time the user comes, and only the pieces that are needed are used.
  • You need a solid knowledge of ES6 first. You could get away with avoiding some features (like "let" and arrow functions) but not all of them. It relies heavily on JavaScript modules and class syntax.
  • If your app will have asynchronous elements, plan those out first. The most obvious example are database and API requests, which take an unspecified amount of time to complete. You'll need to have the rest of your app accommodate those requests and if your app structure doesn't support it, you'll end up rewriting large chunks. If you've never dealt with asynchronous code, Angular is probably not the place to start. First read about JS promises, then Angular Observables, then Subjects and Behavior Subjects. Code real examples of each of those and then move on to the next. Get through all 4 and you'll be golden.
  • Don't confuse ES6 modules with Angular modules. ES6 modules are about separating your code into files, letting the files reference each other, and encouraging OOP practices. Angular modules are how the pieces your app are separated and connected.
  • Also, don't confuse JavaScript imports and exports with module imports and exports. They're largely unrelated. JavaScript imports (usually at the top of the file) and exports (usually before declarations like classes) let the code in different files see each other. Angular module imports and exports let the different pieces of your application use each other. There's some overlap.
  • Take advantage of the Angular CLI._ _ The command line interface will generate many elements for you, and more importantly, it will do it right. It's a push in the right direction of best practices, including unit testing, naming conventions, and file management.
  • The view hierarchy is different from your application hierarchy. The view hierarchy is how the user moves from section to section of your app, while the application hierarchy is how you've structured the code of your application. A user might drill down from one component into another, but those components might not necessarily be parent-child components in your code. However, they often can be as it makes sense to structure your application into logical sections.
  • Understand how the scope of Angular's application hierarchy works. Components are contained within modules, and can only see other components that are exposed to it by the module. But modules can (usually) all see each other. The Angular compiler actually puts all the modules together except in certain circumstances.
  • Think of providers as single instance classes. If different parts of your app need to talk to each other, they can do it through a "service". These are the stable islands amidst your application's shifting seas. Need to track data throughout your app? A service can be your application's data model.
  • Finally, and this applies to most programming learning, don't try and go through an entire training program or online course without getting your hands dirty. The pieces won't conceptually fall into place until you've tried to do them wrong over and over, and finally get it right.

posts.title: Multiple word JavaScript searching
posts.excerpt: The most simple JavaScript search is: haystack.indexOf(needle) . If the result is -1, there's no match, otherwise there is. But this is not very robust. The search string (needle) must be written exactly (order, case, etc.) in the string y
posts.content:
The most simple JavaScript search is:  haystack.indexOf(needle) . If the result is -1, there's no match, otherwise there is. But this is not very robust. The search string (needle) must be written exactly (order, case, etc.) in the string you're searching (haystack). For the auction scraper, I wanted a slightly more robust search. I didn't need multiple searching operators, but I did want to search for multiple words and have it find matches even if they came in a different order. In other words, "1080p tv" should match the item "Westinghouse TV with 1080p resolution". This actually wasn't difficult to achieve: [code language="javascript"]function filter(keywords){ keywords = keywords.toLowerCase(); var keywordArray = keywords.split(' '); if(keywordArray.length==1 && keywordArray[0].length<2){ return; } $('.auction-item .card-title').each(function(){ var remove = false; var i = 0; while(!remove && i<keywordArray.length){ if($(this).text().toLowerCase().indexOf(keywordArray[i]) == -1){ remove = true; } i++; } if(remove) { $(this).parent().parent().parent().hide(); } }); }[/code] A nice way to think of this is that we're removing the non-matches. The basic logic of this function, then is:

  1. Split the search string into separate words
  2. If there's nothing to search, quit
  3. For each item we're searching over:
    1. Assume it's a match
    2. Loop through each of the search keywords
      1. If it doesn't have one of the keywords, it's no longer match
    3. If we get through the last of the keywords, and the item hasn't failed any of these "tests", then it's a true match
    4. If it's not a true match, remove it

posts.title: Developing a PHP based web scraper
posts.excerpt: Let's say a local-based online auction service provides no search capability across separate inventories of 30-200 items each. To address this for my own use, and as a practical development exercise while on paternity leave, I created a PHP
posts.content: Let's say a local-based online auction service provides no search capability across separate inventories of 30-200 items each. To address this for my own use, and as a practical development exercise while on paternity leave, I created a PHP powered web scraper to access the publicly available information and consolidate it into a searchable and easy-to-use database. While I only accessed publicly available information, I did not want to take advantage of their bandwidth. I implemented a local caching solution to reduce queries (to below-normal-web-browsing rates), and chose not to pull images from their CDN. The result is simply a single, searchable database of what was previously separate pages. The benefit, however, is drastically reduced searching time. The source website uses a JSON data source for the listing of auctions, but not of items. This made it easy to get a list of the auctions to poll, but not to actually scrape them. To do the latter, I had to actually scrape the DOMs. Scraping in this manner is liable to break at the slightest update of the source site, but other than using regex patterns as robustly as possible there was no alternative. I wrote the PHP portion in an object oriented fashion. A "scraper" class handles the overall action and stores resulting "auctions". Each auction is made up of some meta-data (i.e. end-time) and in turn stores "items". The interactivity of the page (AJAX calls and searching) is handled via JavaScript. In separate posts, I write a few about interesting lessons gleaned from this project, including multi-term keyword searching, the advantages of CURL requests, and $_SESSION caching. The full source of this project is available on GitHub.

posts.title: StackOverflow Answer: Mouse Up event bottleneck-ing my animation?
posts.excerpt: ## Original question: [Mouse Up event bottleneck-ing my animation?](http://StackOverflow.com/q/46449128) * * * ## My answer: I have a modal window gallery coded by hand, and the performance when loading and unloading the modal is very slow
posts.content:
Original question: Mouse Up event bottleneck-ing my animation?

My answer:

I have a modal window gallery coded by hand, and the performance when loading and unloading the modal is very slow (down to 1-2 FPS) which is very noticeable. That's without transitions; just setting display to none.

I did a performance review, and that's what leads me to my question. When closing the modal, it took 500ms to hide, of which 300ms is "Other". The only other I can find is the Mouse Up event.

Should this take that long (i.e. run the duration of the script it triggers)? Any other ideas what the bottleneck could be if Scripting, Rendering, and Painting is not the issue judging by their times?

posts.title: CSS, The Confusing Bits -- Part 1: Introduction
posts.excerpt: I've always considered CSS to be the wild factor of the 4 web design "quadrangle" of languages. HTML is straight up structure; the browser just works its way down and the elements simply exist without much ado. JavaScript can be tricky, but
posts.content:
I've always considered CSS to be the wild factor of the 4 web design "quadrangle" of languages. HTML is straight up structure; the browser just works its way down and the elements simply exist without much ado. JavaScript can be tricky, but really follows a process and more importantly, you can observe that process one debugger step at a time. PHP (or your server side language of choice) is a bit heavier and harder to observe, but if it's not doing what you think it should, the fault lies with you.

But CSS...CSS lives in the wild. It has such capabilities, from simple layout to amazing animations, and it's rapidly developing. There's even a spec for it, and you can read (in not so pleasant terms) how each of the standards should really work. But out in the wild world of multiple browsers and differing implementations, CSS behaves in unexpected ways. A lot.

An obvious example is the flexbox display model. Take a flex container and simple element:
[code language="css"] .flex-container{ min-height:15em; display:flex; align-items:center; background-color:blue; } .flex-item{ height:5em; background-color:red; flex-grow:1; } [/code][code language="html5"]

[/code]

[caption id="attachment_549" align="aligncenter" width="640"] Ex. 1 - The red flex item is centered vertically, as it should be[/caption]

Yet Internet Explorer, King of All CSS Bugs, renders the red bar at the top of the flex container. Is this a missing browser prefix? A justifiably different interpretation of a standard? No, this is a known IE bug. IE renders the correct height of the flex container, but cannot calculate it correctly to center its items.

[caption id="attachment_550" align="aligncenter" width="640"] Ex. 1b - What gives, IE?[/caption]

Yet, wrap the flex container in another flex container (set simply with a direction of column, thus having no other layout effects) and it all works out correctly. IE can calculate a flex grandparent's height, just not a parent's.

Moving beyond bugs

So much of CSS coding consists of learning, identifying, and remembering these bugs. Even when they're not bugs so much as they are quirks or differences, it's easy to see why CSS coding seems more like an art than a science. It's like you're wrangling a semi-tame beast that sometimes forgets it's being domesticated.

So what can we do, other than write up lists and learn from quite frustrating debugging? Well, we can learn the parts that do make sense better. The more we know about how CSS "thinks" under the hood, the more we'll recognize where a browser is deviating from the norm.

A better understanding of some commonly misunderstood CSS elements will go a long way in improving our coding efficiency. In this series, I'll be looking at:

  1. Z-indexing
  2. Positioning
  3. Width/Height (how it grows and overflows)

posts.title: Passing variables between JavaScript and PHP
posts.excerpt: JavaScript and PHP share many similarities but are fundamentally different. JavaScript code is compiled and executed by the user's browser (at least in the case of websites, although JavaScript can be run on other devices and even by the se
posts.content:
JavaScript and PHP share many similarities but are fundamentally different. JavaScript code is compiled and executed by the user's browser (at least in the case of websites, although JavaScript can be run on other devices and even by the server with Node.js). PHP, however, is compiled and executed by the server. By the time the user receives the page, the PHP is gone. There's absolutely no trace of it on the page. This makes it ideal for secure processing of data, database interactions, user authentication, and basically anything else you don't want users to see, touch, or know about. Understanding that basic difference is fundamental, because often for a web application to work the two languages have to interact. Since one is completely done and gone before the other even starts, you have to think of things differently depending on which direction you want to go.

From PHP to JavaScript

This is the simplest of the two directions, and there's really two different ways to go about this.

Direct PHP to JavaScript injection

Since PHP is done before JavaScript starts, this first method essentially has PHP plop it out right in the middle of the JavaScript. [code language="javascript"] var userIsRegistered = false; [/code]So we have some conditional logic, but all that's happening before the page is sent to the browser. All the browser will see is: [code language="javascript"] var userIsRegistered = false; userIsRegistered = true; [/code] Or, it won't see the second line if the conditional fails. We make sure to always declare the JavaScript variable ahead of time to account for either case. What are the cons here? Well first of all, it's a little clunky. We're mixing languages, trying to keep everything separate, and our end result is kind of funny. Second, we have a possible performance bottleneck. If ...some php code here... involves a complicated query, we're waiting.

AJAX Requests

A little cleaner, but a lot more work, is to create a separate PHP file whose sole purpose is to feed our data.What we're really doing here is messing with the timing of our scripts. Normally, it goes:

  1. PHP
  2. JavaScript

But if at some point JavaScript calls a separate PHP file, that is when that PHP runs. So instead we have:

  1. PHP
  2. JavaScript
  3. PHP file called by JavaScript
  4. The rest of JavaScript from #2 above

Since JavaScript can invoke PHP, we have now call server side code from client side code. The door is wide open. We can extend this and repeat it any number of times. The example above might look a little something like this, using jQuery's helper function for AJAX requests: [code language="javascript"]//Starting our answer as false, it will change to true if AJAX request succeeds var userIsRegistered = false; $.ajax('/getUserData.php',{ //The data we send -- including both the question we're asking and info to determine the answer data: { username: myUsername, function: isRegistered }, //What happens when we get our answer. Also, our answer will be in the 'data' variable. success: function(data){ //Turn it into an object var result = JSON.parse(data); //Make sure response succeeded and didn't fail if(result.response == 'OK'){ if(result.answer){ userIsRegistered = true; } }else{ //Response wasn't OK, so what's the deal? console.log(result.message); } }, error: function(){ //Handle AJAX connection errors } }); [/code] [code language="php"] //separate php file //Standard object to hold our response data var resultObject = new stdClass(); //Start with a default of failure, will be changed to OK if request succeeds resultObject.response = 'Failure'; //Were we asked a question? if(isset($_GET['function'])){ //What question were we asked? switch($_GET['function']){ case 'isRegistered': //Oh, we were asked if a user is registered //Do we have enough information? if(isset($_GET['username'])){ //We have enough information, so we ARE sending back a good response //(We would actually likely want to make sure the connection was good first before assuming this. But that's beyond the example here.) resultObject.response = 'OK'; if(is_user_registered()){ //User was registered, so our answer is yes resultObject.answer = true; }else{ //User was not registered, so our answer is no resultObject.answer = false; } }else{ //We don't have enough information resultObject.message = 'Username must be provided'.; } break; } } //Spitting out everything we're sending back echo json_encode(resultObject); [/code] This is admittedly more complex than absolutely necessary, but you'll see why. First, what exactly are we doing here? Put simply, JavaScript is asking a separate PHP file a question. We're doing this by specifying a function to run (isRegistered) and passing it some data to use to answer the question. The PHP file determines (a) What question am I being asked? (b) Do I have enough information to answer it? and (c) What is the answer? It uses a simple object to store its work, then at the end of the day outputs that object (encoded into simple text, i.e. JSON). The AJAX function of our JavaScript waits for information, which the PHP gives it by echoing out the data. It then has to interpret the response and make sure everything went as planned. You wouldn't want to just check if the result was true/false because...why was it false? So with just a small increase in complexity, we've also upped our capabilities. Now, we could instead create a file whose whole purpose is to return the answer to the question, "Is the user registered?" We might name that file, isUserRegistered.php, and all we'd have to pass it is some criteria on which it would determine the answer (like a username or email). It would return yes or no, and we'd be done. But by abstracting a layer, we get so much more. We call the file something a bit more generic (i.e. getUserData.php), and expect it to handle the answers to a lot of questions about the user. Maybe it can answer "Is the user registered?", "Can the user edit a post?", "What is the user's email address?", and a hundred other inquiries. So in addition to sending it criteria, we also send it the question we're asking (i.e. isRegistered). In exchange, it also does a bit more for us as well. It gives us an answer, but also a helpful error message if it fails. Why did it fail -- was it because a username wasn't provided? We could also build in checks to make sure a failure wasn't because of a database error, a slow server, a non-existent user, etc. So the big advantage here over the first method is the clean, separated layers of code. PHP is in a PHP file doing PHP things. JavaScript does JavaScript things. Maybe that doesn't matter to you, but it will as your application grows. It keeps things nice and neat, and it simply works better and allows for extra capabilities. Furthermore, while we're waiting for that AJAX request to complete, we can also be doing other JavaScript-y things. Note: Each time we do an AJAX call, that's a new HTTP request. So really, we'd probably want to bundle some of these together. PHP could instead return a user object one time, with all of its capabilities clearly spelled out. But sometimes things are more dynamic, depending on user input or dealing with large datasets, and pulling things in smaller pieces makes more sense. And what's more, sometimes things aren't going in this direction at all!

From JavaScript to PHP

If you understand method #2 above, then you may have thought ahead and realized, "Wait a minute, JavaScript is already sending information to PHP in my AJAX request above!" That's right, we've already answered the second direction here. We sent a criteria (username) and a question (isRegistered) in our example above. We can just as easily send any other data to PHP. The important thing to think of here is that with AJAX, we are changing that 'natural' order of events from (1) PHP, (2) JavaScript to anything we want. So if JavaScript needs PHP to update something for us (like a user profile), it can send that to a helper file which doesn't run until that point. We could even use the same file and send it a different function to run (of course it would need some additional data, as well as some solid authentication protocols).

What have we accomplished?

The great thing about the more complete method described here is that in the end, we've basically created an API. It can handle a variety of tasks, and it can handle them robustly. We can extend it, reuse it, and refine it. As our application grows, our API can grow with it. That's a scalable, robust solution!

posts.title: Passing immutable data with encrypted tokens
posts.excerpt: _Update: When I first wrote this, I thought I was so clever for coming up with the concept of encrypting JSON data and using it as a token in the URL. Well, it was clever. So clever that other people had already come up with it. It's referr
posts.content:
Update: When I first wrote this, I thought I was so clever for coming up with the concept of encrypting JSON data and using it as a token in the URL. Well, it was clever. So clever that other people had already come up with it. It's referred to as JSON Web Tokens (JWT) and is an industry standard.

GET & POST Data, in general

The general rule of thumb for passing HTTP data is to use GET for retrieving data, and POST for sending it. (Cookies and session variables are not passed in the HTTP request per se.) POST is harder to manipulate, but is absolutely not hacker proof. It's actually quite easy to simulate POST requests and if a server resource is not hardened against malicious data, then malicious data will find its way in eventually.

The main difference between the two is that GET data is passed as part of the URL. This has some disadvantages (aesthetic and functional), but also a unique advantage -- the GET parameters are bookmark-able and navigable. That means a user can save the results and return later, share it on social media, or navigate back and forth by pages.

Tangent: storing state in the hash

It's this advantage that some developers exploit to hold state. The web is a generally state-less medium, but storing state values in the URL in the same manner as GET variables works surprisingly well. With a library, like jQuery BBQ, multiple parameters can be read and written with ease without even having to deserialize the entire string.

Back to real HTTP requests

Anyways, we tend not to store even quasi-sensitive data in GET/POST requests because they're so manipulatable. We wouldn't care if a user messed with a search parameter, because wherever the form is not confined to the page we would be sanitizing the data. But for protected data, say the amount of a financial deposit, we don't really want that even remotely mutable.

But what if we do want those parameters to be navigable? For instance, we might want to send the page as a link with certain values preset. So we need them in the URL, but we don't want our users messing with them.

Case study: pre-filled employment application

Let's say you've posted a job, and received a resume from an interested candidate. They're a good fit, but you need them to fill out your standard employment agreement.

Now, you could send them a blank form, sure. But maybe your agreement has the hourly wage on it, and you don't want them thinking that's a negotiable item. Wouldn't it be better to send them a customized link, where that data is already pre-filled (and locked in place)?

What not to do

So, you could send them a link like this:

 https://www.yoursite.com/forms/employment_agreement/?name=John+Doe&position=Maintenance+Technician&wage=15

Hopefully by now, you see the problem with this. John might try and get smart, change the wage to 20, and hope you don't notice before HR enters him in the system. Even if you caught it, it's an awkward scenario.

A better solution: encrypted hash data

What we can instead do is the same technique, but with one extra step: encryption. We take the same data stored in the URL, and encrypt it to end up with something like:

 https://www.yoursite.com/forms/employment_agreement/?accessToken=5d189b2278eba41061f2f44ffc6250e2068167677274deea1f8a14360558d4e6d6c0d2b027fa8f3286eb52e700befb1d331b5ff441ad9ff042b09c6701569a

To be clear, we're not encrypting the data because it's top-secret and sensitive. I'm not suggesting doing this with a bank account number, but in our case, we're just encrypting the data so the user doesn't monkey around with it.

We'll use the same private key to encrypt and decrypt this token, and since the user is not privy to this key, he cannot modify or substitute the data. Changing just one character in the string will throw the entire result.

That link with the token appended could be given directly to the applicant, and the page itself will be responsible for decrypting the data, populating the form, and protecting those input fields.

Encrypting / decrypting data

PHP comes with cryptographically strong encryption functionality, openssl, which just has to be enabled on the server. Doing so gives us access to 4 helpful functions:

  • openssl_random_pseudo_bytes -- creates random bytes, useful for creating keys
  • openssl_cipher_iv_length -- returns length of a given encryption method, to be used to kick off encryption method
  • openssl_encrypt -- encrypts string
  • openssl_decrypt -- decrypts string

You don't need a master's degree in cryptography to use these functions and set this up. With just these 4 functions, our basic flow is this:

  1. Create a private key ONE TIME, and store it securely on the server (i.e. in a hidden php variable). We use openssl_random_pseudo_bytes for this.
  2. Each time we need to create a custom token (i.e. send a custom link), we store whatever data we need in a string. JSON is a natural choice. I create a separate, token-generating form for this process. Here we're just using JavaScript.
  3. Before we can encrypt it, we also need something called an an initialization vector each time we want to encrypt something -- the AES encryption method mixes each chunk of the data with the previous chunk. So...the first chunk needs something random to mix with. We store that vector as well as the encrypted data, since we need it to start the unraveling process, and these two together make up the token. openssl_cipher_iv_length gets us the right length to feed to openssl_random_pseudo_bytes, which we're now using a second time.
  4. Now we encrypt it, which requires that private key and the vector we made. Here we use openssl_encrypt.
  5. We save the token, and send it in a link as part of the URL.
  6. When it's fed back to us (i.e. the user clicks the link), we decrypt the string using the SAME init vector, and the SAME private key, using openssl_decrypt. Hey, look! It's our old friend, JSON string!
  7. We do whatever we need to do with the data (i.e. JSON.parse it, then populate the form with it, etc.)
  8. If we need to submit those same values, we pass through the encrypted token to make sure the data it contains is untouched.

For a nearly-complete code example, see the link below which shows all 4 of those functions working together. The only things it doesn't show is the JSON encoding/decoding, and saving the private key for later use.

That's all there is to it! We can now generate a unique token using our special, employees-only form. Inside of that encrypted data is all of the protected information we don't want our prospective employee screwing around with. From the end-user's perspective, the applicant is just receiving a tailor-made custom link. As a bonus, if we've also used it to pre-populate his name, address, etc., he'll be even more impressed with our company for seeming like we have our HR act together.

P.S. The limit for a URL is 4KB. So including our actual URL location, we have 4KB of encrypted data we can store. URL's are ASCII text, which is 1 byte per character. So that means our total is 4,000 characters. In my real-world case that led to this post, I stored 16 property/value pairs in a JSON object, and encrypted it came out to 800 characters including the initialization vector. 

 
Special thanks to:

https://blog.turret.io/the-missing-php-aes-encryption-example/

posts.title: JavaScript vs PHP Syntax Cheatsheet
posts.excerpt: ## Learning new programming languages There are core concepts that carry over to virtually all programming languages. Loops, functions, and variables are part of (nearly?) every modern language. What's more, many _approaches_ one takes to
posts.content:
Learning new programming languages

There are core concepts that carry over to virtually all programming languages. Loops, functions, and variables are part of (nearly?) every modern language. What's more, many approaches one takes to languages largely carry over as well. Knowing what you want to do and how you want to do it is 80% of the art of computer science. The other 20% (which takes at least 50% of the time!) is actually writing the code in the vocabulary and grammar of a given language and getting it to work. The bright side of all of this is that if you really know computer programming, it doesn't take that long to learn a new language. You study syntax, grammar, and a few particularities like memory management and before you know it, you're programming in the new language (crudely, of course, but still). All of this goes to say that it's not all that hard to learn a new language, but it does take time.

Switching back and forth between PHP and JavaScript

On a typical LAMP server (Linux, Apache, MySQL, and PHP) the developer spends most of their time in the realm of JavaScript and PHP. They serve different needs, and they work really well together. They even interact -- JavaScript can call PHP with AJAX, and PHP can communicate back or even directly write out JavaScript code. There are some underlying major differences between the two. For instance, PHP is actually class based while JavaScript relies on prototypal inheritance. But it's the little things that trip you up. All similarities aside, switching back and forth is a real bitch. Thus I present the PHP / JavaScript Syntax Cheatsheet. Only the differences, those nasty little subtleties that drive me crazy, will make it into the list.

 JavaScript PHP
If/Elseif, else if, elseif, elseif, else
Declaration hoistingYesNo
 Including add'tl. filesappend to head :( include() / require() / require_once()
 Logging console.log(msg) error_log(msg)
 Writing to screen DOM manipulation echo, printf, etc.
 Scope Lexical using functions, + this scoping Local unless global specified
 This keyword Depends on call-site, method Current object
Functions are objectsYesNo
Class inheritanceNo, prototype chain instead (reverse of class inheritance)Yes
New keywordCreates object, links prototype chain, sets 'this' to that objectRequired to instantiate object
 Type checking typeof variable is_string(variable), is_int(variable), etc.
 Type castingparseInt, toString, parseFloat(int)variable,(float)variable,(string)variable
 Object creationvar obj = {}; $obj = new stdClass();
 Add object prop obj.prop = ... $obj->prop = ...
 Access object prop ... = obj.prop ... = obj['prop']  ... = $obj->prop ... = $obj::prop uninstantiated
 Looping object properties for(var prop in obj) foreach($obj as $key->$value)
Declaring arraysvar arr = [];$arr = array();
Pushing to arraysarr.push(item)$arr[] = item;
