String concatenation'this is' + 'a sentence' 'this is' . 'a sentence'
String delimiters', "',",<<<EOD,<<<'EOD'

posts.title: Caching Google Maps Geocoding with Wordpress
posts.excerpt: When plotting multiple pins on an embedded Google Map, each pin's latitude and longitude is used to determine the precise pin placement. These can be looked up ahead of time and hard coded, or found on the fly with a geocoding API. Google c
posts.content:
When plotting multiple pins on an embedded Google Map, each pin's latitude and longitude is used to determine the precise pin placement. These can be looked up ahead of time and hard coded, or found on the fly with a geocoding API. Google conveniently provides such a service, however it is limited to 2,500 requests a day before it begins to charge. This seems like a high number until you are plotting maps with 100+ points on them (i.e. real estate listings). It would only take a couple dozen visitors to quickly hit that limit and break the map! An in-between option, and the best option for performance as well, is to using a geocoding API but cache the results locally. Recently geocoded addresses are fetched locally, while new (or stale) addresses query the API. Since this model is entirely reusable across different sites, it's the perfect scenario for a helper plugin. I won't paste my entire implementation here, but there are a few points worth covering.

Plugin Work Flow

The first time I developed this plugin, I gave the front-end developers free reign in using it. There were about 10 different public methods, and most counted on the developer using good async coding practices like Promises. In reality, it led to a lot of developer headaches and troubleshooting. So I rewrote the plugin in a much-simplified module. In the end, the workflow I came up with is essentially:

Application: Hey, helper function, here are my addresses. Can you get the latitude and longitude coordinates for each of them? Helper Plugin: Sure! Let me just run through them real quick. Application: Okay...so um, when you're done, here's what I want to happen: [...] Helper Plugin: Okay, cool. Still working. Application: No problem, I've got other stuff I'm working on. Helper Plugin: Hey Application, I'm all set! I've got each and every address geocoded. Application: Cool! So uh...can I have them? Helper Plugin: Sure! Here you go. But you probably don't need this handy dictionary I'm giving you, because that stuff you told me about earlier? I've gone ahead and done all of that for you!

So, it turns out it's a little hard to write anthropomorphic computer dialogue when async is involved. Hopefully you get the picture, though. The idea here is that the helper plugin is taking care of all the hard work for us. If you're writing the Application, all you really see are the beginning and end of the whole process. The behind-the-scenes portion is really the meat of geocoding, and as such can take a little bit of time for large datasets. Caching the responses locally dramatically speeds up the process. (You could also explore even better performance by pulling the address table down into local code at the beginning, and inserting the additions all together at the end.) One issue that comes up whenever we are dealing with APIs is that we have entered the realm of async. I've come to think the smoothest option for handling this when writing plugins for other developers is to implement a ready function. The application developer sends over the addresses, then queues up their followup code in our plugin's ready function to run when finished.

Behind the Scenes

So what's our helper plugin doing in between that beginning and ending? Hanging out with two of his friends, Database and API!

Helper Plugin: Whoa, Application just gave me 500 addresses to look up! I'll just take them one by one. Okay, this first one here...hey Database, do you know this address? Database: Yep! I learned that address just last week. Here's the coordinates! Helper Plugin: Great! I'll remember it. Now, here's the next address. Database: I know that one too! I learned it 8 months ago. Helper Plugin: Oh...gee, um, thanks, but no thanks. Let's get you an updated record. Hey API, can you geocode this address? API: Sure....let....me....get....that...for...you....here you go! Helper Plugin: Great! A little slow, but thanks! Hey Database, here's an updated record for you. I'll remember it too. Now on to the next address! Database: Sorry, I've actually NEVER seen that one. Helper Plugin: Okay, great..I'll have API get it for us.

And so on.

Hypothetically geocoded addresses shouldn't change, but they might. Roads can be renumbered or even moved, and besides, it's just a good practice to not use very stale data. I personally think a 6 month update window is a good compromise. (Come to think of it, I might go back and randomize my implementation of it +/- a few weeks. Otherwise, the initial big burst of addresses will all expire at the same time.)

On the Front End

Since I am using my the ready() method, my code example for front end developers is rather small: [code language="javascript"]var retailLocationsArray = ['123 Maple Ave, Memphis TN 38117','125 Maple Ave, Memphis, TN 38117']; var retailLocationsGeocoder = new geocoder(retailLocationsArray); retailLocationsGeocoder.ready(function(){ var retailLocationsGeocodedDictionary = retailLocationsGeocoder.getAllResults(); for(var i=0;i<retailLocationsArray.length;i++){ var thisResult = retailLocationsGeocodedDictionary[retailLocationsArray[i]]; //Create marker or other code, using thisResult.lat and thisResult.lng } }); [/code] So again, we're sending in an array of addresses. We initialize a new geocoder with those addresses, and it immediately starts working on them. In the meantime, we start queuing up our followup code. When the lookups are all done, we'll fetch a dictionary of results from the geocoder and use it to plot the results on the map.

Error Checking

Here we are dealing with APIs, dynamic data, and database lookups. Any of those individually should have good error checking; all three of them combined make the need undeniable. We can't allow a bad address (say, with an apartment number included) to throw off our entire program. But that's exactly what will happen if we don't error check.

Application: ...and the third address I want you to lookup is "222 North Maple St (on left side of street above sandwich shop), Memphis, TN 38117"... Helper Plugin: No problem. Database, have you ever heard of 222 North Maple St (on left side of street above sandwich shop)? Database: lolz, nope Helper Plugin: Okay, API, can you hook me up here? API: I AM GOOGLE, AND YOU SHALL NOT GIVE ME THIS CRAP DATA. TAKE THIS ERROR MESSAGE AND BEGONE! Helper Plugin: "Response: Denied", eh? That's a funny latitude/longitude pair. Oh well! Hey Database, here you go! Database: No, wait, what are you doing?!  Great, thanks a lot. Helper Plugin: Hey Application, I see you wanted me to plot this on the map. Here I go! Map, please create a pin at location Response:Denied. Map: That's not a location! You know what? Just take this lousy world map and be thankful if I don't halt your JavaScript engine.

So, we can save ourselves a lot of headaches by implementing a few checks.

  1. It should go without saying that the inputs should also be protected against malicious attacks. If you use wpdb properly, that shouldn't be too difficult (wpdb->insert prevents injection attacks, and wpdb->query can be wrapped in a wpdb->prepare).
  2. When the helper plugin receives the list of addresses, presumably an array, it can filter out any non-string values and even special characters (i.e. the # in APT #).
  3. When Google's API sends back its response, error messages should be captured. At the time of writing it includes a "response" parameter that will be set to such values as "ok", "denied", etc. If one of these are found, the database can be updated with the failure but without trying to force a lat/lng result.
  4. However the helper plugin returns data to the application (I use a dictionary with the address as the key, and a result object as the value), a failure message should be conveyed for bad addresses. I simply include this in my result object: lat/lng/fetch date/success. My application can make sure each success is present before placing it on the map.

Summary

Creating a plugin like this takes a bit of time, but knowing that it will be reused (and used by other developers) is a great encouragement to do things right. The end result is a simple module that requires very little explanation to use. On the settings page for my plugin, I have only two controls. First, a Google API key is required for all this to work so I let it be entered here. Second, for debugging purposes I've added a Reset Cache Table button to mimic a fresh install. If I add a third, it will be a single entry address tester to try out inputs and verify the response from Google. I absolutely love projects like this. The need is clear, the scope is limited, and the result is absolutely helpful.

posts.title: Mockup Scroller
posts.excerpt: _Update 9/17/18:_ The demo below will not function as it was built when the frontend of the site was using WordPress which includes jQuery, and the current implementation of the site does not. I could include it for this page, but that seem
posts.content:
Update 9/17/18: The demo below will not function as it was built when the frontend of the site was using WordPress which includes jQuery, and the current implementation of the site does not. I could include it for this page, but that seems heavy for an example. Sending design mockups to clients--and having them understand the design--is a challenge, especially for long form pages. The ratio of the mockup, usually extremely vertical, is unwieldy for non-media experts. What is the designer's best option?

  1. Send a high-resolution image -- the client may get overwhelmed or be unable to zoom out and see the full image. They may also be confused with the very narrow aspect ratio.
  2. Send a smaller image -- the client won't be able to see the fine details. Here, too, they may also be confused with by the aspect ratio.
  3. Send a quasi-responsive mockup to adjust to the client's browser--- this can be misleading with regards to the actual intended responsive behavior.
  4. Go over the design in person -- this is the best scenario, but is sometimes impossible.

Oftentimes I've sent a large image, but taken care to explain how website mockups tend to be very vertical and that they won't be seeing it as the end user will. Knowing that clients are usually very excited to skip the explanation and open up the mockup, I've never felt very comfortable with this.

$(function(){ $('.outer-mockup-container').each(function(){ setHeight(this); }); $('.outer-mockup-container').resize(function(){ setHeight(this); }); }); function setHeight(that){ console.log('called setHeight'); var thisWidth = $(that).innerWidth(); var thisAspectRatio = $(that).data('aspect-ratio'); $(that).css('height',thisWidth / thisAspectRatio + 30); } To combat this problem, I created a minimalist browser simulator that maintains a set aspect-ratio. The client can scroll up and down within the mini-browser, and actually get a sense for how the page flows. Having a set aspect-ratio also means that intentional above-the-fold design decisions can be conveyed to the client. Behind the scenes, this is simply a stacked container with the very tall mockup image being seen through a window. A little JavaScript checks and maintains the image ratio on browser resize so that it can also grow to fill the available space. At a certain resolution I've taken to hiding the simulator altogether -- I simply don't want my clients trying to view a desktop design mockup on a mobile device. A few browser design cues were given to help the clients intuitively understand what to do. For mobile mockups, a slightly modified design element on the bottom helps create the illusion of scrolling on a phone. So far the effect has been exactly what I had hoped for, and feedback has been fantastic. I've had more concrete discussions with clients about the flow of their sites, and wasted less time explaining how the design will translate into a live browser. The full code for this project is available on the project CodePen page.

posts.title: Demystifing (and replicating!) jQuery's .ready()
posts.excerpt: ## The mystical .ready() function jQuery has become so popular that many new developers learn it right alongside JavaScript (sometimes, I suspect, in place of JavaScript). The .ready() function is one of the first lessons taught in many onl
posts.content:
The mystical .ready() function

jQuery has become so popular that many new developers learn it right alongside JavaScript (sometimes, I suspect, in place of JavaScript). The .ready() function is one of the first lessons taught in many online courses, but with a focus on "how" instead of "why", its users may not fully understand its purpose. In fact, I've seen many questions posted online where the code was needlessly thrown into a .ready() block, even simple function declarations. More seasoned developers will understand its proper usage, as well as its differences from the Window's ready event. But because of its ubiquitous usage, .ready() still maintains an almost mystical status. It's treated and talked about as if it were a special class of JavaScript code, some fundamental method built deep in the bowels of jQuery. We even memorize its invocation form like a grade-school definition: $(document).ready(function(){ ... }); But .ready() is just a function! And what's more, it's not even that complex!

How .ready() really works

Here's what it does:

  1. Accepts a block of code as its argument
  2. Is the document already ready? If so, run the block of code from step 1.
  3. If it's not ready, add the block of code to a holding array.
  4. When the document IS ready, loop through the array and run the code in order.

The holding array technique is elegant and almost exactly as simple as it sounds. Here is the actual function definition from the early 1.2.3 version: [code language="javascript"] ready: function(fn) { // Attach the listeners bindReady(); // If the DOM is already ready if ( jQuery.isReady ) // Execute the function immediately fn.call( document, jQuery ); // Otherwise, remember the function for later else // Add the function to the wait list jQuery.readyList.push( function() { return fn.call(this, jQuery); } ); return this; } [/code] Then, using vanilla JavaScript's addEventListener, jQuery adds a DOMContentLoaded trigger to run the queued up code once the page is loaded. (Okay, it's a little more complicated than that with browser compatibility and such, but this is easily 90% of the code.) So there you go, the $(document).ready spell is broken! It's just a queue, a standard little array. Now...what can we do with this knowledge? We can replicate it!

Replicating jQuery's .ready() approach

If you have ever written a module using asynchronous code, you know that it's hard to make your code accessible to junior developers. To use your code, they too have to understand how async works. I've written many an explanation of basic promise syntax into readme files, and I still had little faith that it would be used properly. Instead, we can duplicate an approach with which even entry-level users are familiar. Let's take the example of geocoding some addresses. We don't want to tell our map to plot out the points until the addresses have been converted to latitude/longitude, and this will involve waiting on an API to get back to us. First, we need some variables: [code language="javascript"] //Stores if the lookup phase is complete var isLookupComplete = false; //Stores functions to execute once ready (that the user can provide) var readyFunctions = []; [/code] Nothing too complex there. We'll also set up our final function that will loop through and run any code that has been queued up, once we're ready. [code language="javascript"] //Run any queued up functions (i.e. from user) function runReadyFunctions(){ for(var i=0;i<readyFunctions.length;i++){ readyFunctions[i].call(document); } readyFunctions = []; } [/code] The third piece is the .ready() function that will accept code from the developer. It's like any other function accepting an argument, but we do need to make sure it's given an actual function. [code language="javascript"] function addReadyFunc(newFunc){ //make sure we've been given a function if(typeof newFunc != 'function'){ return; } //go ahead and run it if we're already done if(isLookupComplete){ newFunc.call(document); }else{ //otherwise store it in an array readyFunctions.push(newFunc); } } [/code] After making sure it's given a function, we just have to see if the lookup is already complete (i.e. we're already 'ready'). If so, we go ahead and run the code on the fly. Otherwise we add it to the array. We'll "rename" the function to "ready" when we export it from our module. Finally, we trigger the ready state once the call to the API is finished. [code language="javascript"] ... // promise returning our async API data ).then(function(){ isLookupComplete = true; runReadyFunctions(); }); [/code] This will run all of our queued up code once our promise is resolved. Note that we also store that the lookup is complete so that future calls to our ready function will run immediately. That's it! It's elegantly simply and super helpful for other developers extending our code. They don't have to worry about async at all. In fact, their usage might be as simple as: [code language="javascript"] myGeocoder.ready(function(){ //Lat and lng coordinates are ready, plot them on map here ... }); [/code] That's a much easier library to pick up and run, and it really didn't cost us much time or effort. It's certainly not a new idea, but if you're going to stand on the shoulders of giants, jQuery is about as solid of a giant as you can find!

posts.title: You Don't Know JS - This & Object Prototypes
posts.excerpt: JavaScript has a reputation for being a novice-friendly language. While a developer of another language, say C#, might study the entire system under the hood, a JavaScript developer might only learn "the good parts" he or she needs to "get
posts.content: JavaScript has a reputation for being a novice-friendly language. While a developer of another language, say C#, might study the entire system under the hood, a JavaScript developer might only learn "the good parts" he or she needs to "get the job done." This is a strength of the language as it really makes programming accessible (see, for instance, the Minecraft JavaScript programming camps). However for the serious developer it is also a weakness. You can't really become a proficient, advanced developer without diving deeper. Trying to do advanced JavaScript without exploring the "deep parts" is a bit like paying no attention whatsoever to politics but then voting once every 4 years. Sure you can do it, but you'll have no idea what's really going on and the results will be unpredictable. That's why I'm so fond of Kyle Simpson's You Don't Know JS series. It's specifically geared towards those developers who are ready to dive deeper. In his third volume he focuses on "this" and objects in JavaScript. I've previously written about the complexities of "this" in JavaScript, but objects deserves their own writeup as well. Kyle begins his chapter on objects by countering the common belief that in JavaScript "everything is an object". This is true in practice (truthy?) but not what's really happening. Primitives like string and number are not objects, but are instead "coerced" into their counterpart object forms when used as such (String, Number, etc.; notice the capitalization). Objects, on their face, are essentially a set of key:value pairs. As those values can themselves be objects, or even references to other objects like functions, their complexity can grow quickly. Importantly, objects are passed by reference, not by value. [code language="javascript"]var objA = { a : 5 }; var objB = objA; objA["a"] = 6; console.log(objB.a); // 6 [/code] In this example changing objA's property also changed objB's. (Also, notice the two separate ways of accessing the property.) This key:value setup is enough information for most JavaScript developers to pass along basic information and work with JSON data. However, that's just the tip of the iceberg with objects. Extending the behavior of objects being passed by reference, we run into the main limitation of using the Object Oriented Programming model with JavaScript. Classes in OOP imply--_demand_--true copies be made. Children classes must be able to overwrite their parent's functions ("polymorphism") yet generally still be able to access them. With JavaScript, though, the child and parent share a reference to the same objects. The child class cannot overwrite the parent, and so the idea of "extending" a class is largely lost. Methods that attempt to simulate this (manually extending classes) will yield partial success but add a lot of bloat. Kyle uses the typical example, a parent class (Vehicle) and child class (Car), to illustrate this well. If Car has a drive() function that also needs to call the parent Vehicle class's drive() function, it ends up looking like this: [code language="javascript"] drive(){ Vehicle.drive.call(this); ...//additional code } [/code] The reason for the obscure function call is twofold. First, we have to use Vehicle.drive instead of just drive so that the parent's function is called instead of the current one. But then, anything the function does is bound to Vehicle, and presumably we want to be operating on Car. So we have to use the explicit .call() technique to specify our context. This brings us to the [[Prototype]] chain. While the class model relies on copies, the prototype functionality of Javascript uses links. We simply establish an inheritance pattern, a chain, that JavaScript will traverse when needed. But again, no copies are made. [code language="javascript"] var spaceship = { currentWarpSpeed : 0, targetWarpSpeed : 1, engage : function(){ currentWarpSpeed = targetWarpSpeed; } } var Enterprise = Object.create(spaceship); console.log(spaceship); // Object {currentWarpSpeed:0,targetWarpSpeed:1,engage:function} console.log(Enterprise); // Object {} console.log(Enterprise.targetWarpSpeed); // 1 [/code] In this example, Enterprise and spaceship are linked on the prototype level by the Object.create technique. Enterprise the object is still empty, yet when attempting to access the target warp speed we still get a result of 1. JavaScript looked at Enterprise first, didn't find anything, and then looked higher up the chain. Is Enterprise extending spaceship? It sort of looks like it, but not truly. If Enterprise gets its own engage() function, it will just "shadow" the parent's engage() and take precedence over it. This prototyping opens the door to some really cool techniques (but not fully the class model). One common usage is with the new operator. [code language="javascript"] function Borg(){ this.isInTheCollective= true; } var taylor = new Borg(); console.log(taylor); // Borg { isInTheCollective:true } [/code] Taylor is an object, but is an instance of Borg so it displays with that label in the console. Using the "new" operator has several effects, including creating a new object, using that new object for any "this" calls in the function referenced, and returning that object. A fourth effect, though, is that a prototype link is established. [code language="javascript"]function Borg(){ this.isInTheCollective= true; } var taylor = new Borg(); Borg.prototype.hiveMind = true; console.log(taylor.hiveMind); // true [/code]So again, when JavaScript's engine can't find "hiveMind" on taylor, it looks up the prototype chain, which in this case includes Borg. (Every function has functionName.prototype, and it is this that objects created with "new" are linked.) So Javascript provides a lot of helpful, advanced functionality for working with objects. But one thing Kyle Simpson stresses again and again in his book is that these capabilities do not add up to true classes. A passing review of some of this might lead one to believe that (i.e. prototype linking has some overlap with class-based inheritance) but that's just the kind of incomplete, vague knowledge that gets JavaScript developers in trouble.

posts.title: Passing the WordPress Theme Checker
posts.excerpt: Every theme that is submitted to the WordPress repository has to pass a [list of standards](https://make.wordpress.org/themes/handbook/review/required/) to be approved. This process ensures both site security and a good user experience.
posts.content: Every theme that is submitted to the WordPress repository has to pass a list of standards to be approved. This process ensures both site security and a good user experience. To pass, the themes will eventually be examined manually by a volunteer in accordance with the published guidelines. Some of these guidelines are required, while others are recommendations or suggestions. However, before a human even glances at a submitted theme, it must first pass a gamut of automated tests. The WordPress Theme Checker plugin runs these tests for the theme developer and shows any discrepancies in detail. Some of these tests are quite serious in nature; for instance, scanning the site code for an eval() block prevents a serious security oversight. Others test for best practices: creating Custom Post Types in a plugin instead of a theme, for example, makes it much easier for a user to switch themes without losing data. Perhaps the test with the widest scope is that no errors can be thrown by the code's PHP or JavaScript. Custom theme developers have absolutely no obligation to pass these tests or comply with the standards they represent. Take for example the requirements to have a fully functioning comment system. Omitting this functionality means the theme will fail at least 4 separate tests. But, if a theme was developed specifically for a client that has absolutely no desire for commenting, then including this functionality is extraneous. However, barring project time commitments, passing these tests can only move your theme in the right direction. I cannot imagine a situation where having included an extra feature or developing to a best-practice standard is going to hurt a theme, and it may end up saving your client a huge headache down the road. More importantly, the plugin encourages developing in the right mindset. Am I keeping up with the latest trends and developing accordingly? Am I cutting corners that will cost my client down the road, even when they switch to a different theme? Will my code play nice with other plugins or future developers? These type of questions don't need to haunt and torment the developer throughout the process. No site is ever going to be 100% perfect and best practices change frequently, but keeping these questions in mind is an important step in developing quality code. Every theme that will make into the WordPress.org repository will have to pass these standards, but even custom themes that are not intended for the repository would do well to run, and pass, these tests. Note: An even higher mark to aim for is compliance with the WordPress coding standards. Separate guidelines exist for HTML, CSS, PHP, and JavaScript. These are much broader in scope and include the community's preferences between valid options to ensure consistency.

posts.title: Actually understanding "this" in JavaScript
posts.excerpt: Many of us have taken a try-and-see approach to using "this" in JavaScript. But, there comes a time when a developer says, "No more guesses, I need to know how that really works." I hope I encourage some others to take that leap with "this
posts.content:
Many of us have taken a try-and-see approach to using "this" in JavaScript. But, there comes a time when a developer says, "No more guesses, I need to know how that really works." I hope I encourage some others to take that leap with "this"! "This" is confusing because it can't easily be learned from context. You can see it used in a dozen code examples, think you know how it works, and be completely wrong. Its functionality skirts right next to how you might expect it to work, but with a "kinda understand it" approach the floor will vanish beneath your feet when you least expect it. In short... "This" does not simply:

  • Refer to the current scope, function, object
  • Refer to the encompassing scope, function, or object
  • Refer to the context of where a function was declared

"This" does:

  • Depend on where and how a function is called

Default implementation

The most basic case of "this" occurs when no other situation applies. In this case, "this" refer to the context from which the current scope was called. Generally that's going to be Window for JavaScript run in a browser. [code language="javascript"] function country(name){ console.log("In country func, this: ",this); //Window this.designation = name; //Added to Window identify(); } function identify(){ console.log("In identify func, this: ",this); //Window console.log("I am",this.designation); //I am the United States } country('the United States'); [/code]In this example it looks like we were trying to add a "designation" to the country function. But it really just got added to the Window variable. So this is really dangerous because it looks like it worked! But it only works because both country() and identify() are both referring to Window. The property isn't stored within context of the country() function. Let's say that you read ahead, and you found out that using the "new" method of calling a function would set "this" to that function. You'd be right, but you still might get thrown under the bus by this first rule. [code language="javascript"] function country(name){ console.log("In country func, this: ",this); //country this.designation = name; //Added to country identify(); } function identify(){ console.log("In identify func, this: ",this); //Window console.log("I am",this.designation); //I am undefined } var a = new country('the United States'); [/code]See what's changed? We've called country() with new, and in fact "this" is now "country" inside of the country function. But it doesn't carry over, and when we call identify() "this" is back to Window again, which doesn't have a designation and returns undefined.

First Exception: Explicit Binding

However, there are a few cases where this default behavior is trumped. We can actually be a little clearer with the JavaScript engine and just tell it what we want "this" to be. To do this, we instead call the function with the .call() or .apply() or .bind() techniques. [code language="javascript"] this.level = 0; //added to global object var fuelTank = { level : 0 //added to fuelTank object } function fill(){ this.level = 100; //who should I fill depends on 'this' } fill.call(fuelTank); //oh, 'this' is going to be the fuelTank console.log(fuelTank.level); //100 [/code]The .call() method, which is a part of any function we create by default, accepts as its first argument a binding context. In our example here, it tells our fill() function to use the fuelTank's level variable instead of the global level variable. We can use this method to get the desired behavior we had with the first example. In other words, we're going to explicitly say that we're referring to the country's designation. [code language="javascript"] function country(name){ console.log("In country func, this: ",this); //country this.designation = name; //Added to country identify.call(this); } function identify(){ console.log("In identify func, this: ",this); //country console.log("I am",this.designation); //I am the United States } var a = new country('the United States'); [/code]The console correctly reads out, "I am the United States", and THIS time it's because designation lives in the country, not the global Window object.

Second Exception: Owner object (implicit binding)

The second, and stronger, exception is if the function has an implicitly bound owner. The closest implicit owner takes priority over the call-stack and even over explicitly bound contexts. [code language="javascript"] var spaceShuttle = { name : 'Endeavor', report: function() { console.log("This is ",this.name," checking in."); } }; function radioTest(){ this.name = "VX-2000 Radio Test Protocol"; spaceShuttle.report(); } var testAlpha = new radioTest(); [/code]When the report() function is called, you might think "this.name" refers to the radioTest's variable of that name. After all, that's where report() was called and we even used the "new" keyword to give radioTest it's own "this". However, since report() is owned by spaceShuttle, that takes priority and the report will output, "This is Endeavor checking in." (I'd be willing to wager that this special case is what skews developers' understanding of how "this" works. See enough examples like this one, and you might think "this" always refers to the current object. Also see enough examples of the default case, and your understanding might grow to "Well, sometimes 'this' depends on where it was called." Like a child learning to speak, you begin to use grammar correctly without understanding the rules. But as a father of 3, I will tell you kids also say a lot of stupid stuff.)

But...not as bound as you might think

Implicit bindings can be overwritten if a function loses its owner. This may seem like a strange scenario until we remember that in JavaScript objects are not duplicated as easily as you might think. If a "copy" of an object (which is really the same object) is called and the owner isn't being used to do so, the function will execute but "this" will not be based on implicit binding. Consider this example: [code language="javascript"] var selfDestructModule = { safetySwitch : true, toggleSafety : toggleButton, }; function toggleButton(myButton){ this.safetySwitch = !(this.safetySwitch); } var backupModule = selfDestructModule; backupModule.toggleSafety(); console.log(selfDestructModule.safetySwitch); // false! [/code]What's happened here? The selfDestructModule and the backupModule are not duplicates. They are the exact same object. When the backup module turns off safety switch, the selfDestructModule's is now off too -- because they're the same. This affects our discussion because even though we might call a function with an explicit owner, once it's copied we don't have a clear owner any more. [code language="javascript"] var selfDestructModule = { safetySwitch : true, toggleSafety : toggleButton, initiate : overloadReactor }; function toggleButton(myButton){ this.safetySwitch = !(this.safetySwitch); } function overloadReactor(){ if(this.safetySwitch == false){ console.log("BOOM"); } } selfDestructModule.toggleSafety(); //safetySwitch = false var quickBoomButton = selfDestructModule.initiate; //"shortcut" quickBoomButton(); //FAIL selfDestructModule.initiate(); //BOOM [/code]Here we tried to create a shortcut to the self destruct's initiate function, just by making a copy of it. Like we saw in the previous example, this set quickBoomButton to the exact same function: overloadReactor (and not just a duplicate of it). That part worked perfectly. BUT, "this" is now different because the owner of overloadReactor is no longer explicit. "This" falls back to the standard behavior, and since quickBoomButton was called in the global scope, it would be set to the global scope (i.e. "window"). The way around this quirky seeming behavior is to "harden" such calls by using an intermediary function that makes the owner explicit.

Hardened Binding

To our previous code, we could add an intermediary function like this one: [code language="javascript"] function initiateSelfDestruct(){ overloadReactor.call(selfDestructModule); } [/code]If our spaceship object had its initiate property pointed to this function instead, our shortcut above would actually work, because our intermediary function is making the binding explicit.

Bringing it all together

There are a few other cases (constructor classes, and arrow functions) but these examples cover the majority of confusing cases. In short:

  1. The default binding context is based on the context of where the function was called
  2. If the .call() or .apply() method is used (explicit binding), the context steals the show
  3. If there is a clear owner (implicit binding), that owner's context takes priority

For a more thorough read, I'd suggest checking out Kyle Simpson's short but packed book, You Don't Know JS: this and Object Prototypes. It goes into much greater depth, and while I don't personally care for the classic foo / bar examples, if you can get through them you'll be at the end of the road to success with "this"!

posts.title: Dynamic Flexbox Gallery
posts.excerpt: Flexbox is great. You can squeeze however many items you want and it will adjust them to fit -- in one direction. Once you start wrapping though (using flex-wrap), you run into a problem. Now that it can move down to a new row, how many col
posts.content: Flexbox is great. You can squeeze however many items you want and it will adjust them to fit -- in one direction. Once you start wrapping though (using flex-wrap), you run into a problem. Now that it can move down to a new row, how many columns should it use before it does so? You're forced to use hard coded widths, or a flex-basis (say, 20%), to let it know how much each item should take up. This flexibility is intentional and quite helpful, but can get you into trouble. With an unknown, dynamic number of equal-sized items (i.e. thumbnails), this is a problem. With 20 items, 5 columns might be ideal. But with 200 items, 5 columns means some really narrow rectangles if you're going to fit them on the screen. To solve this problem requires a bit of JavaScript. Essentially, we can dynamically determine the number of columns based on how many items there are. More specifically, we calculate the width and height ratio of each item, and if it is ever greater than a certain ratio (say, 2:1), have our script add a new "column" by decreasing the flex-basis of every item. This quick example I've set up on Codepen uses a button to add images. If you were pulling from a database, you would just set or update the counter value once you know the number of items.

posts.title: Essential WordPress Plugins for Every Site
posts.excerpt: ## Introduction There's a certain mark of pride for WordPress theme developers using as few plugins as possible. This has a little to do with ability ("I don't _need_ to use them"), and a lot to do with pride ("Damn it, Jim, I'm a developer
posts.content:
Introduction

There's a certain mark of pride for WordPress theme developers using as few plugins as possible. This has a little to do with ability ("I don't need to use them"), and a lot to do with pride ("Damn it, Jim, I'm a developer, not a content builder"). But beyond this, it also follows good programming logic. The less third party code you have floating around your theme, the less likely you are to run into issues and bloating. There are a lot of great plugins, and which ones you should install will depend on what a particular site is meant to do. Nevertheless, there are some plugins that make their way onto my sites time and time again. They make up my essential list (most developers have one), and each of them has proven themselves indispensable. These plugins are either saving me a lot of time, making my workflow smoother, or going deeper into an issue than I have time for. These are the plugins that I have come to rely on, to the point that I don't even really mind handing over the money to upgrade them. However, all of the ones below offer sufficient functionality even at the free level to merit their place on this list.

5. Custom Post Type UI

Custom posts, combined with custom fields, are two of the highly customizable features that have made WordPress a viable CMS instead of a simple blogging platform. I resisted this plugin used by so many colleagues for quite some time, answering their praise for it with pride-filled remarks such as, "Oh, a plugin? I just do it with PHP." (As if I can take credit for instantiating WordPress' silky smooth objects.) But CPT UI does save a lot of time and I've not found any deal-breaking limitations. It may even offer a little too much weight, but it's a fair bet that its output is more compliant than what I whip up in a hurry. The extended (paid) version adds support for formatting and displaying entered data.

4. UpDraft Plus

This plugin (freemium, despite the "plus" in the free version's name) makes backing up your entire WordPress site easy and automatic. It helpfully breaks apart backups into database, theme files, uploads, etc. so that you only have to restore what's needed. More impressively, it seemlessly integrates with numerous online storage solutions including AWS and Dropbox. That feature has been hugely popular with my clients who like seeing (but not touching!) their site backups. The premium version adds free backup storage.

3. Caldera Forms

There are a lot of viable options for your WordPress sites' email form builder. Contact Form 7 is the standard here, but I prefer Caldera for it's quick form-builder and intuitive interface. The developers have included plentiful hooks for extendability, although there is not particularly good documentation and I've had to trace my way through their code to find what I've needed. The pay model is based around add-ons and bundles, but for serious developers you're mostly paying to support their great work and save some time in the process.

2. WordFence

One of the top security plugins, this enables a whole gamut of protections for sites. Even small, low-traffic sites are prone to hacking. A freemium plugin is no guarantee, but it does block some of the most common techniques like brute-force attempts to "guess" the password. The plugin is frequently updated--for instance, it already disables username probing via the WordPress API which was only recently introduced. The premium version ($99/yr) enables automatic IP blacklisting drawn from their ongoing database.

1. Advanced Custom Fields

Okay, so easy custom fields is less important than security (#2 - Wordfence). But this plugin is so prevalent amongst developers, and so helpful in development, that I felt I owed it the #1 spot. Enabling custom fields (text, images, files, boolean, etc., etc.) on specific post types changes they way you build WordPress themes. It is an absolute must if you are creating custom templates for your clients. You can get most of the functionality through the free version, but the pro version enables the repeater field which alone is worth the cost of admission (you can end up avoiding creating a lot of custom-post types using this option). The pro upgrade is $100, but it's a 1-time fee and it licenses an unlimited number of sites.

posts.title: You Don't Know JS - Scope and Closures
posts.excerpt: Kyle Simpson's _You Don't Know JS_ series attacks JavaScript from a brilliant angle. He doesn't just explain code fragments or directly teach techniques. Rather, he explains _how_ JavaScript is working under the surface so that the user kno
posts.content: Kyle Simpson's You Don't Know JS series attacks JavaScript from a brilliant angle. He doesn't just explain code fragments or directly teach techniques. Rather, he explains how JavaScript is working under the surface so that the user knows why its working the way it is. This depth is not necessary for the average practitioner who "just needs it to work," but for those who want to take their skills to the next level it is exactly what is needed. The 6-book series, originally (and still) published through GitHub, is available in ~100-200 page volumes that tackle a particular issue. The first is to ensure readers are up to par with the basics, while this book, the second in the series, jumps into scope and closures. I appreciate that the author deftly toes the line between depth and accessibility. For instance, in detailing the subtleties of the JavaScript parsing engine, Simpson presents the process as a friendly dialogue between its different components. More than just providing humor, this type of thoughtful approach actually makes the concepts clearer. The order of the material makes perfect sense. He begins with how the JavaScript parsing process (i.e. "lexing") works, expands to its implications on scope, details the techniques used to "tame" it, and finally builds to the abstract concept of closures. Here the rest of the book comes together into what Simpson describes as a Matrix-like awakening: that you've been using closures all along, just without seeing them. Simply put, this is a fantastic book that sits just above the knowledge plateau where I've seen so many web developers get stuck. They won't come out on the other side of this read with an abundance of new skills, although there are a few. But they will understand what they've already been doing (or struggling to do) better.

posts.title: Dynamic meta tags on a single page
posts.excerpt: Setting up good meta tags is important if you expect your visitors to share your content on Facebook and other social media, and if your site is actively encouraging such sharing (i.e. providing share links) then configuring these tags is a
posts.content:
Setting up good meta tags is important if you expect your visitors to share your content on Facebook and other social media, and if your site is actively encouraging such sharing (i.e. providing share links) then configuring these tags is an absolute must. If your content is separated cleanly into pages it is generally not a problem to do this. Each page's meta tags will relate directly to the content. However, if you have multiple pieces of content on a single page, each with its own share button, you'll run into problems. With AJAX content this is actually a common scenario. What Open Graph tags should be on such a page? (Remember: if it's just a list linking to content, you would have each button send the item's individual URL and put the respective meta tags there, instead.) Assuming you want each share button to show information about that particular item on social media, and not just information about the list as a whole, you'll have two hurdles to overcome:

  1. A page can have only one set of meta tags
  2. Meta tags have to be present at very beginning of the page load (i.e. before JavaSript runs)

Each of these hurdles has a solution, and they work well together. To handle the first, we can simulate separate URLs for each item with URL parameters. We would set our share buttons to pass along these URLs. For instance: [code language="html5"] Share on Facebook [/code] (You'd probably want that to open up a popup instead, or to use Facebook's actual button generator instead of their simplified sharer.php code.) Social media sites like Facebook will treat URLs like this as separate pages altogether. We can then adjust the meta tags based on the URL, and we'll effectively have one page masquerading as many. The second challenge seems trickier than it really is. By the time client-side scripting is running, it's already too late to set the meta tags. Even if it weren't, some web scrapers won't execute it anyways. So the dynamic setup of our meta tags must already be complete by the time the page is served. For PHP, it might look something like this: [code language="php"] if(isset($_GET['openrecipe'])){ // prevent SQL injection since variable coming from URL $query = mysql_real_escape_string($_GET['openrecipe']); //Query database for specific recipe content based on URL parameter $results_raw = mysql_query("SELECT * FROM recipes WHERE (`title` LIKE '%".$query."%') or die(mysql_error()); //mysql_fetch_array returns first row if not in loop $results = mysql_fetch_array($results_raw); //Grab this recipe's important data for meta tags $thumbnail = $results['featured_image']; $title = $results['title']; $desc = $results['summary']; //Output the dynamic meta content echo ''; echo ''; echo ''; } [/code] Later in our code, we would want to use the same URL parameter to show that particular item to the user, as well. If you haven't figured it out by now, we've effectively implementing a permalink system for dynamic content. The end result is that with the URL parameter, both social media crawlers and your end users are directly served particular content on a single, dynamic page.

posts.title: Building a color naming tool
posts.excerpt: _**Update:** [Head over to the project page to see the end-result](https://www.tmdesigned.com/color-namer/)_ There are a lot of projects that _sound_ simple, but really have all sorts of nuances once you get down to business. Developing a
posts.content:
Update: Head over to the project page to see the end-result There are a lot of projects that sound simple, but really have all sorts of nuances once you get down to business. Developing a tool to name colors is one of those projects. Talking about colors with clients, I've found that having a user-friendly name for the color reduces confusion and actually helps them settle on a choice. "Do you prefer the firebrick red, or the merlot?" The problem for designers and developers is we don't think in terms of those names, preferring the actual code colors or possibly a system like Pantone. Presumably this is why paint manufacturers have gone to the trouble of naming their swatches. Even those of us willing to "translate" to these types of names are faced with a problem. What names do we use? How do we quickly and easily find the closest names to the actual, precise color we want to use in the design? To solve this problem, we'll have to dive into the messy world of comparing colors.

THE UNDERLYING CHALLENGE

[caption id="attachment_331" align="alignleft" width="300"] By Jacob Rus (Own work) [CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons[/caption]The main question here is how do we compare colors. And before we get very far with this, let's be clear about the underlying problem that will no doubt plague us: our colors are at least 3-dimensional. Whether we use RGB or HSL, we're bringing in three separate components. How computers see and think about these components--mathematically, of course-- is different from how we perceive them. This makes finding a "similar" color rather subjective. So we'll want to strive for precise matching, but allow a little flexibility as well. Returning several choices to pick from will be helpful.

COLOR SPACE OPTIONS

[caption id="attachment_292" align="alignright" width="256"] 255 was the maximum number of coins in Zelda for the same reason.[/caption] We can work with colors in several different ways. In RGB, for each of the three color dimensions we have 256 possible values. This magic number shows up all over software design, of course, simply because it is what you get with 1 byte of data (1 byte => 8 bits => 8 1's or 0's => 2^8 => 256). Accounting for zero, this comes out to a max value of 255. In the rgb() CSS syntax, rgb(255,255,255) is pure white. With 3 dimensions, we have 3 bytes (=24 bit color) for a total range of 16 million colors. However, I always prefer thinking in HSL just because it's easier to move around the spectrum in your mind. We tend to say things like, "I want that color to be brighter," instead of, "I want that color to have equally more red, blue, and green," which would mean the same thing. HSL, though, uses different scales. Hue has 360 values while Saturation and Lightness are percentages. This gives us 3,600,000 values instead of 16,777,216. (By the way, CSS3 supports decimal values for the hsl() syntax, so it's not actually limited to those colors.) I daresay that working with 3.6 million colors instead of 16.7 million will be an acceptable compromise for our end-users. Since we're not likely to find a database of even 3.6 million color names, simplifying the user input to that level isn't an issue.

THE DISTANCE BETWEEN TWO COLORS

To run a comparison between two colors, each made up of 3 pieces of data, we're essentially comparing two 3-dimensional points and finding the distance between them. The shorter the distance, the more mathematically similar are the two colors. Lucky for us, that's rather simple to do. In algebra, the distance between two 2-dimensional points is d=∈š(x2∈’x1)^2+(y2∈’y1)^2. Recognize that? It's the pythagorean theorem at work! For 3-dimensional points the equation is similar: the square root of all of the squares of the differences between coordinates added together, which is d=∈š(x2∈’x1)^2+(y2∈’y1)^2+(z2-z1)^2. We could translate this equation to our purposes for RGB or HSL. In fact, since RGB has 3 values in the same range, it would actually be a bit easier. But as I mentioned, HSL is easier to think about, and since we might end up cheating the comparison a bit to return more perceived-similar colors, we'll stick with HSL.

NAMING THE COLOR

The last consideration before we begin coding is how we want to name the colors. Pantone is one option that gives us around 2,000 matches, including some fun ones like "Fuzzy Wuzzy Brown". Sherwin Williams has about 1,000 named colors on their site, and with names like "Heartthrob" and "Papaya" I feel like we're a bit closer. But with either of these, I'd be concerned about copyright infringement. Lucky for us, there is an open-source list of color names pre-packaged as a JSON file. All we'll have to handle is finding the closest match. We only have to do this once per name, so I'm not concerned about efficiency. If I were, we'd definitely want to think through how we're storing and sorting the data. We can at least convert it to HSL ahead of time to save one step, though.

ONTO THE BUILD

We've laid out our project and thought through the biggest strategic challenges. There will be surprises, but that's where tactics come into play. Let the coding begin!

posts.title: The Elements of User Experience
posts.excerpt: ![](/img/uploads/2017/03/elementsofuserexperience-250x300.jpg)Over the past several years I have used many User Experience (UX) tools, but relied on my own instinct and experience to put them together into coherent picture. This book, _The
posts.content: Over the past several years I have used many User Experience (UX) tools, but relied on my own instinct and experience to put them together into coherent picture. This book, The Elements of User Experience by Jesse James Garrett, lays out a map for the conceptual purposes of each type of tool. Put simply, it's the UX book you should read first. I've often told clients the importance of navigating the seas between your business goals and your client's desires. They won't use your site if there's nothing in it for them, and your business gets nowhere if you're just providing a charitable service of information that has nothing to do with your goals. I like how the book refined this further to product objectives. This plane is where a lot of well-known UX tools (market profiles, case studies, etc.) live. The chart that captures the essence of the book, found on p.29, is complex and hard to internalize. But after reading the book it is a reference map to the major concepts. In fact, it's the kind of thing you can pin to the wall by your computer. A few minutes of skimming the chart asking, "Have I addressed each of these things with the client?" would benefit every project. If I were designing a college UX course, I would have them read this, then study the tools for each category. The big project for the semester would be a full fledged project profile using everything they've learned. The final, though, would be applying them to a real-life example where the client doesn't care and there is little time or  budget for these things. That, I think, would be the real test of how much they've internalized the great tools, techniques, and concepts discussed in this book.

posts.title: React.js Game of Life simulator
posts.excerpt: This app utilizes the React.js library and SASS to deliver a functioning life simulator based on the work of John Conway in 1970. I created this project as part of my personal study of the React JavaScript library developed by Facebook. A
posts.content:
This app utilizes the React.js library and SASS to deliver a functioning life simulator based on the work of John Conway in 1970. I created this project as part of my personal study of the React JavaScript library developed by Facebook.

A "Conway's Game of Life" simulator such as this one is based on a 2 dimensional grid of squares. Each square can be thought of as a biological cell, a person living on land, etc. At each generation, each square either lives, dies, or comes to life based on its neighbors.

In this implementation, users can add or remove rows and columns, click each square individually to set up their own pattern, or watch a predefined repeating pattern (i.e. a "pulsar").

The sourcecode for this project can be found on my GitHub repository at https://github.com/tmdesigned/Conway-s-Game-of-Life

A functioning demo of this project can be found here.

pages.title: About
pages.content:
About Taylor

I build software with sharp technical skills, lead projects through clear systems thinking, and manage teams with empathetic yet direct leadership. I currently work at the Georgia Tech Research Institute (GTRI) as a research engineer in the Advanced Concepts Lab. I live near Cincinnati, OH with my wife and kids.

About this site

I created this site in 2019 as a headless WordPress implementation coded in Vue.js. It was a Progressive Web App, pulling posts on demand from the WP API and serving them out of a VUEX store. The site was hosted on an EC2 instance at AWS with a Let's Encrypt SSL.

In 2026, Bitnami was removed from the AWS catalog, and a severe PHP vulnerability was disclosed which together made updating essential and impossible.

I migrated the site to GitHub pages with Decap used to manage local markdown files as the source of data, completely eliminating WordPress as a dependency and removing the need for me to directly manage infrastructure security for a mostly static site.
